div.head: WAR ItZ /I GTON urch
div.p: WAR ItZ /I GTON urch
RELIGIOUS e-SOCIAL
" Men, not Buildings." Rev. H. Ogden on the Extravagance of Modern Christians.

The Rev. H. Ogden preached at Golborne-street, 'Baptist Church on Sunday evening on God's gifts :'' the gifts that never tarnish. " His text was Acts iii. 6, "Silver and geld have I none; but such as I have give I thee : In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk." The preacher asked how much in the practical way had religion done for us ? We adorned our churches until they were tawdry, and the lame, and the halt, and the maimed begged at our doors. There was a stately simplicity about a Quaker meeting-house. Men with God counted more than churches. Souls and not buildings were God's jewels, "I desire sacrifice, and not burnt offerings." Lowell described for us bishops and deans and canons, presidents of Conference, moderators of unions, etc., crowding to meet the Christ. They hustled for precedenca as-society quarrelled for place at Court. The Master led them into the alley and slum. He selected the low-browed, stunted,boggard man, and stemmed the hustle, by inquiring, Are these the images ye make of Me ?' Men were more than buildings. Peter si;d," Silver and gold have I none." Could he return to earth he would not know himself. Probably his sucoessors would not own him. His successors had owned half of Europe and claimed two or three stand- ing armies. Now their possession was a palate that was one of the marvels of the world, and R. 14,000 a year was a neat commentary upon an apostle who was a financial beggar. Probably the Archb6hop of Canterbury found excellent avenues for his income, but whets comment upon the original! A section of the eta:Ty of the Established Church had made frantic appaals to them to recognise the validity of their Orders. The only validity seeded was the living spirit of am living God. But though Peter bad neither silver nor gold, he could in the name of Jesus give what was immensely more than gifts that would tarnish. -

sum at the disposal of our ecclesiastical authorities that boy's education would be undertaken by the Church he would be trained and the payment of his training would come out of a diocesan fund for that purpose. Here in this parish on the Latchford side of the railway embankment we have a thickly and rapidly-growing population, and we are endeavouring to provide a new church for the Mission district. How have we to get the money ? Well, in various ways. Annual sales of work must be held, the Vicar must write to all manner of people ask- ing for subscriptions, weekly collecting cards must be issued, all parishioners are invited to give a donation. But in addition to this we ought to receive a large and substantial sum of money from the church's central fund. But, unfortunately, there is no such thing at present. Now it has been decided that such a fund shall he formed and if the scheme is carried through successfully the Church of England should gain enormously. The scheme is going to be worked on Diocesan lines so that every diocese may have a large sum of money that can be applied to the needs of parishes within its area. How is the fund to be.raised ? By the contributions of churchpeople in every parish. We, that is the clergy, churchwardens and the lay representatives have agreed that St. James' parish shall contribute a sum of at least Xi this year, and we hope that every Church-person in the. parish will rise to the occasion.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Chinch
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Chinch

The 110th anniversary of St. John's Presbyterian Church and third dedication festival of themew church, were celebrated on Sunday, when the Rev. W. Reid preached morning and evening. In the afternoon the sacred cantata "Christ and His soldiers " (Farmer) was rendered by the choir, under the conductorship of Mr. A. G. Lewsey. Mr. Joaea presided at the organ, the principal soloists being Mrs. Milkr, and Misses Smith, Owen and Peacock, and Messrs. Cannon, Gillespie and Mitchell. In the morning, Mr. Reid briefly reviewed the life of John the Baptist, emphasising his preparation for work in a godly parentage and pious home; his message, and • his disat.pointment, and contrasted with the position he occupied, that of the least who to-day occupy and possess the kingdom. In the evening, the preacher spoke of the destruction of the Northern Kingdom of Israel, reviewing some of the historical events found during the thirteen years prior to the fall of Samaria, which, said he, with Assyria was but a side incident of the warfare of the day, but with the sacred writers an event charged with pathos, as telling the story of a ration's death. Viewea externally, the cause was to be found in a short-sighted policy, intrigue and rebellion calling from her own prophets sternest denunciation. What lay behind this and produced the moral and mental paralysis, however, was the nation's easertion of Jehovah, and her distrust of Him who had lived and provided for her, and from horde of slaves had evolved a chosen nation. Polytheism had eaten into the natioa's life, so that she became fit for nothing but to be cast out upon the rubbish heap of the world, and in seeking for the lost tribes it was well to remember that they had not perished through captivity, only a percentage having been deported, but through being merged into Sargon's imported tribes and becoming the substratum of a future population. He reminded his hearers that sin had lost Israel her vocation, and asked that it be remembered that we to-day, as individuals, as citizens, as a nation, and particularly as a Church, had been called of God to witness for Him and His tvuth along lines and through opportunities peculiarly our own.

div.head: Church and Financial Reform.
div.p: The Church and Financial Reform.

The Rev. H. B. Firth, Vicar of St. James', Latch- ford, in the course of his monthly letter to his parishioners, writes :—Old-establisbed bodies are often useful, but they are frequently unbusiness-like ; now the Church is the oldest organised society in England and she is undoubtedly very useful. in a thousand ways the Church exerts an uplifting, refining, humaniz- ing influence over the nation, but the Church suffers grievously because of the unbusiness-like way in which her financial problem has been faced. The Church has lacked a great central fund. which ought to be available for various and local needs. An illustration or two will make my meaning clear. Here, let us suppose, is a very clever boy who has a great desire to become a clergyman; he seems admirably suited for the calling, but he is poor. Be cannot afford to pay for an expensive training at a university or a theological college, and so, because of his poverty an excellent candidate for the ministry is lost to the Church. Now, if there were a large central

div.head: WARRINGTON MOTORIST SUMMONED.
div.p: WARRINGTON MOTORIST SUMMONED.

At the Wrexham Borough Police Court on Monday, Dr. Reginald Smith, Lynton House, 14, Bold-street, Warrington, was summoned on two informations for failing to give his name and address when driving a motor car at Wrexham, and for failing to produce his licence to drive a motor car.—Mr. W. Wynn Evans defended.—P.C. W. Hughes said at 1.10 p.m. on Sunday, May 25th, he was in High-street, when he saw a motor car standing by the Conservative Club. He asked defendant to produce his driving licence. Defendant said he had no business to interfere with him. He told defendant it was his business to ask for it, and he then asked defendant for his name and address. He refused to give them and told him to take the number of the car. He denied that his manner was overbearing.—P.S. Lewis said that on returning in the eveniug the defendant gave him his name and address, and said the reason why he refused to give it earlier in the day was that the officer was insolent.—For the defence, Mr. Wynn Evans submitted that Dr. Smith committed

no offence when he refused to give his name and address, because he had not previously committed any offence against the section dealing with reckless driving, &c.—The Clerk said he agreed with that view.—Mr. Wynn Evans said he should therefore ask that the summons be dismissed. As to the summons for failing to produce the licence, he should like to say that Dr. Smith was the police surgeon for the county borough of Warrington, and for the county of Lancaster, and that be had held these appointments for sixteen years. He had never had a wrong word with the police in his life. He had always found them respectful and civil. He did not expect tbe police to be servile, but he intended to ask the Bench to say that he was justified in what he said, because of the conduct of the young constable. He thought the magistrates would not convict defendant because he forgot to carry his licence, which was a perfectly clean one.—Dr. Smith, Mr. F. H. Preedey, and Mr. J. L. Pearson gave evidence for the defence.— The Mayor said the charge of refusing to give the name and address would be dismiss ed. For failing to produce the licence defendant would be fined 10s. 6d. and costs.

An over-banging pall oc smoke has so long been accepted as the inevitable in industrial centres, that it is refreshing to be confronted with unmistakable evidences of the practicability of successfully conducting large manufactories with- out the emission Of velurnes of black smoke. For many years Messrs. Joseph Cr osfield and Sons, Ltd., have borne the proud title of owners of "the works with the smokeless chimneys, " and they are entitled to no small credit for having led the way in the anti-smoke movement in our town by the adoption of the latest scientific appliances. We are pleased, however, to state, that Warrington, or its immediate environs, can now boast a second large works from which the output of smoke is practically nil. The Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Co., Ltd., have now in full use at Grappenhall a works covering nine acres of land and considerable extensions are contemplated in the near futute. In the building and equipment of those premises one condition which the firm have had in mind from the very outset is that the works shall be smokeless,and, as far as the completed section is concerned, they have succeeded to the utmost of their hopes. net e are three chimneys, but observers assure us that very seldom, indeed, do they emit smoke to any appreciable extent. Throughout the works gas is used for power purposes, thus enabling boilers to be entirely dispensed with. Those ovens and furnaces which necessitate the use of coal and slack are arranged in such a way that practic- ally no smoke is sent forth. The achievement is the more notable when it is borne in mind that the works embodies a large number of varying trades. Foundries, fitting and grinding shops, and japanning departments are some of the chief sections. Even those firms which hesitate to supersede existing methods might, without inconvenience, con- sider the practicability of adopting smoke-consuming appliances when extending their works or installing new plant. They would thus be helping on the , realisation of that ideal, which at prt sent may seem very remote, of a smokeless, yet busy and prosperous Warrington.

div.head: militarism " Anti-Christian." Rey. W. Cooper Condemns the Compulsory
div.p: militarism " Anti-Christian." Rey. W. Cooper Condemns the Compulsory
Training Movement

A striking address on " Militarism "was given at the meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society on Sunday afternoon by the Rev. W. Cooper. He introduced his subject by reminding his hearers that a deliberate and open attempt was being made to capture the P.S.A.'s for this anti-Christian movement. He was opposed to militarism on several grounds. First, it was un-Scrip- tura). True, in its earlier stages militarism was enunciated as a religious duty. The Deity was con- ceived as a man of war, but with fuller revelation came the idea that de was of quite another nature, hence the prophetic protest. It was, however, only in New Testament times that militarism received its death blow. Jesus Christ was the Prince of Peace, and no militarism could be squared with the ringing message of brother- hood proclaimed in the Sermon on the Mount.

div.head: BAR OF PROGRESS.
div.p: THE BAR OF PROGRESS.

Secondly, militarism had always been the bar of progress. Europe to-day would have been in a more advanced condition had it not been for Napoleon. This inhuman monster plunged the Continent into turmoil and strife, was responsible for the murder of something like 5,000,000 souls, and put back tbe clock of progress. Again, modern Christianity and modern militarism were quite incompntible. Wbat could the real followers of Jesus Christ have to do with war or its accessories ?

div.head: BOYS' BRIGADE CRITICISED.
div.p: BOYS' BRIGADE CRITICISED.

A week ago he was about to enter his pulpit in Legh- street when some drums began to beat, the discordant blare of bugles was beard, and he knew that it proceeded from some young brigade who thoughtlessly had com- menced to be schooled in the use of arms; and to lend an air of respectability to the anti-Christian movement; they were on their way to a Christian service. Such a travesty on the teaching of brotherly love filled him with revulsion. Personally, he could never act as chaplain to militarists, as he could never bring himself to preach to the soldier as some men did to-day. Further, militarism denied the sacredness of human life. Our law regarded the life of the citizen as inviolable. Even before receiving capital punishment, the criminal must be tried before twelve good men and true, in order that no mistake might be made. Militarism swept all this to one side, and schooled men to slay their brothers with the quickest dispatch. His feelings had been harried only a few weeks ago by the narration of an eye witness from the Egyptian campaign, who described bow the invader had pitch- forked the natives on their bayonets.

div.head: LESSON FROM NEW ZEALAND
div.p: A LESSON FROM NEW ZEALAND

In conclusion, the speaker pointed to New Zealand, where the shackles had been placed upon the inhabitants and all were compelled to serve regardless of conscientious scruples. In reply to a question, the Defence Minister admitted that he had been unable to conceive any legislation to meet the case of the conscientious objectors. He warned his hearers to retain their liberties and not be influenced by those who were attempting to bring us into bondage. The meeting was presided over by the Rev. T. T James, who made reference to the Rev. W. Cooper's impending departure from Warrington. Mr. Walker sang" Lead, kindly light," and "Come unto Me," which were feelingly rendered, and greatly appreciated. Mr. Payton was the accompanist. Mr. C. Cotton read the lesson, and Mr. A. Healey led the prayer. One new member was welcomed. The Secretary (Mr. B. Farrar) proposed a very hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Cooper for the willing services he bad rendered to this Brotherhood during his ministry in Warrington. They wished for him God speed and blessing in his new sphere. Mr. J. Himsworth seconded, and the vote was carried with enthusiasm.

div.head: NEW SMOKE ABATEMENT BILL,
div.p: A NEW SMOKE ABATEMENT BILL,

The advocates of smoke abatement have often been described as unpractical visionaries, but t!tey have now come forward with concrete proposals by which they hope to rid tbe community, to a large extent, of what everybody agrees is an unpleasant feature—to say the least—of our commercial life. The Smoke Abatement League is responsible for the drafting of a comprehensive Parliamentary Bill, which was laid before the House of Commons in April by Mr. Gordon Harvey, M.P. for Rochdale, and ordered to be printed. Its authors claim that it embodies the suggestions and opinions forwarded to them during the last three years from the sanitary authorities of mcst of the large towns. Efforts have been made to interest the President of the Local Govern- ment Board (Mr. John Burns) in the measure, and, if possible, to have it adopted by the Government. An interview with him at the House of Commons led to his promise to consider the matter in his office, but no further action has been taken. The League fears that there is no prospect of the Bill coming into law during the session of 1913, and is accordingly supporting the London Coal Smoke Abatement Society in an attempt to obtain the appointment of a Royal Commission to inquire into the subject. • THE LAW AS IT STANDS.

Although the Bill as it stands will probably not find its way to the Statute 1300 k in the eaily future, it should serve a useful purpose in educating publia. opinion on the question, and will doubt- lesS form the basis of legislation by which even our drab manufacturing towns may be made pleasant and attractive. tinder the Public Health Act, the emission of black smoke in such quantities as to be a nuisance is punishable by fines, but there is an important saving clause to the effect that "Nothing in this Act shall be construed to extend to mines of different descriptions so as to interfere with or obstruct the efficient working of the same; nor to the smelting of ores and minerals, nor to the calcining, puddling and rolling of iron and other metals, nor to the conversion of pig iron into wrought iron so as to obstruct or interfere with any of such processes respectively." This is commonly held to amount to the exemption of the trades specified, but it would appear that the mug rests upon the manufacturers of showing that the adoption of smoke-consuming appliances would obstruct or interfere with their trades. This view receives emphasis from another clause which states that where a person is summoned in respect of a nuisance arising from the emission of smoke, "The Court shall hold that no nuisance is created within the meaning of this Act, and dismiss the complaint, if it is satisfied that such fireplace or furnace is con- structed in such a manner as to consume, as far as practicable, having regard to the nature of the manu- facture or trade, all smoke arising therefrom, and that such fireplace or furnace has been carefully attended to by the person having charge thereof." WHAT THE NEW BILL PROPOSES.

The new Bill would make it incumbent upon the owner, occupier, or user of a furnace to have such furnace constructed so that it will consume its own smoke; and the emission of smoke or grit from such furnace or its chimney is constituted a nuisance. At the same time the Local Government Board are given power to make special exemptions in those cases in which it is impracticable to avoid making smoke in carrying on a business, but such power to exempt is limited to ten years from the passing of the Act, and an exemption itself must be renewed every two years. The Local Government Board are authorised to set up local smoke abatement authorities in those areas in which the local sanitary authorities are failing to carry out their duties with regard to smoke abatement. Local smoke inspectors may be appointed by the local authority, subject to certain requirements as to experience, and to the control of the Local Govern- ment Board. The Lcal Government Board are given the right to inspet . the recore-4 of offences under the Act, in order to see if the local authority is properly/ carrying out its duties, and, subject to such obliga- tion being satisfied, the Local Government Board may pay not more than half the salary of local smoke inspectors by way of grant in aid. The Bill also requires the central authority themselves to appoint Government smoke inspectors, and authorises such inspectors to prosecute in cases where the local authority has failed to do so. Existing powers as to the abatement of smoke nuisances are expressly preserved. THE MAYOR CRITICISES THE BILL. "BRISTLING WITH DIFFICULTIES."

Interviewed by a representative of the " Examiner " the Mayor (Coulicillor Dr. Joseph), expressed the view that the new Bill seemed to bristle with difficulties and objections. In the first • place, his Worship regards as a retrograde step the taking of the management of lccal affairs, to some extent, out of the hands of local authorities. "It seems to be pulling the wires from the centre in London, " he said, " whereas decentralization is more in keeping with the spirit of the times. If a properly constituted local authority is worthy cf being entrusted with the conduct of its

His Worship's next objection was that scientific knowledge on the subject of smoke prevention is not sufficiently advanced to make an enactment compelling the adoption of smoke-consuming appliances of any great advantage. The Bill practically said, "You must provide means of consuming your own smoke," whereas he maintained that that could not be laid down, as a general rule, with any degree of certainty. By limiting the exemption of special processes to ten years, the Bill was venturing into the legion of prophecy as to the progress of science in a certain direttion. No one could say with accuracy th at in ten years chemical science would have advanced to such an extent as to render it possible, or easy, to prevent the emission of smoke from all works. His Worship farther commented UpDll the fact that domestic smoke is specifically excluded from the purview of the measure, although in most large communities the greater part of the smoke came from dwelling-houses. "I should think that more than half the smoke in Warrington," he added, "comes from houses rather than from works." Any measure which professed to deal with the smoke problem and which failed materially to affect the emission of smoke, in unreasonable quantities, from dwelling- houses, must be regarded as inefficient.

McDonald.—The officer stated that the prisoner was in company with three other men, and they appeared to be under the influence of drink. THEFT FOLLOWS LoaN.—Mary Elizabeth Cann' 13, Lilford-street, was charged with having stolen ss. from a box in the house of Hugh Tyrer, 6, George-street, the previous day.—The Chief Constable said that prosecntrix received 10s. from her husband the p-evious morning. After purchasing some commodities she placed tie remaining money in a box in the parlour. ID the after- noon prisoner borrowed sixpence which prosecutrix got out of the box. 31 re. Tyrer went out, leaving her daughter in charge of the house. Prisoner came in during her absence. She went into the parlour and the girl heard the chinking of money. On the girl going into the parlour prisoner turned round and looked out. of the window, making some remark about the garden. —Mrs. Woodward, 61, Catherine-street, gave evidence to the effect that later in the afternoon Mrs. Cann tendered a half-crown for a loaf and she said she had drawn 58. 103. from the Co-operative Stores. One of the half-crowns was an old one.— The Chief Constable said that one of the half-crowns which Mrs. Tyrer had missed was an old one.—Prisoner said the little girl was behind her all the time. She never took the money.—ln answer to prisoner, Mrs. Woodward admitted that prisoner had tendered a sovereign at the shop on the Thursday night. Prisoner alleged that there was not a neighbour who would go near the house because Mrs. Tyrer accused them of staling money.—The Chief Constable : We could call a number of witnesses who would discredit that statement. Prisoner, he added, had been before the Court previously on charges of stealing. She was well known to the police as being a pilferer of that description.—Mrs. Cann was fined 405., or in default one month's imprisonment.

div.head: " OVER-RIDING" LOCAL AUTHORITIES.
div.p: " OVER-RIDING" LOCAL AUTHORITIES.

An objection upon which his Worship laid special stress was that the Local Government Board had power, in cas- s where they considered local authorities were failing to do their duty, to over-ride them by the appointment of special smoke abatement authorities. It was important that local health authorities should work in harmony with the central authority in London, and he believed that such an enactment would lead to distrust and strained relations. It was not inconceiv- able that the Local Government Board might, upc unreliable or prejudiced evidence, hold that a lee& authority was not doing its duty, and one case cf that kind would inevitably create uneasiness and bad feel- ing throughout the country. The same objection applied to the appointment of smoke inspectors by the Local Government Board, and he did not think the apportionment of the salaries between the local and central authorities would work satisfactorily. An inspector who felt that he was partially independent of the local committee might be disposed to act in an overbearing manner towards them.

div.head: WHEN THE MILLENNIUM ARRIVES.
div.p: WHEN THE MILLENNIUM ARRIVES.

"I should like it to be understood," added his Worship, "that although I have been looked upon as an advocate of smoke, I am as anxiou, as anyone to reduce it to the lowest possible extent. At the same time, I think it is vexatious to expect anything more than that. Practical commonsense is, at this juncture, of more value than anything else in dealing with the question. When the time arrives that some certain means of consuming smoke irwead of emitting it into the atmosphere has been evolved, it shoutd be applied to houses as well as to works. Then no doubt the millennium will have come—at any rate, with regard lo the smoke question. No one looks upon smoke as an absolute advantage, but a great many of the best and keenest observers are of opinion that it is not injurious to health to anything like the extent that strong advocates of smoke prevention have represented."

div.head: ALDERMAN BENNETT WELCOMES TETE BILL
div.p: ALDERMAN BENNETT WELCOMES TETE BILL

Alderman A. Bennett has for many years taken a leading part in the anti-smoke crusade, and his views on the new Bill, as expressed to an " Examiner" reporter, were in many respects in direct contradiction to those of the Mayor. ".1 cordially approve of the main provisions of the Bill," said Alderman Bennett, "and sincerely hope that a strenuous effort will be made to get it passed through Parliament as early as possible. The matter is of infinitely more importance than many of the questions over which the rival parties seem to delight in wrangling. Practical measures of this character are lost sight of, whilst the time of Parliament is wasted in futile controversy over problems which, in many instancas, do not appreciably touch the average daily life of the people. "The principal weaknessjof tbe present law is that it practically exempts certain industries which mainly contribute to the nuisance, and that its administration is left almost entirely to the discretion of the local authorities. These in many cases, in their anxiety not to interfere with the trade of their respective localities, or to offend the important industrial undertakings, do not carry out the law with any real vigour or deter- mination. I understand that under the new Bill the various Councils may still act as the local smoke abatement authorities in their respective districts, but that the Local Government Boara are to have power to constitute special authorities, acting in such areas as they may determine and consisting of members elected by the local Councils, with power to co-opt outside individuals who are interested in the question or have expert knowledge concerning it. These authorities will be required to appoint expert smoke inspectors, with the widest possible povvers,aod will pay one half their salaries. The Local Govern- ment Board will also appoint a number of Government inspectors, experienced in chemistry and engineering, for the purpose of stimulating the work of the local authorities and reporting to the Local Government Board thereon.

div.head: STIMULATING AUTHORITIES TO ACTION,
div.p: STIMULATING AUTHORITIES TO ACTION,

" But the really important provision is that in case the local authority fails to do its duty in any area, the Government in3pector shall have power to prosecute any offender against the Act, and to debit the local authority with the expenses of such prosecution. In other words, where local authorities are sufficiently alive to their responsibilities, matters will proceed pretty much as at present, the only difference being that they will have considerably extended powers, especially in the case of metallurgical and other pro- cesses, and the emission of ash and grit from the offending chimneys, and that half the salaries of the insrectors will be borne by the Local Government Board. If, on the other hand. they fail to carry out the provisions of the Bill, the matter will be taken out of their hands by the Govern- ment inspectors, the law will he enforced and the defaulting local authority will have to bear the costs occasioned by their negligence. For the first time in our experience, we shall then be sure that this grave nuisance will be adequately dealt with. The marvel to me is that the public have stood it in silence so long, for it is not only detrimental to health and utterly destructive of the amenities of every manufacturing centre, but is also a source of incalculable waste and loss. Only the other day, one of the largest manufacturers in Warrington, whose firm carry on a great variety of processes, assured me that it was perfectly possible to prevent blaek smoke altogether by the introduction of proper appliances, and that his own firm had been able to deal with the matter quite successfully. The imposition of an occasional fine would, I am confident, have the most salutory effects, and our manufacturers would begin to give serious attention to a problem which it is their absolute duty to face, in the interests of the community. An even more serious nuisance is fo be found in the fact that deleterious fumes are allowed to escape from many of our local chimneys, apparently without control, and in several parts of the town the result of this may be seen in the gradual decay of all the neighbouring vegetation."

On May 11th Mr. Forster saw the boots in the bedroom, but on returning home at the week end, after being away, he missed them. On the 17th May the father taxed both prisoners with the offence and the elder prisoner produced a pawn ticket eaowing that the boots had been pledged with Mr. Houghton Mersey-street for 49. 7A. He gave him the ticket anSnothing was heard ot him until the previous day vaien Detective Sergeant Reddington found the elder prisoner in the Workhouse. He said, "I pawned the boots to get food. I thought I should have got them out before Saturday." The younger prisoner said, "I carried them out of the house and my father pawned them, giving me sixpence of the money." Illustrating the meanness of the theft, the Superintendent said that the father of the prosecutor took the prisoners into his house and kept them for two or three weeks, not charg- ing them anything. —ALL ABOUT AN ACCOUNT.—The stary of an exciting scene in a !hop was unfolded, when William Fairhurst, of the Wetnt, Buttermarket-street, was summoned for having assaulted Jane Briscoe, greengrocer, 37, Butter- market-street, on Juno 4th, and further for having assaulted her sister, Agnes Welder. Mrs. Briscoe was summoned for having assaulted Mary Jane Fairhurst, wife of the defendant Fairhurst. Mr. Steel appeared for Mrs. Briscoe. and Mr. Swallow for Mr. and Mrs. Fairhurst.—Mr. Steel said that on the day in question Mrs. Fairhurst accompanied by her mother, MTP. Kilcourse, went to Mrs. Briscoe's shop to ask how much she owed. Mrs. Briscoe replied, " You know as well as I do." In the ensuing argument Mrs. Fairhurst used bad language. birs. Briscoe asked her to leave the shop, and as she would not do so, she pushed her. A few minutes afterwards Mrs. Briscoe started to go to the house of the Fairhursts in reference to the account that wan owing, when she was met by Mr. Fairhurst, who, without making any remark, struck her a violent blow in the moutb, causing her to fall to the ground. Mrs. Briscoe's sister, Agnes Welder, saw the assault and asked defendant why he bad committed it. After striking the girl in the mouth, Fairhurst put her bead under his arm and gave her several blows on the face. —For the defence, Mr. Swallow contended that the disturbance commenced in the shop, and that Mrs. Briscoe struck Mrs. Fairhurst. Mr. Fairhurst, who was upstairs at the time, came down and told Mrs. Briscoe and her sister to go away, but they refused to do so. Mr. Fairhurst alleged that Mrs. Briscoe and her sister struck him. rle denied having struck the complainant. —After bearing a great deal of evidence, the magistrates dismissed the case against Mrs. Briscoe, but fined Wria. Fairhurst Li for the aesault on Mrs. Briscoe. The charge of assault on Agnes Welder was dismissed.

div.head: HECKLING THE PREACHER.
div.p: HECKLING THE PREACHER.
Rev. A. M. Mitchell's Suggestion to
Revive Interest in Sermons.

The Rev. A. N. Mitchell, Vicar of Burtonwood, writes in his parish magazine on a proposal recently advanced by a corrtspondent in the Press that preachers should be heckltd, the pew to catechise the pulpit whilst the discounts is being delivered. Our sympathy (he writes) is not with the suggestion to treat the sermon as the lecture, the pulyit as the platform, the preacher as the debater. We fear for the preacher, may be, that too frequently he might be "knocked into a cocked hat." But this is no real objection; let the preacher stand or fall according to h;s ability. The wrong point really is that sermon heckling, in the particular manner proposed, is greatly to be deprecated as not serving the interests of decency, zeverence, and order • it might give rise to heated debate, unseemly display of temper, angry recriminations, un-Parliamentary personalities besides helping to deplete a congregation of its mere docile and peaceable members. Questionings about preachments is quite another matter, and might, perhaps, bs cdopted with some advantage to both preacher and people ; indeed, for ourselves we are convinced something of the kind ought to be introduccd into our Churches if the setmon as a means of instruction, as well as of awakening is t survive, if it is to maintain and develop its usefulness, it is to keep "up to date " and be abreast of the times. The preachers who study and work out problems are far too few ; the mental and spititual horizon of congregations is much too "cabin'd, cribb'd, confined." In every church where sermons are preached the right (it is not only a privilege) of asking questions and of having them publicly answered should be recognised. This can be done very easily without the giving or mentioning of names, wathout any breach of reveience and order. The questions could be written out and put in a box conveniently placed for that purpose. These the preacher, in due course, would receive, and answer at the following service, or at a still later service if found more convenient.

Questions arising out of a morning discourse might be dealt with at the evening service, if the same pr(acher cccupied the pulpit ; questions suggested by the evening subject could be taken in the morning or evening of the next Lord's Day. There should not be the slightest difficulty or con- fusion in carrying through such a simple, helpful, and desirable arrangement ; the benefit would be great to the more thoughtful of churchgoers ; the declining interest in sermons would be revived : miserable pulpit platitudes would be abandoned. Heckling the preacher in this sensible and reverent fashion would certainly tend to make our Church in town and country centres of Christian thought and influence, to which, as thing are and the sermon is, they cannot make in EID many ca3es, tbe slightest pre- tention. It must, however, be acknowledged that congregations to whom "the heckling" offer is made are not always ready to accept it.

div.head: HOUSING DEADLOCK AT LEIGH.
div.p: HOUSING DEADLOCK AT LEIGH.
Master Builders at Variance with
the Council

The Leigh Town Council some time ego decided to build 100 houses in view of the house famine in the town. No tenders have been received in response to the Council's invitation, however, and at Tuesday night's meeting of the Council Mr. Gregory moved that in view of the refusal of the master builders to tender for the erection of municipal houses the Council should instruct the Housing Sub-committee to erect the houses by the employment of direct labour. The master builders, he said, were not prepared to tender because the Council had passed a resolution stating that the contractors should pay the bricklayers labourers not less than 61d. per hour. It seemed to him there was an understanding between the property owners and the master builders for the purpose of keep- ing a limited supi ly of houses in the town. The master builders were being dominated by two or three builders who had axes to grind. It was said that if the Council decided to build by dir,ct labour some of t a men working on the job would run the risk of being boy- cotted. Mr. Boydell denied that there was a conspiracy to defeat the scheme. The master builders' contention was that the Council had no right to [lx the wages to be paid to workmen in the town. That was a matter for the employers and the trade union to determine. The resolution was defeated by 22 votes to 6.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, June 14, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, June 14, 1913.
FARM AND GARDEN,
Farm Labourers' Strike Reaches the Crisis Point To-day,
NOTICES TO BE HANDED IN.

Aftcr several weeks endeavouring to get concessions from their masters in regard to conditions of service, the West Lancashire farm 14bourers, through their organisation, the National Agricultural Labourers' Union, have decided to test the issue by a strike, and to-day notices to cease work, which will expire next Friday evening, will be served on the farmers in all the townships within the triangular area formed by Liverpool, Southport and Ormskirk. Over 3,000 labourers will be affected by the notices, and the effect of a strike in a fortnight's time can only be fully appreciated by those who have had experience of the difficulties indissolubly associated with the intensive farming operations as carried on in this arable area. Particularly is the situation a trying one at harvest time, when on all the farms extra labour is requisitioned to gather in the crops, and as the expiration of the notices will be at the start of the hay harvest and early potat ) lifting the position of affairs, should the lock-out be a serious one, will mean heavy losses in unharvested crops. It would be idle to pretend that the farmers regard the announcement respecting the notices with indiffer- ence, but their opinions in regard to "collective bargaining," which the Labcurers' Union insist on, are as rigid as ever. If the weather is at all favour- able during t',.e bay harvt st, f irmers say they will get through somehow, but otherwise if the men remain loyal to the union, which the masters greatly doubt— some understandicg will have to be c me to or severe lneses must ensue. Labour at present is anything but plentiful owing to the boom in trade in the towns, and Irish harvesters do not immigrate in anything like the numbers they did four or five years since.

div.head: STATEMENT BY THE FARMERS.
div.p: STATEMENT BY THE FARMERS.

In an authoritatite statement issued on behalf of the South-Wtst Lancashire farmers it is denied that they have declared war against their farm setvants. On the contrary, they maintain that there is practically no grievance between them. Tle men, they say, are well paid compared with the carters in Liverpool and Manchester, and their wages far exceed those paid to agricultural labourers in the southern counties of England. The day workmen are receiving wages of from 20s. to 255. a week, and teamsmen 21s. to 255. per week, with allowances. The maste.s believe that many of the men will reluctantly hand in notices to their employers, for whom they have worked since leaving school.

div.head: VANISHING MILKMAID.
div.p: THE VANISHING MILKMAID.

At Sleaford Hiring Fair, one of the largest in England, thousands of servants of both sexes attended from all parts of the country, but not cue girl in a hundred seeking a farmhouse situation would under- take the duties of milking. The milkmaid may now be said to have almost disappeared. Men are engaged to do this work. Wages all round were higher, and girls eeeking situltions in the town secured from £4 to £5 more per year than those remaining in the coun!ry.

div.head: COLOURING OF SHEEP.
div.p: COLOURING OF SHEEP.

It is an unpleasant duty examining some show sheep, so "thickly " is the colouring matter laid on, says "Farm and Home." It is time that exhibitors gave this matter their serious attention, for it is doubtful if it results in any god. It would be difficult to assign any valid reason for colouring an animal in such a way that it looks sit, gether differect from its natural self ; those accustomed to it may think it improves the al pearance, but the general public do not think SO, and we are not willing to believe that a competent judge can be Muer ced by the process. It is simply a fashion, which is troublesome to the exhibitor, and serves no useful objet. THE FEEDING HABITS OF BIRD 3.

Experience has shown me that expressions of opinion with nit examination as to the feeding habits of birds are not only useless but often most misleading; e.g.—A fishing txret t who has long taken an interest in gulls sent me a black-headed gull from the North with the information : Fishing in burn, just taken a small trout. On examination in gullet was the water- beetle (Dytiscus marginal's). In the gizzard several earth-worms, elytra of beetles and two fresh-water shrimps. Again, herring gulls were sent, stated to have been fishing for spats in shoal-water, and on examination were found to contain Inittle stars. In both instances the gulls were destroying enemies of fish ova. The feeding habits of the black-headed gull is a most imprtant question, from the farmer's point of view, in consequet.ce of the e xtraordinary rate at which they have reccntly increased.—Dr. Francis Ward, in "Country Life."

div.head: VALUE OF THE HAY CROPS,
div.p: VALUE OF THE HAY CROPS,

Althou Dli not now so completely Cy( r shadowed by the corn harvest as it formerly was, says the " Times " the hay harvest is still looked upon as of secondary import- ance. Neither in magnitude nor in value is it on a level with the group of cereals, but hay fills a place in the economy of the farm of far greater significance than is commonly supposed. Probably few realise that the aggregate output of bay in Great Britain is about equal in money value to that of all the three cereals, and it is only when the value of the straw of the latter is added that the collective grain crops gain an appreciable advantage. The annual hay harvest in England, Wales, and Scotland is at a moderate estimate reckoned at £31,750,000, as compated with £32,750,000 worth of wheat, barley, and oats, to which has to be added £12,500,000 for the straw. These calculations are not unduly favourable to the hay crop, as the price is reckoned at £3 103. a ton for rotation hay and £3 for meadow hay, and in recent years the selling prices have oftener exceeded these figures than fallen short of them. This aggre- gate sum, derived from 7,500,000 acres, does not represent a large return from the acre, the average being a little over 53, but it should not be forgotten that this is not the whole revenue for the season from the acreage mowed. There is often a second crop, and always an aftermath to be cut or grazed, and in many cases this is a substantial item, difficult to reduce to a money equivalent, but extremely service- able for supplementing the pastures when glass is short, for hurdling or for soiling.

div.head: S 3ARCITY OF LABOURERS.
div.p: S 3ARCITY OF LABOURERS.

The scarcity of labourers is causing serious incon- venience in many districts. It is with difficulty that the full c >mplement of regular hands can be main- tained, and, except near the villages, day workers are almost unobtainable. It is not merely weeding and hoeing that suffer from a deficiency of workers ; similar trouble is afflicting the dairying counties, with the result that mechanical appliances are being adoptcd from necessity rather than from choice. It is fortu- nate for both the producer and the consumer of milk that the milking machine has been brought to a reasonable state of proficiency; for it looks as if nothing but this invention could prevent many from relinquishing dairying for some other business less exacting in its demands upon labour,

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

ASTERS AND INSECTS.—Now that thousands of asters are being planted out for summer effect, we would warn readers of the danger that is usually lurking unseen among them. Too often we hear complaints of plants with their young foliage curled and crippled, and this is usually due to mites or aphides. As each plant is lifted from the box, it should be dipped into some weak insecticide and moved about in it, so as to thoroughly wet the whole of the foliage. This simple task now will in many cases mean the difference between success and failure later on. ---" The Garden." SWALLOWING A STONE Ent;.—T. W. Walker tells the following story in "Country Life" : —" One of my helpers, when trapping vermin last week, set a trap on a marshy piece of ground. He put a sham partridge egg on a forked stick, showing the egg above water. Of course the trap, as you know, was set on a patch clear of water. The trap was set for a hooded crow, but a heron was caught instead. Well, of course, that might easily happen, but the sham partridge egg had disappeared. To make a long story short, the heron had swallowed it, and my helper, Harry Dickson, squeezed it out of the heron's long thrapple. Now I don't mean to say herons are hunters for game eggs, but it appears that if they came on a nest of game eggs they would make a meal of them.

POSES AND GREEN FLY.—We do not remember seeing roses so badly infested with green fly or aphis as they are this year, and judging by reports received, the trouble is very widespread. Undoubtedly the best method of combating this pest before the flowers are actually open is to spray with any of the insecticides
Continued in next column.

advertised in our pages. When tho blooms are open, however, they are apt to become soiled by such treat ment, thonEh even then it is better to sacrifice a few than to let the pest get the upper hand. Where a g ,od force of water is available, a severe hosing will dis- lodge large numbers of insects, and if repeated two or three evenings in succession, will do much towards cleansing the plants and cause no injury to the open flowers—' The Garden."

ROSES.—These should receive a dressing or two of liquid manure as soon as the buds begin to form. Keep a look out for mildew, and t, hould any of the trees be affected, dust them with flowers of sulphur or spray them with a solution of liver of sulphur. Dis- budding is recommended for such varieties as Frau Karl Druschki, Mrs. John Laing, Killarney, Caroline Testout, and Marquis Litta ; even where exhibition blooms are not required it is far better to have a few good blooms than a quantity of small, overcrowded ones.—" Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review,"

div.head: INSURED LANCASHIRE.
div.p: INSURED LANCASHIRE.
County Committee Discusses Malingering.
SOME STRIKING FIGURES.

Some remarkable figures were printed at a meet- ing of the Lancashire Insurance Committee held at Preston on Monday, indicating that about 700,000 persons are insured in the administrative county alone.

div.head: HOW THE MONEY IS SPENT.
div.p: HOW THE MONEY IS SPENT.

Mr. Ormerod (acting chairman of the Finance Com- mittee) presented the quarterly accounts. On medical benefit account, panel doctors had been paid £15,777 and chemists £6,887, the latter being at the rate of 3d. per prescription. It was proposed to pay the doctors monthly in future. The treasurer's estimate of funds required to June 301 showed : Adrninist a- tion account : Staff, printing, &c., £1,500. Medical treatment: One month (May), at 7d. per person per month, 632,000 insured persons, £18,433 ; one quarter at Is. 9d. per head, for 93,600 insured persons not yet allocated to doctors, .£8,190 ; district 22, 50,500 insured p,rsons for the first quarter, at is. 9d. per head, .£4,418. Dugs and appliances : 6,1. per person per quarter, 632,000 insured persons, £15,800; less plyments made to date, £6,839. Sanat rium benefit : Treatment, &.c., £l,OOO. Total, A:42,502 ; less balance in hand, £21,027.

div.head: PART-TIME CLERK.
div.p: PART-TIME CLERK.

In conclusion, the committee made this reference to the appointment of Mr. Harcourt Clire as part-time clerk at a salary of L5OO a year :—" Your sub-com- mittee have received twenty letters from certain approved societies, urban councils, , objecting to the appointment of a part-time clerk by the Insurance Committee, and these letters were laid before your sub- committee. After considering the matter' your sub- committee saw co reason to recommend the Insurance Committee to re-open the queotion of the appointment of clerk. Your sub-committee have to report that the Insurance Commissioners have sinctioned the appoint- ment of the clerk and staff."
Upon this vosli )11 of a part-time clerk the chief debate arose. _

Mr. Walkden (Lancashire Miners' Federation) moved, as an amendment, that the paragraph relating to the clerk's appointment be referred back. The appoint- ment, he declared, bad been sprung upon the com- mittee, and in the name of 60,000 to 70,000 miners, and as a ruerns)er of the Ashton-in—Makorfleld Urban District Council,of which he was a member, he objected. The amendment received 18 votes, while nearly 30 !rinds were raised against, the sub-committee's report being adopted in its entirety. INSURANCE MALINGERING. CERTIFICATE DISPUTE : SUGGESTED COMPROMISE.

The Clerk (Mr. Harcourt E. Clare) reported that at a meeting of the Medical Benefit Sub-committee that afternoon the following resolution had been passed, as being a reasonOple compromise with regard to doctors' certificates : _ _ .

"It shall be treated as a breach of a doctor's agre, meat if he knowingly gives an insured person a certificate for sickness or disablement benefit under the Act, (1) in respect' of an industrial disease, (2) if the illness is caused by tLe patient's own misconduct. 'rho doctor shall state en the certificate the nature of the disease in every case of a disease notifi rble to a local authority; and also in every Case unless, in his opinion, to do so would militate against the patient's recovery ; but, if in such a case he refrains from stating the witure of the illness on the certificate, he shall, if requested, give his opinion of it in writing to a medical man who may be emplo3eJ by or on behalf of an approved aociety. The (lector all stite on each certificate whether, in his opinion, the illness has arisen from natural causes or from an accident." _ _

Dr. Oldham urged that the Committee should post- pone consideration of the matter. The preposal was not likely to to accepted by the doctors' committee. The medical practitioners had already offered to give the certificate which would state that the di-A3ase was not an industrial one, and not duo to the misconduct of an individual. He would like to have an opportunity of meeting the representatives of the approved societies upon the question of malingering. The labelling of tl.e disease on the certificates would Dever help the medical men or the approved societies' agents in discovering or checking malingering, but would difftrentilte between insured and non-insured patients. Unless a doctor could absolutely prove an insured person had not got the a hes and pains that person compliined of he bad to accept the patient's word, but the agents had a better chance of seeing if the patient was ill by his attitude at home.

Mr. Hallsworth said the appoved societies were not having fair treatment. They could wive the doctor considerable time in regard to a malingerer if they knew the nature of the illness. As it was, they were face to face with a code of rules which would enable their auditors to refuse to sanction the payment of bendirs. He (Mr. Hallsworth) had had two glaring cases of malingering tint, week. A fortnight ago a man told him he would be ill that day (yesterday) and be would be going on his holidays. (Laughter.) A few days ago be saw a certificate, in which the word illness simply was given, which had been granted to a woman, who, be was told, was busily engaged in making preparations for her wedding. (Laughter.) After further discussion, the Committee, by 18 votes to 14, decided to approve of the general principle of the suggested compromise as the basis of a scheme of settlement, and appointed n deputation to meet the County M,dicial Committee on this basis.

div.head: PROTECTING AMERICAN WEALTH.
div.p: PROTECTING AMERICAN WEALTH.

One of the stock phrases of the standpat Republicans is "protecting American labour." Of course, it is Ametican wealth that is really protected. The pro- tection is for commodities not labour. The fallacy inherent in this slogan has never been so well expressed as in this extract from a letter from Mr. Rseph McDonald of Providence, R. I. " Workmen have their labour to sell and they must sell it in a flee trade market. The only protection which American labourers have against foreign labourers is the pr ice of a ticket from foreign countries here. The foreign 'pauper' labour which our workmen need to fear is the pauper labour which stands at our mill gates and competes with the labour already in said "Collier's National Weekly," U.S.A., June 13th, 1913.

A Local Building __Society's Successful
Year.

Another successful 3-ettr was under review at the annual meeting of the Warrington Workingmen's Permanent Benefit Building Society, which was held in the Golborne-street schoolroom on Monday evening. Mr. H. Hope presided over a good attendancs of members, end nearly all the officials of the society were present. THE YEAR'S WORKING.

In their 43rd annual report the managers fit ted that during the year the sum of £1,184 148. 31. had been received as subscrictiona ; £2,517 3s. id. f r re-payments ; and .C 7 ('s 51. entrance fees, flne, &c. ; bnd banker's interest, £l9 3., making the total receipts £4,058 Os. 9d. ; the working expenses being £B2 is. 7d. The withdra-sals amounted to .C 1,227 10d.ond the sum of £3,150 had been advanced to members. There were 228 subscribers, holding 310 shares ; and 57 borrowers, holding 216 shims ; making 285 members, holding 556 shares. The bonuses this year amounted to £551 ss. on the amount lent, of which sum £ICO 16s. was divided as profit, and £l5O 9s, carried to the Prospective Interest Account. The total arn,unt remaining owing upon mortgages was £13,063 16s. 101., of ,ahich only £11,564 19s. could be regarded as capital, the balance of £1,503 17s 10d. representing the proper- tiona'e amount of interest thereon, calculated for the number of years the several mortgages have still to run. The profits for the year, including £l2 55. 2d. from last account, after deducting working expenses, amounted to £461 3. The total amount owing to the society on mortgages was £13,068 16s. 10d. The valuation of the property upon which the advances have been made was £2i,50. The w11;10 of the managers retired; Messrs. div.p: s
THE ANCIENT HERO.

It 4 curious, writes Mr. F. Day in the West- minster Review, to notice the nature of the influ- ence which religion brings to bear on its different followers. and also to consider how it comes to pass that the growth of civilisation and pros- perity seeras invariably to undermine and weaken the religion of a. nation. In bygone times it was customary for a knight, on the eve of battle, to pass the hours from sun- set to sunrise in prayer before the altar; and in the middle of the twelfth century King Roger the Norman, on escaping from shipwreck off the, coast of C-ephalti, in North Sicily, during his con- quests there, at once set to work, and as v. thank-offering to God raised that glorious cathe- dral which still enthrals with wonder and admi- ration the feelings of all who gaze upon it. His son and successor, William 11.. also erected the beautiful cathedral of Monreale, near Palermo, an exquisite poem in mosaics, far finer and more extensive than those at St. Mark's, in Venice, one mosaic picture representing him receiving him crown from Christ himself, by no means in a. spirit of braggadocio, as the humility and devoutness of his portrait testify. Notwithstanding the piety of these ancient heroes, after a nightlong vigil passed in prayer,. they would be guilty of the most terrible cruel- ties towards their enemies, an anomaly whiclx seems ine-cplicable,

"BRUTAL COMPULSION."
Rev. A. M. Mitchell Says Authority Has Been Wrested From the Parent

div.head: CRITIC OF OUR EDUCATIONAL SYSTEM.
div.p: A CRITIC OF OUR EDUCATIONAL SYSTEM.

Under the heading of" Those wicked parents," the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, vicar of Burtonwood, in the current issue of his Parish Magazine, di,,cusses the question of the alleged decline of parental authority. He writes :—With the parent lies the grievance rather than the blame, for parental authority has been wrested from the parents' hands by force and violence. The Education Authority has stepped in between the parent and the child ; it says, "this child is ours for five days of the week, for so many hours of each of those five days—the greater part of its life between five awl fourteen. You are not to interfere, you are not to judge what is good for the child, physically, mentally, spiritually; that is our business ; the child is more ours than yours, be must obey the authority: you must feed and lodge him. You must wash and clothe him, if you don't we'll make you; he must obey us and do our bidding. If you isterfere 'twill be the worse for you. Obedience to the State is heaven's first law : the fifth Commandment has gone out of fashion: the parent is a nonentity."

div.head: "BRUTAL COMPULSION."
div.p: "BRUTAL COMPULSION."

This beautiful system of brutal compulsion, dignified by the name of " education, " is now producing its natural sad abundant crop of disobedience, insolence, lawlessness, and misery. The parent has been thrust aside, the attendance officer has usurped the parents' place—the place c.f authority and control. When we get back to origins there is no reason at all why we should wonder at the casting off by the young of parental control. Wbat we now see and experience is the harvest of interference between parent and child. We are but reaping what we have so successfully sown. The children have been quick- witted enough to see that .the Education Authority comes first and must be obeyed: that the parent may be ignored but not the school officer.

div.head: IN BONDAGE TO THE STATE.
div.p: IN BONDAGE TO THE STATE.

All this clamour about the decay of parental control is in the circumstances the merest clap-trap. The unhappy helpless parent is first put in bondage to the State, and then enslaved to the children. If parents are robbed of their parental rights can they reasonably be expected to bring children into the world; why look to them to maintain the nation's birthrate? There would seem to be no limit to the blindness'of leaders and guides, moral and spiritual, who strike at the parents with the one hand and "the love of pleasure" with the other. The love of pleasure is abroad, but as an indication of the joy of life, the just heritage of every child, it only needs patient aud wise direction to bring in the social, ethical, and spiritual npliftment of juvenile democracy. llow can the Church consistently find fault with "the love of pleasure" which is abroad? Usa she not helped to create it,and afterwards done her utmost to foster it ? We find no fault, we cast no stones, only we think our memories should be sufficiently long to have in mind our bazaar frivolities end dissi- pations, our gambling transactions, our stage efforts, our whist drives and card parties. Religion, as we practise it, is not free from the charge of the love of pleasure. "Those wicked parents " may, after all, be justified in the retort direct—"those wicked Pharisees."

div.head: DEATH OF DR. L. S. FORBES WINSLOW.
div.p: DEATH OF DR. L. S. FORBES WINSLOW.

Dr. Forbes Winslow was a member of a family which has achieved distinction in several generations, and was especially proud of the fact that he was a lineal descendant of the Edward Winslow who set sail in the Mayflower and became the first Governor of New Plymouth. He had many medical associations, both his father and one uncle being well-known medical men. He was educated at Rugby and Down- ing College, Cambridge, of which University he was M.B. and LL.D. ; in later years he received the D.C.L. of Oxford. From the beginning of his medical career Dr. Forbes Winslow turned his attention to the study of mental disease, a subject on which he afterwards attained a world-wide reputation. This bent of his mind seems to have been determined by his intense interest in humanity. &sides several purely technical books and papers he was the author of works on "Spiritualistic Madness,"" Uncontrollable Drunkenness," "Eccentricity of Youth Leading to Crhue," " Mad Humanity," and other works which may considered contributions to the literature of sociology as well as of the subject which he had made peculiarly his own.
