div.head: Examiner, Saturday, June 14, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, June 14, 1913.
A BANKRUPT PARTY.
Tories Have Only Protection and Conscription to Offer.
PROGRESSIVE LABOUR LEAGUE.

The wretched weather made it impossible for the Warrington Progressive Labour League to hold its usual open-air meeting at Bridge Foot on Monday evening. However, a number of enthusiasts went to the Liberal Club, where the Rev. Harry Ross, of Hyde, delivered an address. He said he did not remember, in all his knowledge of politics, such a situation as the dountry was faced with to-day. They had one great party bankrupt of leaders, policy ani prospects. Such a situation was not a healthy one for the political life of the nation. The great danger was that Liberals would become over- confident. If they studied the speeches of political leaders, they would see the shifts and devices to which the Tory party was being reduced in order to galvanise into some kind of life the opposition that they talked so much about. When they realised how little the Tories were able to accomplish, with all their twistings and turnings, with all their changes of leaders and policy, Liberals were apt to regard the enemy with con- tempt. It was a great mistake to under-rate the enemy, because old-fashioned Toryism was not dead. It was engrained in British human nature, and, whAtever else Toryism stood for, it stood for those who had got possessions sticking to them. That was the bottom fact in the Tariff " itefcrm" propaganda. EARLY ELECTION WELCOMED.

The first policy of the Tory party at the present time was "Turn the Ooverument out by any means you can." According to that evening's paper, they were in high hopes that there would be a general election within the next two months. (Laughter.) All be could aly was that he sincerely hoped their desire would be realised, because he believed that, in spite of the Insurance Act, dummy guns, drilling in Belfast and the illegal importation of arms, the Tory party, if they were to face the electorate this summer, would receive the soundest drubbing they had had since 1906. (Applause.) He had, hovrevdr, no hope or expectation of that event, desirable though it might be, transpiring this summer. Tariff " Reform " was not dead and done with. It might be in a trance or in a comatose condi- tion, but with the very first bad winter it would revive miraculously. A great many people had put big stakes into Tariff " Reform," and the landlord stood to gain immensely by its adoption.

div.head: WIIAT TARIFFS DO FOR LANDLORDS.
div.p: WIIAT TARIFFS DO FOR LANDLORDS.

When Germany aiopted its scientific tariff, the great estates in that country appreciated in value to the tune of £500,000,000. The great landowners of this country would not have been so ready with their £l,OOO sub- scriptions if they were not hoping for a subatantiAl return on their investments. Having expressed the view that Mr. Joseph Chamberlain's object in beginn- ing the Tariff "Reform " agitation was to drag a highly scented red herring across the trail of disaster and doom which had followed the South African war, the speaker said he believed that if Mr Chamberlain had boot able to retain his commanding position in politics Tariff "Reform" would have been utterly smashed and entirely removed from the sphere 01 practical politics for a century to come. Mr. Chamberlain, when he thought it had served his pur- pose, would have been clever enough to turn to some other aide-issue. THE MILITARIST CAMPAIGN.

The only other constructive policy which the Tory party had to offer was the proposal of Lord Roberta, which was even madder than Tariff "Reform." Were we in free England, with our magni- ficent navy and our great tradition; were we, the sons of men who had died for the liberties that we possessed rather than put themselves under the heel of any military or aristocratic oligatchy, were we, in the twentieth century, prepared to sit down quietly and see our sone, fur whom we Lad been making sacrificts in the hope that theirs wculd be a better England than had existed in the pa 4, placed under the heel of the drill sergeant? He was prepared to use every power he potsessed to hicder and stop that policy. (Applause.) Moreover, he claimed to be as patriotic as Lord Roberts, and to have as great a stake in the country as any landowner. A COUNT'S COMMENTS. •

The speaker went on to repudiate the remarks of Count Uleichen, commanding the Belfast mili•ary district, who, in replying to the toast of the services at a dinner given to the officers of the Fi:st Battle Squadron, now at Bangor, county Dawn, by the Lord Mayor of the city said "There were people like Mr. Keir Hardie, Mr. Carnegie, and various peace presidents who said that because you had a big army you introduced militarism and you induced war. To that he gave a flat contradiction. He failed to follow the argument put forward by these people to the effect that if you had a big navy you had peace' and if you had a big army you would have war. People of that sort, however well meaning they might be, could only be said to be suffering from softening of the brain, lie was delighted to see that the Government proposed to bring forward in the next session a Bill for the care of the feeble-minded, and he would recommend to their first charge the gentlemen whose names he had mentioned." He (the speaker) ranged himself with Mr. Kier Hardie and air. Carnegie on the militarist question, and he warmly resented the insinuations of Count Gleichen, whose position ought to have precluded him from offer- ing any ()pinion on current political questions. (Applause.) The only argument that Count Gleichen, who would call himself a gentleman, had to advance against his opponents on the question was to descend to the gutter and talk about softening of the brain. Were it not for the position he occupied, his remarks might have been allowed to pass unnoticed, but, as a public servant, he should be severely reprimanded for giving vent to such remarks. They were, however, a fair sample of the kind of argument to which we were accustomed from the "gentlemanly" party. He (the speaker) was tempted to reply that, if the atentsl Ddiciency Bill were passed, it seemed to him that those who needed the care of the authorities that it would create were gentlemen who were opposed to Mr. Carnegie and Mr. Keir Hardie, if Count Gleichen might be taken as a representative of them. (Applause.) Finally, the speaker raid be was delight/ad to bear that the Liberal forces in Warrington were in good heart, and that they were not content to mark time, but were doing what they could to enlighten and instruct their neighbours and friend,. They had a magnificent policy and a grand leader. (Applause.) Whatever Mr. Asquith had promised be had performed. (Applause.) Much as the Liberal party had accomplished, its programme was not yet exhausted, and they were glad to know that electoral reform and the land question were soon to be tackled. (Applause.) The speaker instanced the case of agricultural labourers in Warwickshire whose wages wore only 10s. per week, and, after giving an example a rural tyranny, he added that the day was coming when it would not be possible for any landowner to turn a man out of his home and livelihood because of his political opinions. (Applause.)

div.head: LAW-ABIDING SUFFRAGISTS.
div.p: LAW-ABIDING SUFFRAGISTS.
[By One of Them.]

We law-abiding Suffragists often meet with people who say to us, "I shouldn't mind if women did get votes, but I won't join you until you learn how to behave yourselves. I will have nothing to do with people who set fire to houses." Our answer to this is, " Everyone has a right to his or her own opinion, but nobody has a right to form his opinion without looking at the facts of the case a little more closely than that." In the first place, the Suffragists who break the law, usually called "The Suffragettes," are a very small minority of the women who are working for Woman Suffrage. Those NI ho have gone to prison number a few hundreds, while those who have been convicted of serious offences in connection with this agitation are fewer sill.

div.head: MILITANCY REPUDIATED.
div.p: MILITANCY REPUDIATED.

The great national Union of Woman Suffrage Societies, of which Mrs. Henry Fawcett is president, is quite distinct from the militant societies in its constitution and its tactics. It has repeatedly con- demned methods of violence in political propaganda. In comprises more than 400 law-abiding societies with a total membership of over 42,000, and has been increasing lately at the rate of over 1,000 a month. In the second place, the militant movement, being sensational, has attracted much more attention from the Press than the work of the law-abiding Suffragists. While the news of a militant outrage is shown in largo head-lines and on the posters of every newspaper, the most important meetings of constitutional Suffragists receive scant attention from editors on the look-out for exciting 'copy," and many thousands of orderly meetings pass unrecorded by the largo dailies. The men and women who take their opinion from headlines have only themselves to thank if their knowledge of the Woman Suffrage movement is super- ficial,but it is unfair to the many thousands of women, whose desire for the vote is as keen as their conduct is orderly that their cause should be so hastily judged. EXTREMISTS IN EVERY GREAT MOVEMENT.

In every great movement there will be Lund some extremists and we cannot fairly repudiate a just cause because some men and women, maddened by delays and by the tnishanding of a great question by patty politicians, have gone beyond the bounds of reason in its advocacy. If we did this, Christians would cease to be Christians because of the many crimes committed in the past in the name of Christianity. And to come down to the present-day politics, the followers of neither of the two great parties can honestly deny justice to Suffragist i on the score of militancy, for then Home Rulers would have to for- swear Home Rule because there has been cattle driving among the Nationalists, while Unionists must forswear the union because some of them have broken the heads of Nationalists in Ulster. But neither Liberals nor Conservatives would con- sider that such a denial of their principles could reasonably be expected of them, and constitutional Suffragists ask that reason shall also be applied in their case, and that Woman Suffrage shall 1)3 judged on its own merit a and not by the excesses of the extremists.

The best way to crush out militancy is not by useless recriminations or vindictive punishments, but lay just dealing- with the Suffrage question. The gimuine, thorough-going Anti-Suffragists, who, having thought the matter out, honestly disbelieve in Woman Suffrage, must be left to their own conclu- sions, but there are rainy more who will not trouble to think, and for their opinions we can have little respect. But does no blame attach to those others who, admitting their belief in the principle, have done nothing to put that ptinciple into practice? Who make their disapproval of militancy the excuse for their refusal to help?

div.head: COURAGE AND COWARDICE.
div.p: COURAGE AND COWARDICE.

We say to them, 'Have the c urage of your opinions, join in your thousands, aid make the pressure ef public opinion in favour of this reform more urgent than ever; then justice must prevail and militancy cease." Is it not cowardly to hide your true opinions, leaving the work to others, and then when the struggle is over to come out and say, as we know that millions will do—" Oh, yes, I was with you all along " ? When such theoretical ‘''uffragisti as these refuse us their aid in this great hpi ritual and moral fight we are reminded of the words of Henry V : . . . . And gentlemen in England now abed Shall think themselves accursed they were not here, And hold tht ir manhoods cheap while any speaks, That fought wito us upon St. Crispin'a Day." Gentlemen of Wartipgton, we ask you to join us now, the Society in your town is ready to welcome YOU most heartily, and later when our great battle is won, there will be no chance of you bolding your " manhood@ cheap," but you will join with us in the glory of victory for the good of our race.

div.head: STORY OF DANTE'S TOMB.
div.p: THE STORY OF DANTE'S TOMB.

In his book on Ravenna Mr. Edward Hutton tells the comparatively little-known story of Dante's tomb. Dante died in exile in Ravenna in 1321. His body was laid in a stone chest and placed by his friend Guido Novello da Polenta (the nephew of Francesca da Rimini) in the Church of the Minor Friars. Guido died before he could carry out No intention of raising a monument over the poet's ashes. Fulfilling Boo- caccio's prophecy, Florence soon repented her treatment of Dante, and she made repeated de- mands for his body. These were acceded to in 1520. when Ravenna had become a papal city and the Pope was a Florentine. But when the coffin was opened it was found to contain only some withered laurel-leaves and a fragment of bone. In 1865 some workmen found built into the wall of a chapel adjoining the tomb a wooden box, which contained a skeleton, and bore an in- scription indicating that the body bad been hidden by the Franciscan Friars in order to evade the claims of Florence. The skeleton corresponded with Dante's well-known figure and the skull with his death-mask. The remains were re-interred in state in the original stkno chest and tomb.

div.head: TOWN HALL ABLAZE.
div.p: TOWN HALL ABLAZE.
Clock Tower Wrecked at St. Helens.
EXCITING SCENES.

A disastrous fire at St. Helens on Monday destroyed the fine spire anc:, a cmisiderable portion of the Tow° Hall. In preparation for the visit of the King to St. Helens next month workmen have been engaged in renovating the tower and spire, and the work has necessitated the employment of painters, who, it is stated, have been burning off the old paint with blow lamps in order that repainting might be done. Steeplejacks have also been engaged in connection with the work on the tower and spire.

div.head: FIRE BRIGADE'S DIFFICULT TASK.
div.p: FIRE BRIGADE'S DIFFICULT TASK.

About ten o'clock on Monday morning, while men wcre working on a scaffold placed round the clock face, fire was di covered in the spire thirty feet above. An alarm was at once given. The fire station is situated at one end of the building, and the brigade came to the scene of the fire. The height of the epire from the ground is about 120 ft., and it was found that there was not sufficient, pressure of water to enable the firemen to reach the flames, which by this time were burning fiercely round the clock and in the spire above. The fire brigade from the chemical works of Messrs. Pilkington and Co near at hand, turned out, and rendered what aid they could, but it was realised that there was little hope of saving the clock tower and the spire, and attention was directed to the rest of the building in the immediate vicinity of the tower. Firemen ascended the fire escapes and did their best to throw water high enough to reach the burning tower, but it was found impossible to throw a jet higher than the clock face. In less than half an hour from the moment when the fire was dis- covered the whole of the spire above the clock had practically burned out, all that remained being a skeleton of blazing timbers and ironwork, which presently fell with a crash upon the roof of the Town Hall. Burning wood and twisted ironwork fell upon the assembly-room in the rear, setting it on fire, and upon the offices of the borough treasurer, which are covered with a glass roof. At this time fears were entertained that the whole of the building was doomed, and much excitement prevailed. A high wind which was blowing greatly increased the difficulties of the firemen. The clerks in the treasurer's department had been warned and were fortunately not in the offices when the spire fell. A PERILOUS CLIMB.

News th,t the- Town Hall was on fire spread quickly through the town, and a great crowd gathered in the square, of which the building forms one side. Within the space kept clear by the police the firemen threw volumes of water upon the portions of the burning buildings they could reach. While the fire was at its height Mr. Pennington, the contractor for the work which was being carried out, climbed by the perpendi- cul4r ladders fixed to the side of the tower for the convenience of the workmen, taking a hose with him. He ascended to the scaffolding round the clock, and though the flames were unpleasantly near he endeavoured, by pushing the nozzle of the hosepipe through the broken clock face, to get at the flames. In this way be rendered goodfservice. Mr. Pennington occupied s.. position of considerable peril, and the crowd loudly cheered him for his plucky conduct. In the meantime Corporation officials were removing valuables from the interior ot the Town Hall. The Council Chamber contained a number of valuable portraits, including one by Ilerkomer of the late Sir David Gamble, and those were got out with all speed. Fortunately, the Chamber was not damaged, and one side of the hall apparently has escaped injury. On the other side, however, which includes the treasurer's department and the police and fire stations, a good deal of damage was done, and the holes observed in the roof after the fire was extin- guished showed that the whole of this portion of the Town Hall had had a narrow escape from demolition. Despite the efforts of the fire bilged° they were unable to save the roof of the assembly-room, a large portion of which fell in about twelve o'clock. The fire burned on until early in the afternoon, and it was then found possible to ascertain, to a certain extent, the amount of the damage that had been done. The most serious part of it has apparently been caused to the assembly. room, where portions of the burning roof fell upon the chairs and furniture beneath and rendered the apart- ment practically a wreak. The spire and clock are entirely destroyed, and much damage, caused by fire and water, has been done to other parts of the building.

div.head: DAMAGE.
div.p: THE DAMAGE.

The Town Hall, which is a brick aul atone building, was opened in 1876, and it is said to have cost about £60,000. It is a singular coincidence that the Town Hall in use before the present one was destroyed by tire. The amount of damage which has been done cannot at present be accurately estimated, hut it is variously stated at from £lO,OOO to £20,000. No explanation can at the moment be given of the cause of the outbreak, beyond the suggestion that the lights used by the workmen caught some portion of the wood- work and were fanned by the wind into a flume.

div.p: "MINIMUM RELIGION."

In his sermon at Fartn•street Church, London, on Sunday, Father Bernard Vaughan said that the very minimum dose of religion for any sane man was belief in a personal God and in the immortality of the soul. Canon Alexander, preaching at St. Paul's, said that three things essential to a living Christianity were the belief in God, in the historic Christ, and in personal immortality.

cruisers under his command. Mr. Jenkins, it is easy to understand, succeeded in catching the eye of his superiors. He was promoted to the Commodore Secretary's office, and had the satisfaction ot writing a despatch of Wilmot's visit to the King of Dahomey, which was copied in Captain Burton's "Life and experience on the coast of Africa," where he occupied the position of British Consul. Mr. Jenkins was afterwards transferred to H.M.S. " Pioneer " and saw service in the Pacific. Mr. Jenkins is a native of DevOnshire, and the fact that he was born among the granite rocks on the borders of Dartmoor probably accounts for hi 3 love of horses, of fishing, of open-air life, and his continued youthfulness, buoyancy, and interest in human affairs—although he has been a lawyer for so many years. He has written a book, "How Tom Jeffrey saw the world," in which he tells us, in thrilling form, the story of his early life, in much the same manner as Tom Hughes tells the story of his career at Rugby, in "Torn Brown's schooldays." Mr. Jenkins's book is not likely to be a standard work like that of Judge Hughes's, but it should be in the hands of every Warringtonian who wishes to know more about one who will leave his impress upon the history of the town.

Short History of the Camp. During the ten years preceding 1903, a number of Warrington boys had been sent to the Birkdale Camp, owing to the kindly interest of Mr. A. H. Lea, tapestry manu- facturer, and a Christmas treat tor poor children had been in existence through the initiative of Mr. Jenkins. These two gentle- men inevitably came together, and a consul- tation resulted in a decision to call a meeting with the object of establishing, if possible, a Warrington children's summer camp. On the 23rd of June, 1903, a meeting was held at the Town Hall to discuss the proba- bilities of establishing a camp to be devoted solely to the children of Warrington. It is worth recalling who were among those attending this momentous meeting. The Mayor, who that year was Mr. J. Charlton Parr, presided. His Worship was accom- panied by the Mayoress, and there were also present, the Revs. W. Bracecamp, J. Davies and B. Percival, Fathers Whittle and Wilson, Mrs. Henry Roberts, Mrs. Carleton, Alderman Monks and Messrs. F. Monks, J. Moore Murray (Director of Education), Henry Taylor (Police Court Missionary), A. H. Lee and W. H. J. Jenkins.

Little difficulty was experienced in con- vincing the meeting of the " desirability and feasibility "of the scheme, and a committee was appointed consisting of Mrs. Henry Roberts, Miss Pierpoint, the Rev. W. Brace- camp, Father Whittle, Alderman Monks,and Messrs. F. Monks, J. Moore Murray, J. W. Parker, J. H. Smethurst, Henry- Taylor, A. H. Lee and W. H. J. Jenkins to make investigations. The first camp was formed in July at Moreton, in Wirral, and 66 boys went under canvas in charge of Mr. F. J. Emson, who, as chief officer, had the assistance of Messrs. T. H. Aukland, A. Malcolm, G. Dawson and A. Chappell. During the second week 84 boys were in camp, and it was felt that the holiday had been of the greatest value to the children. The result was an incentive for increased effort. The Advantages of Prestatyn.

div.head: W. H. J. J.
div.p: W. H. J. J.
The man whose love for children impels him to DO something for the poorest of them.
RE
AL
Do ye hear ihe children weeping, 0 my brothers, Ere the sorrow comes with years? Wien Mrs. Browning wrote of the cry of the children, who

are weary ere they run, she had undoubtedly in mind the offspring of the poorer classes who, in this happy England of ours, are sadly handicapped both as to their immediate well-being and future prospects.
But the child's sob curseth deeper in the silence Than the strong man in his wrath, is the terrible ending to her terrible indict- ment of our social conditions.

Fortunately for the children, and happily for the good name of humanity, there are many whose love for their fellows dictates the desire to ameliorate their condition so far as may be in a tentative kind of way, while we are waiting for the "good time coming" of which the poet sings. More fortunately, still, this feeling, so far as War- rington is concerned, has found a pivot upon which it can work, and has worked most successfully, in the person of Councillor W. H. J. Jenkins.

There is now, thanks to the organising ability and enthusiasm of Councillor Jenkins, a summer camp that stands on " four statute acres of land at Towyn, in the parish of Melidin," according to the musty-fusty lawyers' lease under which the land is held. The camp is known popularly, in every sense of the word, only as the" Prestatyn Camp" for Warrington children.

A Great Transformation. With its back to the sea, but sheltered by the sand hills, for which the coast between Pres- tatyn and Rhyl are so famous, with its front to the everlasting hills and the sunshine that floods up in its perpetual glory from the south, the camp is a veritable children's paradise. Who shall say what will be the ultimate effect of placing in such surround- ings a child who has never seen any- thing but bricks and mortar and dirty gutters? No one can tell; but, in imany cases, a glimpse of God's fair earth, in its fairest form and grandest setting, must move the imagination of the child for good on a scale that will be incalculable. From the street to the golden shore, from the entry to the open sunshine, from, hard and harsh conditions to freedom and plenty, and to sights that had been undreamed of, make up a sudden transformation that may well give the child-mind a start upon a new and better path with infinite possibilities. For immediate purposes, however,a week's break in the year for the greater part of a thousand boys and girls makes the Prestatyn Camp a valuable social asset for Warrington. A glance at our picture will show the number of smiles that one of the four weeks in camp can provide, to offer full recompense for the money and personal service that are given so freely and fully year by year. The Man. Councillor Jenkins is well known in town for many good qualities, but he is chiefly known because of his keen sympathy for, and interest in, his fellows, and especially the younger and poorer portion of them. Like , most real workers and well-doers, he does not take all the credit to himself. Most generously he recalls, upon all seasonable occasions, the fact that it was the late treasurer of the camp, Mr. Arthur H, Lee, who first asked him to give a helping hand in the work which has since become his own; most enthusiastically does he recall the real help he has always received from Mr. J. A. Ransome, who succeeded Mr. Lee as treasurer, and has had the great advantage of the active assistance of Mrs. Ransome. The committee and the workers in camp claim Mr. Jenkins's warmest praise; but all these will admit, that, as we have said, Mr. Jenkins, who from the first has been the hon. secretary and a kind of manag- ing director, is the pivot upon which the whole scheme centres, and looks—not in vain —for capable direction. Strange it is, that this children's man— who is looked up to and honoured by all but the most thoughtless of the many who pass annually through the camp—is a bachelor. Strange! Though it may be that a childless man may have memories that will spur him on in other children's behalf with an intensity that cannot be felt by his neighbour who is a family man. These are sacred considerations into which we may not enter. It is sufficient to know that Mr. Jenkins, bachelor, is content to engineer a scheme, and keep it going from year to year, that will give new life and interests to so large a proportion of our youthful com- munity. As Slave Chaser. In his younger days, Mr. Jenkins was engaged upon much more grim work than this. He went to sea, his boy friends will be greatly interested to know, and served on Her Majesty's Ship "Rattlesnake," a 22-gun corvette, under Commodore Arthur P. Eardley Wilmot. Many and varied were the adventures of young Jenkins, but the most exciting bear on the story of the part he took in suppressing the slave trade on the West Coast of Africa. On one notable occasion
HOLIDAYS BY THE GLAD SEA WAVES.

div.head: ENJOYMENT AT PRESTATYN C
div.p: ENJOYMENT AT PRESTATYN C

the "Rattlesnake" captured the ".Maraquita" in the Congo with 500 slaves on board, for which, after leaving the sea, Mr. Jenkins received a considerable bonus for prize money. The saving of slaves, it will be admitted, was a suitable training for one who, in after life, was to turn his attention to the children of his own land.

During the first Ashanti war a landing party had to go ashore at Cape Coast Castle, for the protection of the Colony against the AQhantis, and Wilmot, being the senior officer in the West African Squadron, had twenty

div.head: AMP.
div.p: AMP.

lines was the right and proper thing, that they forthwith began to consider the ways and means for establishing a permanent camp. Several sites were selected for inspection, including one at Delamere and one at South- port. At length the choice lay between Southport and Prestatyn, and everything pointed to Prestatyn being the most accept- able from every point of view. Whereas the Southport site was a long way from the sea, whose " intention seems to recede further," the Prestatyn site "abuts on the seashore with practically an unlimited extent of good clean foreshore and sandy beach for bathing. It is covered on. the north and west by sandy ridges, well covered with grass. On the south and within easy walking distance are high hills with charming, rural scenery and exhilarating surroundings. Immediately adjacent is a large area of common land, dry and beauti- fully situated, adjoining the sea. Over this children could roam and play without let or hindrance. There are natural grounds suit- able for cricket, football and other games." There was a plentiful supply of good water, which could be laid on to the camp at small cost.

It was resolved to take steps for the estab- lishment of a permanent camp at Prestatyn, with a view to its being used as a convales- cent home for Warrington children when out of ordinary use. A start was at once made, and the system of sending girls as well as boys was introduced, the girls who went during the last week being placed under the charge of Mrs. Wilkinson, with the following as assistants :—Misses Em son, Bailey, Haley, Laurie, Dickenson, Fairclough, Jefferson and Taylor. The experiment proved a decided success, 260 boys and 72 girls being sent. Steps were then taken to place the under- taking on a permanent basis, and it was eventually arranged that the land should be leased from Lady McLaren for 14 years from January Ist, 1906, at £lO a year for the first seven years, and £l2 subsequently, plus rates. Wooden huts, presented by various • donors, took the place of tents, and a large assembly hall, to be used as a dining-room, concert hall, and a comfortable place of refuge in bad weather, was erected by Lady Greenall. For Warringtonians.

In 1907, Mr. Lee made a suggestion that the camp should be let during the time the children were not there to any respectable persons whether resident in Warrington or not, but, as the wbole scheme had been built up on the lines of having a Warrington camp for Warrington people, this suggestion was not entertained, and Mr. Lee resigned as hon. treasurer, a vote of thanks being accorded him " for his most generous efforts in the past." The venture has gone on growing and prospering at a normal rate, until last summer 259 boys and 257 girls, or a total of 516, enjoyed the pleasures of camp life by the sea, under the auspices of the committee, in addition to many who hired the camp before and after the school holidays. The girls occupy the camp during the first two weeks of the summer holidays, and the boys during the last two. They are selected on well understood lines. First, the teachers, who necessarily understand their young charges and their several necessities, make sugges- tions. The Director of Education and his staff deal with these suggestions with a sympathetic touch that is born of the most kindly interest in the welfare of the children, and a rare devotion to the movement which bespeaks their best endeavour. These officials decide upon the boys and girls whose names are to be submitted to the camp authorities, and then all goes merry as a marriage bell—for the fortunate ones. These fortunate ones up-to-date number nearly 5,000. As we mentioned those who took charge of the earliest camp, so we record the names of those who officiated last season—volun- tary workers to whom the warmest thanks of the community are due : Girls' fortnight.—Mrs. Hill (superin- tendant), and the Misses Mary Emson, Maude Emson, M. Morley, L. Jefferson, E. Walker and D. Wainwright. Boys' fortnight.—Mr. J. J. Firth (superin- tendent) and Mrs. Firth, and Messrs. E. England, T. V. Groake, E. J. Mee, S. Parsonage, F. S. Phillips and Inspector Wainwright. The balance sheet is assuming substantial dimensions. Last season the total expendi- ture was £323, and when balances and receipts were taken into account it was found that there was a debtor balance at the bank of £35.

The chief expense is, of course, food, which stood at £164, or about half the whole ; railway fares absorbing a further £64. The income was derived as follows :—Subscrip- tions, £l3O ; visitors to camp, £120; donations, £57 ;I collecting books, £27; collecting boxes, £1 15s.

Those who wish to do good, and fear that their kindness may be misplaced, will have a ready way out of their difficulty if they will communicate upon the subject with either Mr. J. A. Ransome, Shirley, Hill Cliffe ;or Councillor Jenkins, Winwiek-street. Here is a cause that all may safely support.

div.head: 'UNITY AND HARMONY IN LIFE.
div.p: 'UNITY AND HARMONY IN LIFE.
The Mind as an All-Important Factor
In Evolution.
NOT A SERVANT OF "SURVIVAL.

lAnyone who desires an exercise in hard thinking would do well to study this latest . work by Professor Hobhouse, whose name Ishould be familiar in Warrington on account rof the brilliant lecture on "Biology and i Politics," which he delivered here some little i; time ago. Unlike certain other philosophers, [Mr. Hobhouse is not afraid of revealing to ' the public gaze the innermost workings of his mind, and those who care to follow him ' through his various philosophical writings, •of which the present volume is a kind of culmination, w:111 enjoy the privilege of witnessing many of the inner processes through which a peculiarly fine and sensitive mind may pass in the con- sistent endeavour to meet difficulties and solve problems which are certain to face anyone who thinks seriously of life at all. 1 Professor Hobhouse was trained in that school of thought which swayed English philosophy during part of the last century, the school, namely, for which the mechanical categories of science seemed all-sufficient to explain the mystery of life. Scientific evolu- tion seemed likely to reduce mind to a nonentity, a mere function of brain, and to dethrone all ethical and religious values : it denied all purpose in the natural world, and subjected the whole, human life and activity included, to the domination of inevitable .necessity. Against this tendency there battled only a somewhat discredited theology on the one hand, and a transcen- dental and little understood idealistic philosophy on the other. Professor Hob- house could accept neither of these ways of escape from scientific determinism, nor, on the other hand, was he prepared to regard the exclusion of mind and teleology as final. He, therefore, took in hand the task of show- , ing, from the very basis of science itself, that admitted processes of development, known as elements in evolution, can only be made intelligible by the assumption that such pro- cesses are guided by purpose, and conse- quently that, for the proper understanding of evolution itself, we need not only mechanical but also teleological categories. There must be not only necessity and determinism in the evolutionary process, but purpose and selection as well; mind cannot possibly be reduced to a mere nonentity in the business, but, on the contrary, must, from the moment it appears on the scene, play a deciding part. The Mind as a Factor in Evolution. In order in this way to justify the place and significance of mind in evolution, Professor Hobhouse found it necessary to undertake what was really a history of mind, in its progress from the lowest step of consciousness to the highest point of per- sonal and social realisation. The main lines and results of this study are briefly sum- marised in the first part of the present volume, and the reality of the presence of mind as a significant factor in evolution is enforced by a wonderful wealth of argument and illustration drawn from sciences like biology and psychology, with which Pro- fessor Hobhouse appears to have a thorough acquaintance. In the course of evolution, what we call mind is seen to emerge, first, as "a means of securing the permanence of the species " : this is the biological function of mind which it never loses, but with which it is never content. Instead of remain- ing the mere servant of survival, and the mere slave of the natural order, mind from the outset begins to assert its mastery and independence, and to build a world of its own, so that, in the end, the development of mind has to be regarded "not as a side product of natural selection, but as the central fact of the history of life upon the earth." Thus, as it were, at a bound,the position of the old pseudo scientific philosophy, best known as Materialism, is reversed, and mind, instead of being a negligible accident, becomes the controlling and all important factor. The presence of mind means that the movement of the world, which we call the process of evolution, has reached a point when it has become conscious of itself, and capable of self direction and self realisation; evolution is no longer the mere result of non-spiritual forces,but the conscious labour of intelligence and will. In reading evolution in this way, Professor Hobhouse is in agreement with the general scientific and philosophical tendencies of our day, which, all make solidly for a spiritual interpreta- tion of life. "There is a spiritual element integral to the structure and movement of Reality," and evolution is the process by which this principle asserts its mastery over all others: the history of the world and life is the record of the victory of mind and will. Harmonious and Unified Social Living.

In the second part of the book, Professor Hobhouse develops the thought that the significant progress of mind is towards unity and harmony in every realm of life; the mind of science gives us a unified and harmonious outer world; the mind of morality should give a unified individual life; the social mind and will should make for a harmonious and unified form of social living. These latter are especially the tasks which still lie ahead of mind. This effort after unity and harmony, so essentially characteristic of mind, might suggest the presence in Reality of a mind for which complete unity and harmony existed as a realised ideal. Such a mind has been posited by most idealistic systems of philosophy, and is familiar to the religious consciousness under the name of God. Professor Hobhouse, however, will not go quite so far as this: if I there be any such " Divine mind," it must , pass through the process of development that can be traced in the world, and cannot be eternally and transcendentally complete in itself, and if, again, we are to have any knowledge of such a mind, that knowledge can come only through study of the mind of humanity; the central or divine mind is revealed, if at all, in the concerted labours of mankind towards higher unity and harmony. , Professor Hobhouse, whilst asserting the final significance of mind, is anxious all along Ito allow to mechanism its due and proper place: mind and purpose are controlling factors in the whole, but not themselves the whole. So far his argument takes him ; but he will not go further towards idealism and religion, which seek to reduce even mechanism to a form of mind and make spirit completely supreme. Still, the vindication of the rights of spirit which Professor Hobhouse has here made is surely welcome, and all the more welcome because of the strictly scientific manner of approach. If science leads us to place mind and spirit first, then we have little to fear, and our ethical and religious life can develop fairly, being no

div.head: *THE WAR UPON WAR.
div.p: *THE WAR UPON WAR.
War in the Light of Modern Conditions and Modern Thought.
ITS PLACE IN CIVILISATION.

The matter of these pages has taken shape from a paper originally read at the First Universal Peace Conference held at West- minster Town Hall in 1890. In a preface the writer probably speaks very truly in saying that the ideas presented found little welcome at the time. They constitute, however, in their present form, and developed through the intervening years, a valuable contribution on a subject very pertinent to the hour. This book is a consideration of the value of • war in the light of modern conditions and of modern thought. It is in reality a well- reasoned plea for peace as the only rational • policy for the civilised world, and it is an • argument based on sound and scientific grounds. By a process of clear thinking, Mr. Graham demonstrates the false application too often made of the blind law of natural selection to the conditions of modern civilised com- munities. Civilised life cannot come to its goal by a survival of the fittest in the sense of physical struggle unmodified by sympathy or humanitarian feeling. As a matter of fact, since man became a self-conscious being, and gained moral conceptions, the whole history of civilisation has been a modification of the blind forces of natural selection by death. The story of man has been an upward march, and in the progress all our social aspirations, our institutions such as the Poor Law, and all efforts to deal with the unfortunate or the unfit, have been a denial of the brute law.. The writer proceeds to investigate the claims of war to a place in the life of modern civilised races. As a starting point, he is willing to admit the contribution which war has made to the evolution of the race, giving full place to the moral qualities it has produced, and the end it has accomplished in welding peoples together and enthusing them with a national consciousness. Its present utility, however, is absolutely denied, and its function regarded as now at an end. On the one hand, the absorption of different peoples into races has gone far enough, and indeed too far, for modern wars have often involved the setting up of powers within which no sort of cohesion or common consciousness is possible, and it would be better if Poland, Finland, Alsace Lorraine, Armenia, Crete, Trieste, Georgia, were free and independent peoples. On the other hand, the modern world has become industrial, and the world of in dustry offers a field for the development and exercise of all those qualities of endurance and heroism which the demands of war once produced in human character. The view is maintained that in the realm of government Militarism and Autocracy stand over against Industrialism and Popular Government.

Empire and the Lust of Possession. In the light of these ideas a close examina- tion is made in these pages of the effect of Imperialism upon the national life, and of the results of Empire seen in the races brought under our dominion. An analysis of what the writer terms the dangerous classes of the community is here attempted. These are labelled under the heads of capitalists, officers of the services, certain types of newspapers, manufacturers of material for war, and the jingo elements of society. The spirit of natural friendliness expressed in the ordinary relationships of English and German workmen is contrasted with the financial speculations which lie at the root of modern warfare; the practice of news- papers which manufacture war scares, with a view to circulation, is held up to condemna- tion; and there is an interesting examina- tion of the make-up of the ordinary triusic hall audience of the" Rule Britannia" order. The conclusion reached is that the Empire from its inception to its completion is a class interest. At its best it is a questionable good, as witness our problem in India. It would be all to the good for the races concerned if the lust of possession could be checked. It is desirable that its spirit should be arrested before it finds a new field of operation in China. The whole of the modern speculation in war is demonstrated to be not 'merely futile for the purposes of progress, but a disastrous hindrance to industrial develop- ment. Modern war is the war of the capitalist, and it serves no good purpose for the race. The real battle for the future is between capital and labour, and it will be fought by peaceful and constitutional methods. This is a book to be read carefully. Mr. Graham does not fill his pages with unfounded assertions. He has followed modern history with clear vision and under- standing. His arguments are usually borne out by verifiable facts stated with clearness. There is, indeed, a wealth of reference to the events of our time, which reveals a mind in touch not only with the concerns of our own country, but with a grasp of all international relationships. Nor is this an argument against militarism based on mere sentiment. It is put on ground where reason and high principle coincide. It is a trenchant criticism of the modern situation in which the burden of war causes an increasing restlessness. It is a book scientific in spirit, sane in outlook, and wise in conclusions.
T. T. JAMES.
4- EVOLUTION AND EMPIPE. By J. W. Graham, MA_ London : Headley Bros. 24.
'ECCENTRIC WISDOM.

How utterly foolish some modern faddists must think the public to be For the former would have us believe that in the Christian era alone there have been nineteen centuries of folly, with but a few years of wisdom in the yet young twentieth century. What colossal impertinence to accuse the never idle workshop of Nature of having neglected the human race. On the contrary. see how Nature has always provided well for humanity. Examine the properties and virtues of a little growth, like the popular Currant ; that small yet ndarvellous food-stuff, entirely natural, absolutely pure and unadulterated. Men of science were so interested in its remarkably high nutritive power that they resolved to analyse it to find out what it contained. The result was a revelation, for the Currant is nearly all grape-sugar—the most nutritious and digestible of all foods—and tartaric acid, a natural germicide or pre- ventive of disease. That is why people who eat plenty of Currants enjoy robust health and strength, and do not know the miseries of indigestion. Currants pro- vide the body with what it requires, and surely it is wiser to trust Nature than the charlatans who pretend to have improved upon her.
longer threatened with reduction to a mere natural or illusive level.

Professor Hobhouse's book is extra- ordinarily crowded with interesting and important matter, and almost every page of it invites to long discussion. We can only, therefore, here apologise for the brevity and lamentable incompleteness of this notice. STANLEY A. MELLOR. *DEVELOPMENT AND Purosr,. By L. T. Hobhouse, London: Macmillan and Co. 10s. net.

div.head: SOLWAY PRINCE.
div.p: THE SOLWAY PRINCE.
Admiralty Court Sequel to Ship Canal
Collision.

In the Admiralty Court on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Bargrave Deane, sitting with Trinity Masters, the owners of the steamship Solway Prince (the Man- chester, Liverpool, and North Wales Steamship Company, Limited) sued the owners of the Glasgow steamship Rossmore to recover damages arising out of a collision between those vessels in the Manchester Ship Canal near Thelwall Ferry, shortly after mid-day on March 22nd last. - - -

_ The defendants, who denied liability,counterclaimed for damages. The Solway Prince was at the time bound from Partington to Malpas, Cornwall, with a coal cargo, and the Rossmore from Cork to Partington in ballast. The plaintiffs' case was that the Solway Prince, owing to the jamming of her helm, got out of control, and they complained that the Rossmore instead of stopping con- tinued on, causing the collision. As a result of the damage she sustained, the Solway Prince sank. On the other hand, the defendants attributed the collision to the neglect of those on the Solway Prince in allowing their vessel to get out of control, and in not taking steps to avoid the accident after this occurred. The hearing was adjourned.

div.head: HOME RULE PROGRESS.
div.p: HOME RULE PROGRESS.

A great deal of noise is being made by the Opposition but the sound they are making proceeds from a cause that is usually described in brief and apt language. Boys whistle to keep up their courage when

passing a churchyard; a Conservative Opposition, in these degenerate days, try to obscure the real state of their doubting mind by shying books at Mr. WINSTON CHURCHILL, playing at treason with real and dummy implements of war, and saying what they cannot, if we are to pay their intelligence an average amount of respect, believe to be true. Their latest comforting reflection is that the country is going against the Govern- ment. It would be safer for them if they made the assertion and refrained from trying to provide the proof. The proof they profess to see in the by elections. What are the facts? This week the Home Rule Bill has passed a second reading by 98 votes. This differs only by three votes from the second reading a year ago. As the PRIME MINISTER pointed out, since the Home Rule Bill was introduced there have been twenty-one

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, June 14, 1913.

by-elections contested by Liberal and Labour candidates. The Government have lost four and won one. The four. seats were North- West Manchester, where Sir George Kemp could not be accounted a supporter of Home

Rule; Midlothian and Crewe, where the Labour Candidates took the votes that would have provided substantial Progressive majorities; and Newmarket, where Home Rule was of little moment so far as the Unionists were concerned. On the other hand the Government win was in Ulster itself and revealed the awkward fact that even Ulster has a majority in favour of Home Rule. The votes cast at these elections are :—For Home Rule candidates, 121,269 ; for Tory candi- dates, 105,568; majority for Home Rule, 15,701. So that the country, as well as tl-e House, seems fairly content with the policy that is being pursued by the Government. It is a conclusive answer to the parrot cry that the Parliamentary majority for the Bill does not represent the opinion of the country if we point to the election results. We are told on the one hand that Home Rule ought to be submitted to a General Election before being thrust upon the Orange Counties of Ulster, but Mr. WALTER LONG and the Carson-led " loyalists " declare that if a General Election gave a British majority for Home Rule the " loyalists " would still fight. These facts about Ulster and the political situation, so far as it bears upon Home Rule, are so mixe d up as to remind one of the figures about Tariffs and " reform " that emanate from the same party. Hopeless floundering is not politics, any more than a" political circus," as managed by Sir EDWARD CARSON, can, with reason, be called statesmanship.
Developed.
SECTION THE KING MAY OPEN IN JULY.

The first portion of the new Warrington Bridge is now approaching a very interesting condition, and a good idea may be formed of what the completed structure will be like. Apparently, much greater progress has been made lately with the erection of the struc- ture, but, as a matter of fact this is not so. Most of the heaviest and really most important part of the structure is buried, but as this was to a certain extent uninteresting, outsiders were inclined to think that progress was slow, because there was no indication of the bridge proper. A near inspection of the earlier works, under the guidance of the resident engineer, would have shown the extremely interesting nature of them, and the "slow progress" complaints from the top of a tramcar inspection, would have proved to be quite unfounded.
How the Graceful Span Over the Pilersey has Recently
Photograph by Burrell. FIRST SECTION OF NEW BRIDGE NEARLY COMPLETED. ARCHES OF THE OLD BRIDGE IN THE REAR.

pointed out that the Mayor would be unable to take part in the proceedings at the bridge, as he would have to be in readiness to receive their Majesties on their arrival at the Town Hall. The happy suggestion was then advanced that the King might open the bridge by pressing an electric button on the stand at the Town Hall, and Lord Derby undertook that his Majesty should be asked to give favourable consideration to this proposal. In conversation with an " Examiner " reporter, the Mayor said that, should his Majesty consent to open the bridge, he was sure that great satisfaction would be felt by the people of Warrington. He regarded the completion of the first portion of the structure as the most appropriate stage for the opening ceremony to be performed, as that half of the bridge would immediately come into use, and the charm and novelty of crossing it would long since have worn off when the entire structure was finished.

His Worship added that he had submitted the names of the engineer of the bridge (Mr. J. J. Webster) and the contractor (Mr. Alfred Thorne) for inclusion in the list of ladies and gentlemen to be presented to their Majesties.

div.head: Passing Week.
div.p: The Passing Week.
THE KING AND WARRINGTON BRIDGE.

The Mayor is entitled to the warm thanks of the community for the public spirit which prompted him to obtain Lord Derby's promise to lay before the King a proposal that his Majesty should, on the occasion of his visit to Warrington, formally open the first complete section of the new Warrington Bridge. There is, we understand, every probability that Royal recognition will thus be conferred upon the most important undertaking to which the Corporation has applied itself in recent years, and great satisfaction will be felt by the townspeople at this crowning feature of a visit which promises to be for ever memorable in the annals of the borough.

MR. CROSFIELD'S WARRINGTON HOIJSE. During the week Mrs. A. H. Crosfield, accompanied by Miss Crosfield, has been in town superintending the furnishing of the house in Bold-street that she and Mr. Crosfield are to occupy. The house is to be ready for use by the date of the King's Visit.

THE PROPOSED NEW GRAMMAR SCHOOL, It does not appear that much progress will be reported to the meeting of the Education Committee on Monday, respecting the con- ference on the new site for the Grammar School. We learn from the minutes of the School Management Committee that on the 3rd inst a further letter was read from the Governors of the school, and that the Director was instructed as to the reply he was to send. There is not much substance in that. Monday this week was the date named for the holding of this momentous meeting, but the conference did not take place. The School Management Committee, we are informed, feel that something more explicit,with regard to their proposals, should be submitted by the governors for the consideration of such conference. With that object, correspond- ence is passing. _ _

This question of the higher education of the children of the town is of the greatest importance. It has the deepest concern for the whole of the people and, in that sense, is not a question for the Governors, even with the assistance of the Education Committee and the Board of Education to settle. It is a question upon which the general public are well qualified to speak—as they are fully entitled to speak—and we place our correspondence' columns at the disposal of our readers for the purpose of discussing the subject from all points of view. A public examination of all the facts would do much good and would assist those who have the matter in hand to discharge their trust to the best advantage.

div.head: WHAT IS THE ATTRACTION?
div.p: WHAT IS THE ATTRACTION?

Last week we gave our readers a picture showing a large snake that had been found and captured alive by some of the men engaged upon work connected with the new Warrington Bridge. On Thursday this week a hare was captured at the same spot, or within a few yards of it. At about a quarter past nine in the morning a hare was seen I\ running about in Friars' Green and, as hares were made to be chased whether in town or country, a number ,of persons, among whom it is hinted were a few Policemen, were soon engaged in the delights know to harriers. Barbauld-street and Arpley-road witnessed moving scenes and the hare made for War- rington Bridge s where one cf the workmen fell upon it and ended its urban. jaunt. A snake and a hare in two weeks is a good record for the new bridge. We are looking forward with high expectation for next week's bridge surprise.

div.head: "I WOULD NOT IF I MIGHT."
div.p: "I WOULD NOT IF I MIGHT."

I would not, if I might, Have one continuous day : A constant stream of light Would bring its own decay. I would not, ill might, Have life sans pain alway : Sorrows are lessons bright, To teach the better way. A trouble bravely met, Is danger safely past: A purpose firmly set Earns its reward at last.
W.

The Editor's invitation to his readers to send in their original poetry has met with a good response. The quality of the verses received encourages him to renew the invitation. Contributions in verse will be most welcome.

div.head: AN R.A.'S OPINION.
div.p: AN R.A.'S OPINION.

The main ribs can now be seen to their full advantage, and form a graceful and strik- ing contrast to the smaller arches of the old bridge. The vertical columns carrying the floors are of a neat design, and no extravagant mouldings have been adopted in any part of the structure. In the opinion of a well- known R.A., who recently visited the works, the proportions of the structure throughout are excellent. ARTISTIC PANELS.

The concrete floors have been laid, and as soon as the various gas, water, electric and other mains have been fixed in position, the handsome parapet will be completed, and the roadway and footway paved. The tall pedestals at the entrance to the bridge will form interesting features, the larger ones being surmounted with a handsome lamp standard, and the smaller ones having an ornamental vase. The panels of the pedestals 'will be well suited to receive the very appropriate descriptive panels suggested by Mr. Alderman Bennett.

A very interesting and novel detail in the construction of the main ribs was the temporary hinge at each end and at the centre of each rib. This may probably have been ,noticed in the three gaps which were visible in the ribs at the points mentioned. At these points all the concrete was left out, except a small section in the middle, which had additional steel reinforcement. The other steel reinforcement was exposed, and was free to deflect or deform if there was any undue stress upon it. By this construction, the arch was in a position to adapt itself to its load. If the arch had been built com- pletely the whole way at first, when the load came upon it, the material would probably have cracked, under the effect of theinternal stresses. There is now no fear of this happen- ing,the gaps in the ribs not being permanently filled until the whole dead load was being carried by them. READY FOR THE ROYAL VISIT.

Unless something unforseen happens, we are assured by the engineer. Mr. John J. Webster, M. Inst. C.E., that the first portion of the bridge will be ready for the opening ceremony on the occasion of the Royal visit in July. TO BE COMPLETED EARLY NEXT YEAR.

The second portion is well in hand, and when the old structure is removed the work will be carried out apparently much more quickly than the first portion, the templates, shuttering,&c.,of the first portion being avail- able for the second. The piles are all made, also the balusters of the handrailing, and as there are no preliminary arrangements to make, the whole bridge should be completed early next year. We feel quite satisfied that we shall then have a structure worthy of its associations and of credit to the engineer and all concerned.

div.head: ROYAL VISIT.
div.p: THE ROYAL VISIT.
The King Asked to Open Warrington Bridge.
CEREMONY AT THE TOWN HALL.

There is every probability that the visit of their Majesties the King and Queen to War- rington on July 7th will be rendered additionally memorable by a ceremony of unique civic interest. Lord Derby has promised to submit to the King a suggestion that his Majesty should open the first portion of the new Warrington Bridge, which is now rapidly nearing completion. Should his Majesty be pleased to give his sanction to the proposal, general satisfaction will be felt in the town at this bestowal of Royal favour upon Warrington's important municipal undertaking. The proposal took definite shape at a meeting called by Lord Derby and held at the Town Hall, Preston, on Wednesday, for the purpose of rehearsing some of the cere- monial attendant upon the Royal tour through Lancashire. Representatives of several boroughs attended and were enlightened as to the formalities to be observed on their presentation to their Majesties. The Mayor informed Lord Derby that the first portion of the new bridge would be com- pleted in time for the Royal visit, and asked whether there was any possibility of arranging for his Majesty to open the struc- ture. Lord Derby readily agreed that such a ceremony would be highly appropriate, and promised to place the idea before his Majesty. In the first place the possibility was raised as to whether his Majesty, while en route from Arpley Station to the Town Hall, might stay for a few moments at the bridge in order to perform the ceremony. It was, however,
For the holidays, DRESS BASKETS, TRUNKS, SUIT CASES, &C.--,L S. GARLAND, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: ARRANGEMENTS FOR THE CEREMONY.
div.p: ARRANGEMENTS FOR THE CEREMONY.

When his Majesty presses the electric button on the stand at the Town Hall, the current will sever an ornamental rope placed across the north end of the bridge and simul- taneously fire a Royal salute of twenty-one guns.

At a meeting of the Bridges Committee yesterday afternoon the action of the Mayor in asking Lord Derby to include the opening of the bridge in the arrangements for the Royal visit to Warrington was heartily approved. When the bridge is opened, no civic representative will be in attendance on the site, owing to the ceremonies at the Town Hall. It has, however, been arranged that immediately after his Majesty's departure, the Mayor, members of the Coun- cil, and invited guests shall proceed from the Town Hall to the bridge and walk across it. The police will, accordingly, keep the bridge closed for a short time after the rope has been severed. The Church Lads' Brigade and Boy Scouts will head the procession to the bridge.

div.head: CHILDREN'S GREETING.
div.p: THE CHILDREN'S GREETING.

The school children will play a prominent part in the day's rejoicings. As the arrange- ments at present stand, 9,000 scholars will be massed on the lawn, and will thus be in a position of vantage to witness the presenta- tions to their Majesties. The children Will be provided with red, white and blue hand- kerchiefs, which will be waved on their Majesties arrival and departure. It is hoped that time will also be spared for the singing of a verse of the National Anthem immediately the presentai ions are over. In order to ensure that everything shall pass off smoothly, a rehearsal will take place a few days before the Royal visit. After the King has left the Town Hall, the Mayor will present to the successful schools the special commemoration shields awarded for pro- ficiency in athletics. We understand that the Schools Committee have accepted the tender of Mr. F. Hallett, Bridge-street, to provide three silver challenge shields.

div.head: DECORATIONS.
div.p: THE DECORATIONS.

The Decorations Committee have con - sidered schemes for the decoration of the route which their Majesties will traverse. It has been decided to erect five triumphal arches in the following positions—across Arpley-road on the west side of Friars-green ; at Market Gate ; at the east and west entrances of the Town Hall grounds; and at the borough boundary, Sankeyßridges. The work has been entrusted to Messrs. C. T. Brock and Co., of Crystal Palace fame, who were responsible for the exquisite decoration of the town on the occasien of the visit of the late King Edward VII. and Queen Alexandra. An appeal has been issued to residents and occupiers of property along the line of route to assist the Corporation in making the streets as attractive as possible. On the recommendation of the Chief Con- stable and the Borough Surveyor, the Traffic sub-committee has decided to barricade certain streets. The whole of the line of route wilt be closed between certain hours.

div.head: PENKETH WELCOME.
div.p: PENKETH WELCOME.

At a meeting of the Penketh Parish Council on Monday the Chairman (Dr. Murray) introduced the question of the King's visit, and inquired if the Coun- cil intended making some arrangements for the day when the King passes through the village. After a little discussion, it was decided that the Clerk should communicate with the head teachers of the respective schools in the district, namely : Penketh Council School and Friends' School, also Great Sankey Council Schools, requesting them to make arrangements for the scholars to line the village.

div.head: COMPANY' NOTICES.
div.p: COMPANY' NOTICES.
LIPTON, LIMITED.

The Directors of Lipton, Limited, state that the profit for the year ended 15th March, 1913, after pro- viding £41,091 for depreciation, is £162,544. They recommend a final dividend of six per cent. per annum, making, with the interim dividend already paid, six per cent. for the year. The sum to be carried forward is £31,702.

Crosfield's band will occupy the stand in Bank Park, to-morrow (Sunday) afternoon, commencing at 3-15 p.m.
New Books.

Our reviews of two important books, by Professor J. W. Graham, on "Evolution and Empire," and by Professor Hobhouse, on " Development and Purpose," appear on page .1 under the respective heads "The War upon War " and " Unity and Harmony in Life."

Bishop's Clerical Birthday. The Bishop of Liverpool on Wednesday, laid the foundation-stone of a new chancel at Holy Trinity Church, Ashton-in-Makerfield. He mentioned that that was a notable day to himself, for on St. Barnabas' Day forty-two years ago he was ordained a priest, and admitted to the full ministry of the Chtych of Christ. Messrs. W. Hodgkinson Ltd.: Employes' Outing.

The first summe-r outing in connectii:m with the above firm took place on Thursday, when a happy party of employes at.d fliends journeyed to Chester, and by boat to Eccleston for tea. Afterwards the river and the country were enjoyed to the full by their respective devotees, all meeting again on the 6.45 steamer for Chester. The party reached Warrington safely at 9 o'clock, having been favoured with ideal weather and a delightful time.

Warrington Photograpnic Society. Under the leadership of Mr. J. H. Kertland eleven members took part in the outing to Helsby on Saturday afternoon. The 2 p.m. train from Bank Quay took them on the outward journey, arid from Helsby a fine breezy walk over the hill sides was enjoyed as far as Frodsham. Many new pictures were obtained of this ever-varying country, and everyone was ready for tea by the time Frodsham was reached. During the long light evening several late exposures were successfully made, and so delayed the return till the 9 p.m. train. Value of Libraries.

- Representatives from Leeds, Liverpool and other Lancashire and Yorkshire towns attended tbe Library Association meeting at the Rylands Library,Mancliestdr on Wednesday. Mr. Charles Madeley (Warrington) presided. Mr. Henry Guppy, librarian of the Rylands Library, said libraries were among the most valuable assets in the world. The library was a university which it was never too late to enter, and there a man could obtain the best part of his education. Literature was the viaduct which bridged the present to a know- ledge of the pat by a vital record of what men had felt and thought in life.

Women Liberals : Sewing Class Picnic. About 150 members of Mrs. Osborne's sewing class, accompanied by the Committee, had their second annual picnic to Southport, on Thursday. A capital dinner was served at Fletcher's, in Lord-street. and the time between then and tea was cccupied in drives and enjoying the delights of the promenade. After tea the prtv were joined by Mrs. A. H. Crosfield and Miss Crosfield, who had been engaged at the Cockbedge Sale of Work and they delivered short addresses to their friends. Mrs. Osborne also spoke and propcsod a vote of thanks to Miss Booth who, as treasurer of the picnic, had done much to assure the success of the outing. The day was fine and the trip was greatly enjoyed.

div.head: Presentation to Miss Jessie Dobson.
div.p: Presentation to Miss Jessie Dobson.

The staff of the engineering department of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co. have pre- sented Miss Jessie Dobson, Black Bear House, Latch- ford, who for eight yea's has been telephone operator at the works, with a handsome silver cruet, on the occasion of her leaving to be married to Mr. J. Potter, another member of the staff. The interesting event took place yesterday in the office at Dallam, the gift being handed over by Mr. Fred T. Light, whose eulogies of the recipient were well seconded by Mr. R. G. S. Finney. Mr. Potter responded on behalf of his future wife. The wedding takes place at Christ Church, Latchford, to-day, and the honeymoon will be spent at Aberystwyth.

div.head: Relic of the Patten Family.
div.p: Relic of the Patten Family.

A. large auction sale, which is of some interest to Warrington people, has been held at Winmarlegh Hall, the home of the Patten Family. Much of the furniture sold once filled the chambers of Bank Hall, and some of it adorned the old Patten House mentioned in recent issues of the "Examiner." Three days were occupied by the auctioneer in the disposal of pictures, furniture, and other art objects. —A story of one of the Wilson Pattens attaches to an old bureau which was put up for sale. It is said that as a youth he was locked up in one of the rooms as a punishment for some wrongdoing. He employed his enforced leisure to carve his name upon the lid, the process being carried out by the aid of a penknife and heated poker. He accomplished P A T in effective but not very artistic letters,and had shaped out a second T when disturbed. This bureau has come back to Warrington after its sojourn at Winmarlegh Hall, and may be seen at the antique shop of Messrs. Buckley, Wilderspool Cause- way, who have also become the possessors of many other relics of the Patten family. Very much more valuable from the collectors point of view, is an oriental jar, of porcelain, adorned with lotus and peony flowers and what are known as Ko Ko birds. This dates from 1682, and belongs td the K wan Yin period of Chinese art. It is for a collection of similar oriental articles that Mr. W. B. Lever has recently paid £275,000.

div.head: s" Round the World in Two Hours."
div.p: s" Round the World in Two Hours."

In addition to being a popular source of amusement, cinematograph pictures have also an educational value, as all who have witnessed "Round the World in Two Hours " at the Picturedroine this week will testify. It is a wonderful film, and large houses have derived pleasure and profit from the imaginary tour. Mr. Richard Saker is the lecturer, and his piquant and instructive comments give an added interest to the views. The journey is made all the more realistic by the fact that one sees the actual start from Warrington. 1' A motor car conveys Mr. Saker (the lecturer), Mr. Clifford and Mr. Cooper (the local manager) down Sankey-street and Horsemarket-street to Central Station, where the party leave for Liverpool. Sailing from the seaport by the Baltic, Queenstown is quickly reached. but not before we have seen some beautiful sea effects do we reach New York. The beauties and munificence of this New World city are enjoyed to the full, and then we have views of the principal Canadian towns, the roaring Niagra Falls and Mexican cities. More picturesque scenery is seen in New Zealand, after which we "do " the Australian cities, Japan, China, India and Africa. Arriving in Europe we see the wondrous beauties of Athens, Rome, Naples and Venice. Next we find our- selves in turn in Germany, Austria, Norway, Sweden and Spain. Making further north, we stay in Paris with its architecturally beautiful I)ouleva'rds, and noble buildings. Finally we arrive inLondon, and after "seeing the sights " in the metropolis, we return to Warrington via Bank Quay Station. The star picture for Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday next is" The minister's daughter." On the remaining evenings of the week Toy of destiny" will be shown. '‘

div.head: DEATH OF MR. RALPH BURROWS.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. RALPH BURROWS.
Grappenhall worthy passes away suddenly.

By the death of Mr. Ralph M. Burrows, Grappen- hall loses one of its most interesting old inhabitants. He was found dead in his room by his niece on Thurs- day morning, having been ailing for only a Couple of days. He had lived a quiet, unobtrusive life—in fact, he was almost a recluse. Mr. Burrows had several hobbies, amongst which were reading and studying botany. He could often be seen wending his way homewards on a summer's evening with a collection of wild flowers. Many of his collections found their way to the botany room at the Warrington Museum. He was also fond of writing verses, and a volume of his poems gives a wealth of interesting historical informa- tion about the parish in which he had lived the greater ptrt of his life. His political tendencies can best be described from two lines headed "The Tory Party," which are found written in the;fly-leaf of a copy of his poems : "This is thq British party of stagnation, __Quite out of date in the progressive nation."

The news of his death came is a shock to many people in Grappenhall and district, by whom he was highly respected. Only as late as Sunday last he was completing a contribution for the pages of the " Examiner "on Grappenhall ancient and modern. We hope to publish this in our next issue. Meanwhile, we tender our sympathy to all his relatives and friends.
