div.head: INCREASED WAGES IN THE IRON TRADE.
div.p: INCREASED WAGES IN THE IRON TRADE.

In spite of the lull in the demand and the marked depression in prices in the iron trade which is now 'apparent, the return for March and April of the accountants to the Midland Iron and Steel Wages Board, which controls iron workers' wages in North and South Staffordshire, Shropshire, Lancashire, York- shire, and South Wales, shows an increase of 4s. 2d. per ton in the average net price of iron produced by the 17 selected firms, and in accordance with the sliding scale iron workers' wages are advanced 21 per cent. They are now increased to 10s. 9d. per ton, and with the bonus of 6d. per ton which was granted by the Board in the middle of last year the actual rate for puddling is us. 3d. This is exactly 2s more than was paid in March and April last year, and to find a parallel one has to search the returns for nearly half a century.—" Times," June 2nd.

div.head: BRITISH COAL TRADE
div.p: THE BRITISH COAL TRADE

There are few industries in this country in which prosperity at the moment is greater than it is in the coal-mining industry, or any in which the prospects over the year are brighter. Wages have been advancing at a more rapd pace than they have done at any period since the great boom of 1000-01 ; employment was never more regular or more plentiful; the profits earned by colliery companies are exceedingly good ; and the foreign demand for export coal is so great that coal exporters and colliery owners are clamouring for greater dock accommodation and quicker despatch. . . Great though the increase in the ccst of pro- duction has been in this country during the past five or six years, the increase in the cost of production in Germany—our only possible serious rival in Europe—has been greater. Compared with the average pit-mouth price for the quinquennial peticd 1886-1890 in the United Kingdom the average for the five years 1906-10 showed an increase of about 2g. sd. per ton (from se. 10d. to Ss. 3d.), but German coal prices for the same period showed an increase of 4s. o,ld. per ton (from ss. 91d. to 9s. 10d.), Belgian prices an incre9se of ss. 2d• per tn (from 7s. Sd. to 12s. 10d.), and French prices an increase of 3s. 3d. per ton (from Ss. 11d, to lEs. 2d.). All these ate permanent factors in the supremacy of British, and particularly of Welsh, coal in foreign competitive markets. The United States, it is true, is able to pro- duce coal at nearly half the price it costs us, but, owing to the great distances separating pit from poi t, the price at which American coal can be shipped in the States is on an average higher than that at which British coal can be loaded free on board, and- in any case the United States cannot, except perhaps temporarily, become a great coal-exporting country till it has reversed many of its trades and has become a great bulky raw material importing country.--From "The Times," June 4.

div.head: ALEXANDRA DAY.
div.p: ALEXANDRA DAY.
Arrangements For Local Celebrations.

It is expected that. 300 ladies will be selling artificial wild IN ses in the streets of Warrington on June 28th, which is being kept as Alexandra Day. Fifty thousand button-holes are to be disposed of, and the funds of the Infirmary should benefit con- siderably by the effort. There was a large attendance of ladies at the Infirmary on Thursday, when further arrangements were made. Mr. J. H. Smethurst (chairman of the Infirmary Board of Management) presided, ,and was supported by Mrs. Henry Greenalt (secretary) and Mrs. F. Monks (treasurer). Representa- tives of all the wards in the town were present, and the flowers were tastefully displayed for their inspection. The Chairman answered numerous questions from which we understand that in each ward there will be a depot where flowers can be obtained. When that is closed, the ladies will have to go to the head office at the Infirmary, where their baskets will be renewed. The baskets and badges, which are of appropriate design, are to be sold to the workers at fourpence each, instead of sixpence each, as was originally stated. Each basket will contain twelve dozen penny flowers,six fourpenny ones,and three sixpenny ones. The flowers which are exquisitely pretty, will also be sold in the various places of amusement. To the question " Can the policemen wear the flowers ?" the Chairman replied that Mrs. Greenall would inquire of the Chief Constable. Another lady suggested that probably the soldiers would have a special permission to wear the roses. A further meeting will be held on Thurs- day next.

div.head: FIGHTING CONSUMPTION.
div.p: FIGHTING CONSUMPTION.
A Phthisical Care Committee for Warrington.

The Phthisical Care Committee, to which reference has been made More, seems well on the way to being launched. Naturally when such a committee is selected on a representative basis, it takes some time to constitute, while the various constituent institutions are choosing their delegates. The committee is composed of the following members, viz :

REPRESENTATIVES. APPOINTED BY Alderman James Evans, Health Committee. Mrs. Jackson Holmes, Education Committee. Mrs. Annie Bell, Insurance Committee. Mr. F. Hodson, Insurance Committee. Mr. F. Aylmer Frost, Chamber of Commerce. Mr. Holman Kingdon, Chamber of Commerce. Mr. E. Bandies, Trades Council. Mr. S. H. Sinitb, Trades Council. Mr. Roee,r C. Parr, Infirmary. Mr. J. ii. Smethurst, Infirmary. Mr. F. W. Monks, Guild of Help. Mr. C. E. Parker, Guild of Hetp. Mr. T. Wadsworth, Guild of Help. Ex-OFFICIO MEMBERS. Dr. G. W. N. Joseph Medical Officer. Mr. J. M. Murray, Director of Education. Mr. A. E. Harrison, Manager of Lab. Exchange. Mr. A. Tilling, Clerk to Insurance Corn. Mr. W. J. Rowland, Secretary to Guild of Help. The formation of the committee is the outcome of a resolution unanimously passed at a Conference held several months ago to consider the question of Sanatorium Benefit and the care of phthisical patients generally. Somewhat similar steps have been taken in other places, e.g., Portsmouth and Hampstead. In the former town there is a voluntary association for the Care of Consumptives working in very close con- tact with the Health Authority, the headquarters being at the Municipal Dispensary. The Warrington scheme contemplates co-operation with local authorities, and the provision of food, clothing mad employment where necessary to phthisical patients.

div.head: WEDDINGS OF THE WEEK.
div.p: WEDDINGS OF THE WEEK.
PHAIL---BES WICK.

A marriage which aroused considerable interest took place at Wycliffe Congregational Church on Thursday, when Mr. George Priail, son cf Mr. and Mrs. W. Phail, Crow-lane, West, Newton-le-Willows, was married to Miss Avice Annie lieswick, daughter of Mr. William Beswick, Manchester-road, Warrington. The bride is a member of a arnily which has long been associated with Wycliffe Church and she herself has rendered devoted service to the Church and Sunday School. The Pastor (Rev. 'l'. 'l'. James) officiated. The bride, who was given away by her father, was charm-

ingly attired in soft cream satin, and brown hat trimmed with ostrich feather trount. Miss Cissie Whitfield. who was in attendance as bridesmaid, wore diess of Wedge,wood blue silk. Her ornament was a gold ring, the gift of the bridegroom. Mr. J. Buchan, of t. Helens, discharged the duties of best man. The newly-married couple, who were the recipients of numerous and beautiful presents, left for Fairbourne, where the honeymoon is being spent. div.head: BENNION---CLARKE.
div.p: BENNION---CLARKE.

Bennion, of Moore, was married to Miss Annie Julian Clarke, daughter of the late Mr. John Clarke and of Mrs. Ellen Clarke, Manchester-road. The bride was until recently in charge of the telephone room at the Post Office. . The Rector (Rev. Canon Willis) officiated. Mr. F. M. Darby, Mug. Bac., was at the organ, and as the bridal party left the church he played Mendelssohn's Wedding March. The bride was given away by her eldest brother, Mr. Herbert Clarke, of London. She was beautifully attired in champagne coloured silk, with hat to match, and carried a bouquet of white roses and lilies of the valley. Her ornament was a gold pt-ndant, the gift

of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids were the Misses Mabel and loreuce Clarke (sisters of the bride). Mi-s Mabel Clarke wore a grey silk dress, with hat of pink and black ; and Miss Florence Clarke was attired in pale blue silk, with hat of 'Pagel straw, trimmed with roses. The bouquets were composed of pink carnations, and they wore gold brooches, the gifts of bridegroom. Mr. J. H. Graham (brother-in-law of the bridegroom) acted as best man. The reception was held at the home of the bride's mother, after which the newly-married couple left for Scarborough, where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride travelled in a grey costume, with hat to match. Mr. and Mrs. liennion were the recipients of upwards of fifty hand- some presents. The bride'sg,ft ti the bridegroom was au opal scarf pin.
Llandudn,,, the bride travelling in a navy costume, with hat to match. Many handsome presents were received.

Mr. Salmon acted as best man. The reception was held in the Baptist schoolroom. Later, the happy couple left for

div.head: Burdett---Skelton.
div.p: Burdett---Skelton.

There was a pretty wedding at Stretton Church, on Thursday, the bridegroom being Mr. Walter Burdett, son of Mr. and Mrs. S. Burdett, Warrington, and the bride Miss Elsie Skelton, daughter of the late Mr. William P. Skelton, Warrington. The Vicar (the Rev. the Hon. C. F. Cross), officiated. The bride was given away by her uncle, Mt. J. 11. Fletcher, of Stockton Heath. She was tastefully attired in a white serge costume, with pink hat. Miss Besbie Whitlow, who acted as bridesmaid, wore a pale blue voile dress, and Tuscan hat trimmed with black velvet and roses.

Mr. llub?rt Finney discharged the duties of best man. Amid the good wishes of their friends. Mr. and Mrs. Walter Burdett left for London and Newquay, where the honeymo-in is being spent. The bride trAvelled in a navy blue cisturne. The happy couple were the recipients of many useful and iaandsome presents.

div.head: PRESBYTERIAN GARDEN PARTY.
div.p: PRESBYTERIAN GARDEN PARTY.
Successful gathering at Newholme, Latchford, to further Bazaar Work.
AN IDEAL AFTERNOON.
I'hotoyrapli by A. l'ri,ce.

div.head: GROUP OF CHURCH OFfICIALS.
div.p: GROUP OF CHURCH OFfICIALS.

The office-bearers and congregation of John's Church, Warrington, have for som months past been engaged in arranging for bazaar in aid of church funds. The chairmf of the bazaar committee is 'Mr. W. Russe, " Newholme," Latchford, who is presbyter; elder at St.Uohn's, and in connection with thk work of bazaar organisation Mr. and Mrs. Russell very generously arranged garden parties at their residence on Thursday and Saturday of this week. The first of the two functions was held on Thursday and was favoured with brilliant sunshine, under which the extensive grounds of "New holme " looked their best. The members and friends of St. John's formed a large company, which included the Rev. W. Reid, minister, who after the assembly of the guests, expressed in a few words, their gratitude to Mr. and Mrs. Russell for such an opportunity of coming to- gether amid pleasant surroundings. Every provision had been made by the host

Back Row, Left to Right: P. H. Brown, J. Hunter, R. Mungall, T. Stringer, J. H. Owen, W. M. Walker, G. Miller, A. G. Lewsey. Front Row, Left to Right : T. Ferguson, B. Williamson, W. Russell, Rev. W. Reid (Pastor), J. Snailham, J. Bennett, C. Barlow.

and hostess for the entertainment of their guests. An orchestra discoursed excellent music during the afternoon. Bowling was engaged in on one of the lawns, whilst an enjoyable feature of the proceedings was a cricket match ladies v. gentlemen, which re- sulted in a draw—no centuries being scored. A shooting-range and hoop-la stall had been erected in the grounds by the bazaar com- mittee, and not only provided a good deal of enjoyment but also netted a fair sum in aid of the bazaar funds. Tea was served on the lawn, and was partaken of under most de- lightful weather conditions. Later the company assembled on the lawn where some photographs were taken by Mr. A. Price, Wilderspool Causeway. It was , late in the evening when the party broke up, after having spent an ideal afternoon. It is hoped the weather may again be favourable for the concluding function this (Saturday) afternoon.

div.head: WESLEYAN QUARTERLY MEETING.
div.p: WESLEYAN QUARTERLY MEETING.

The quarterly meeting of the Warrington Wesleyan Methodist Circuit was held on Thursday at Moore. The Rev. W. A. BeCiett presided, and announced an increase of 53 members on the quarter. The Circuit Stewards (Mr. P. A. Harris and Dr. Ferguson) reported a satisfactory balance ;n hand, and Mr. Harris stated that the Rev. I'. W. Derry, of Bury, had accepted an invitation to succeed the Rev. W. A. Beckett in 1914, and the Rev. A. T. York, of Lancaster, would succeed the Rev. H. Middlewood in the same year. The Chairman stated that the amount raised locally for connexional funds was 492 Os. 63., a small increase on the year. Mr. Withinshavv reported that the proceeds of the bazaar for the Norris-street scheme amounted to £974 is. 9d. It was reported that the Synod was due to be held in Warrington in 1914. The next quarterly meeting, on September 11th, will be held at Lymm.

div.head: COCKHEDGE MISSION,
div.p: COCKHEDGE MISSION,
Sale of Work for New Building Fund.
MISS CROSFIELD AND THE SPIRIT OF THE AGE.

The workers of Wycliffe Cockhedge Mission have this week made an effort, by means of a two-days' sale of work, to complete their promised contribution of £2OO to the fund which is being raised for the new school chapel now nearing completion in Padgate- lane. Great interest had been taken in the project, and when the sale opened on Thursday afternoon the room, with its tastefully arranged stalls, presented a most inviting and cheerful appearance. The arrange- ments were admirably carried out by a committee, with Mr. W. H. Wallington as president, Mr. W. Berry as vice-president, Mr. J. W. Slqck as treasurer, Mr. F. Morrall as corresponding secretary, and Mr. A. Ashton as organising secretary.

div.head: TUE STALL-HOLDERS.
div.p: TUE STALL-HOLDERS.

The stalls were in charge of the following:— Ladies' sewing Class.—Alesdames Ashton, Shaw, W Berry. Sunday School.—Mesdames W. H. Wallington, F. Berry, Misses Annie Clayton, L. Brown, L. Pearson, E. Berry, H. Shaw. Congregational.—Miss Joynson, Mesdames Wells, Leathley, Atherton, R. Smith, Miss N. Atherton. Novelty Stall.—Mesdames Syers, Crozier. Plants, Flowers and Fruit.—Messrs, W. Berry, W. Middleton, Misses Nellie Smith, M Gamble. Advertising Stall.—Messrs. A. Evans, By. Clayton, Misses W. Evans, M. Evans. Handkerchief Stall.—Misses A. Wright, A. Taker, E. Warhurst, G. Hughes, Alice Looker. Refreshment Stall. —Mesdames Morrell, Phtunix, Daniels, Middleton, Misses G. Clayton, F. Senior, A. Senior, L. Barton, G. Holbrook, Lillian Smith, Ethel Smith, A. Leathley, E. Leathley, M. Senior, E. Holbrook, A. Hankinson, Annie Locker, M. Ashbrook, Bessie Rushton.
Village Pump.—Misses Ethel Wells, Elsie Middleton, Mr. James Phwnis.
Electric Battery.—Messrs. John Phcenix, J. Pearson. Cockhedge Post Office.—Messrs. H. Corlett, Joseph Phomix, junior, W. Phenix. Weighing Machine.—Messrs. H. Wilson, S. Wilson, F. Dutton.
Shooting Range.—Messrs. J. W. Brown, G. Senior. THE OPENING CEREMONY.

The sale was opened on Thursday by Miss Crosfleld, who was accompanied by Mrs. A. H. Crosfleld. Coun- cillor Peacock presided, and amongst others present were the Revs. T. T. James and John Yonge, Mr. and Mrs. Ziba Armibage, Mr. J. Longland, Mr. W. Beswick and Mr. E. S. Garbind. "A BLESSING IN DISGUISE."

The CHAIRMAN expressed the satisfaction which it gave him to support a Mission possessing such a grand and noble record of work as Cockhedge. When they considEred the conditions under which they worked and how limited was their accommodation, the results must be gratifying to all who were anxious for the welfare of the ueighbourhood. On viewing the new school chapel now in course of erection, be could not help thinking that the circumstances which compelled the abandonment of the present premises—the fact that Messrs. Armitage and Rigby wished to build on that spot—were a blessing in disguise. He felt that, witts their splendid band ot workers which would undoubt- edly be enlarged in their new sphere of usefulness, the work they would accomplish would bs of far-reaching benefit. The flourishing state of the Mission reflected great credit upon the workers, who must have been very ambitious and have experienced trying times in attempting to raise the grand total necessary for the new building scheme. It was gratifying to know that in a neighbourhood, which was one of the poorest in Warrington, the people were so enthusiastically banded together to promote the success of that religious enter- prise. Referring to the presence of Miss Crosfield, Councillor Peacock said that if there was one family which was generally respected in Warrington it was the Crosfield family. (Applause.) He did not, however, forget that the name of Armitage was held in equal respect—in fact the two families seemed to run in double harness. (Laughter and applause.) He did not know what Wycliffe Church—and especially Cockhedge Mission—would have done without the generous help of the Armitage family, who had subscribed handsomely both personally and through the firm, towards the present scheme. (Applause.)

div.head: "IN THE FOREFRONT OF CIVILISATION."
div.p: "IN THE FOREFRONT OF CIVILISATION."

Miss CROSFIELD conveyed the good wishes of Mrs. Crosfield, who was unable to attend, as she was at present abroad. Continuing, she said Mr. Morrall had told her son et ling about the Mission and the work it had accomplibned for the last forty-three years. She knew something of missions, too. She did not suppose any of those present were race-goers— probably very few of them troubled as to which horse won the Derby. But if they were in the habit of attending races, they might say it was a.. neck-and-neck race between Cockhedge Mission and the IVorkingmen's Mission. (Laughter and applause.) She knew well, from long association with Thewlis-street, that grand, cheerful feeling which spread a halo round the spot where people gathered together for love of their fellow-creatures and did good work voluntarily. She was sure that atmosphere as just as strong at Cockhedge Mission as at Thewlis-street. In her view, places which could spread such an atmosphere stood in the forefront of modern civilisation. (Hear, hear.) it had been said that the keynote of the nineteenth century was individualism—that was " Make your own way at all costs ; push other people on one side, so that you may get in the forefront." The keynote of the twentieth century, how- ever, was to be fellow ship, not merely pushing one's own individual interests, but all working collectively for the good of humanity. (Applause.) She was particularly strtick with the half-penny fund in aid of the building scheme, which had been such an extra- ordinary success that it had been the means of accumulating Lloo. (Applause.) That was something to be proud of. It reminded her of a Greek saying which her sister-in-law was fond of quoting: " Bean on bean fills the sack." In the eyes of Europe one of the virtues with which the English-speaking race was not. credited was that of thrift. The achievement of the workers at Cockhedge Mission gave the lie to that reproach. Temperance was one of the strong features of the work at the Mission, and she was pleased to hear that they hada flourishing Band of Hope of 50) members —the strongest, she believed, in NVarrington. (Applause.) In this connection, Miss Crosfield emphasised the importance of fighting the drink evil by turning the tastes of the people towards something higher. Finally, she congratulated the workers on the delightful bazaar they had got together, and wished the enterpriss every f•uccess. (Applause.) HOW THE FUND STANDS.

Mr. F. MoRRALL (secretary) pointed out that the new building was to cost £2,500. The congregation at. Cockhedge had agreed to contribute £2OO, and they had already raised about £125. He did not think they would rest satisfied by making up the total to the guaranteed amount, but hoped to raise over £lOO by the sale. (Applause.) The Rev. T. T. JAMES, in proposing a vote of thanks to Miss Crosfield and Councillor Peacock, said the erection of the new chapel was an important under- taking. They looked forward to the future and they were tinder a debt of obligation to those who had taken a prominent part in that effort. (Applause.) Mr. J. PHCENIX seconded. He said the new building effort had been in their minds for many years. and now they were on the eve of its realisation. (Applause.) No matter how long they had striven to raise funds, he did not think they could have secured a finer buirding than the one which was in course of erection in Padgatio- lane. (Applause.) Mr. ZIBA ARMITAGE briefly supported the vote of thanks, and said Miss Crosfield and Councillor Peacock were only giving another example of that kindness and generosity for which they were so well known. (Applause.) The vote was heartily passed. Entertainments were given at intervals, Mr. R. Wallington being at the piano. Miss Lloyd Williams' orchestra played selections.

div.head: Yesterday's Proceedings.
div.p: Yesterday's Proceedings.

Yesterday's proceedings were opened by Alderman A. BENNETT, who said that there ought to be no sectarian jealousy; they were all fighting for the same Master and working for the same cause. Councillor J. T. LOCKER, who presided, hopel that in their new chapel they would maintain those traditions which were so worthy of all those who had taken an interest in the mission.

A hearty vote of thanks was accorded both gentle- men, on the proposition of the Rev. T. T. James, seconded by Mr. W. H. Wallington, and supported by Mr. Morrell, who said that the proceeds of the previous day amounted bo £59 2s.

div.head: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.

These sessions were held at Stockton Heath Police Station on Tuecday. The presiding magistrates were Conncillor El. Roberts (in the chair), Messrs. James Hepherd, F. Monks, G. Dakin, T. Baxter, H. Gordon Roberts and J. A. Ransome. NOT COMING TO STOCKTON HEATH AGAlN.—Walter Fitter,Hood-lane, Sankey, was summoned for being the owner of a heavy locomotive waggon, which was i:a7dllng along Grappenhall-mad with four waggons, without having a sufficient number of men to attend to same. Inspector Bra ese said the four waggons belonged to a threshing machine. The driver was the defendant's son and he had two men on the engine and that another was NNith the waggons. On being told that he should have had four men he said, " I won't come through Stockton Heath again." Defendant said they had never had any more than three men in charge of the locomo- tive for over 25 years. They travelled all over the country, but there was only trouble at Stockton Heath. The Clerk : They are more accurate in Stockton Heath. Defendant was ordered to pay 10s.—Daniel Fitter, the son of the last defendant, was summoned for allowing the waggon to he drawn without having any com- municating cord from the rear waggon to the engine. Inspector Breese said that %%hen stopped, defendant said he did not know he should have had such a cord. —ln answer to the Clerk, the witness said that the by-law bad only been in force since the 7th April. Defendant's father said he did not think the by-law came into operation until the end of the present month. Defendant was ordered to pay the costs. ALLEGED NEGLECT OF CHILDREN.—Itoger and SITIO Tickle, Pickering's oth' Boat, Dutton, were snmmoned for having neglect,d four children, aged 13, 11, 5, and 3 years respectively, in such a manner as to cause them unnecessary suffering.—Mr. W. E. Hough (Runcorn), who appeared for the N.S.P.C.C., said that the defendants lived in a lonely spot and had been warned by officers of the society who had visited the house. The children were verminous and the clothing was ragged. There was very little frirn;ture, the bedding was filthy, the smell most offensive.— Inspector Evans, of the N.S.P.C.C., said the whole house was filthy from top to bottom and the stench was abominable. On one occasion when he went into the house there was no fire and nothing with which to make the children a cup of tea when they returned from school over a mile and a half away. There was very little furniture in the house.—ln answer to Mr. 11. N. Linaker, who defended, witness admitted that on one occasion when he went into the house there was half a pound of breed and butter.—Mr. Linaker : And you suggest the children were hungry and not given sufficient food ?—Yes.—Mr. Linaker: If they were not given sufficient food they would have eaten the bread and butter.—lcspector Turpin (N.S.P.C.C., Northwich) said the hones was in a horribly filthy condition. There was no attempt at cleanliness and fowls were allowed to run in and out of the house. Dr. McDonald (Runcorn) who had visited the house, said that he found the children scantily clothed sod that whole house was in dirty state. There were a couple of broken chairs, and the beds, which con- sisted of straw and chaff, were very dirty. There was also a most offensive smell. The mischief wss owing to the want of cleanliness in the bedroom.—ln answer to Mr. Linaker, witness said the hair of the children was clean and well nourished. The health of the children, with one exception, was good.— Mr. Linaker suggested that the care should he adjourned for three months as the male defendant's employer would take an oversight of defendants and the children.—The magistrates adjourned the case for three months, the Chairman remarking that they, as well as the society, were desirous of doing what they could in the interests of the children.--Mr. Linaker : I don't think you will have cause to regret what you have done. A BROKEN MRLODV.—An Italian named Dement° was summoned for assaulting Thomas Geddings, at Moore, on the 29th May. —A witness stated that the com- plainant was playing outside a house. All at once the tune stopped and he came out and saw defendant thrashing the complainant very severely.—Defendant was fined 10s. and costs, or in default 14 days' imprison- ment.

TEMPER PLEADED AS EXCUSE FOR ASSAULT.—Henry Nichols, signalman. 4, Alfred-street, Stockton Heath, was summoned for having assaulted Margaret Nichols, Brackley-street, Stockton Heath, on the lit June.— Defendanticlid not appear at first, but a warrant having been issued for his apprehension, he arrived in about half-an-hour and pleaded guilty.—Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for complainant, and said she was a relative of the defendant, and wife of Thomas Nichols, a tram conductor to the Warrington Corporation. On the day in question the complainant went to have tea with the defendant's mother, who resides next door to bin'. Shortly after her arrival the defendant came into the house and said," Who author- ised you to come here ?" She replied that defendant had nothing to do with her visit. At this stage of the hearing, in consequence of faintness, complainant had to be carried out of Court. She revived in time to give her evidence.—Continuing, Mr. Steel said that defendant threatened to kick the complainant out of the house, and attempted to strike her. The mother intervened and endeavoured to persuade him not to commit an assault. After using a number of threats the defendant took up a folded tablecloth that was lying on the table and struck the complainant a severe blow with it on the side of her head, " dazing " her for few moments. She was in a delicate state of health at the time and under the care of a doctor, and in con- requence of the assault had been unable to sleep or take food.—Complainant gave evidence in corroborating this statement.—The defendant, who admitted that he struck the complainant, pleaded that he did so while he was in a bad temper. Ho promised not to repeat the offence.—The Bench convicted him of an aggravated assault flood him 10.. and costs,which, with the advocate's fee, amounted to 10e., and bound him over to keep the peace for 12 months.

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. THE EDITOR of the "Examiner " invites correspond- ence on all subjects of public interest. LETTERS should be brief and pointed. Their object must be to impart or seek information, not abuse. LETTERS must, in all cases, be accompanied by the name and address of the writer. COMMUNICATIONS received early in the week—except urgent matters—can always be given the best attention.

AMBULANCE WORK AT THE KING'S VISIT. Sir,—l hear that the Chief Superintendent of tbe Warrington Corps of the St. John Ambulance Brigade requires twenty nursing sisters for duty on the day of the King's visit. It is rumoured that the Cheshire Red Cross Bearer Co. have applied to be allowed to occupy a position in front of the Town Hall steps, where they will have a good view of the principsl ceremony. The Chief Constable has approved of the twelve ambulance stations in the town according to the probable needs of the day; and if the Red Cross ladies—most of whom do not reside in Warrington, but come from Grappenhall, Daresbury, Sc.— would volunteer to do street duty with the Brigade they would have a good opportunity of rendering good service.
FIRST AID.

div.head: "THE TRADE' AND SWEATING,
div.p: "THE TRADE' AND SWEATING,

Sir,— At a temperance meeting held at Warringt n last week, a notice of which appeared in your issue of Saturday last, Mr. Taylor said they should oppose and crush the drink traffic because there was no trade in the country which sweated its workers like the drink business. " The trade worked its employes longer hours and paid less wages in proportion to its capital than any other industry." The argument that the drink trade pays less wages, or employs less labour, as it is sometimes put, in proportion to its capital than any other trade, has long since lost its force. Indeed, as far back as 1896 the argument was practically abandoned by Mr. James Whyte, the secretary of the Alliance. In an article written that year Mr. Whyte said, " I believe that the liquor trAde gives much more employment than Dr. Burns and Mr. Hoyle were disposed to allow. In this Iby no means stand alone among temperance men." As a matter of tact a larger percentage of th.) money spent on alcoholic drinks is paid away again in wages than would be the case if the money were spent on teetotal drinks. EDWARD TUCKER. June 12th, 1913.

div.head: WOMAN SUFFRAGE AND MILITANCY.
div.p: WOMAN SUFFRAGE AND MILITANCY.

Sir,—lt seems only fitting that some woman should thank Mr. Ogden for his fine article of last week about the Militant Suffragist selling papers in Manchester. Since then, events have brought the t•ubject even more forcibly before us. Probably to many the death of Miss Davison has caused considerable heart searchings. We may strongly disapprove of militancy (as indeed I do), and yet we must admire the heroism and self-sacrifice of her action.
These are the questions that arise : Are those of us who are and always have been in favour of Women's Suffrage, doing all we ought to further it ?
_ Is it in any way our tesponsibility that the repeated delays in granting the vote have driven some women frantic? _

Personally, I believe if all, who are nominally in favour of Women's Suffrage in acme form or other, had really cared to do a little work for it, that we should have had the vote long ago and should have been saved frcm these deplorable mistakes. It is so easy to say we do not approve of militancy, but are we making equal sacrifices or even any sacrifice at all for this great movement for the raising of Womanhood? (MRS.) HELEN M. RANSOME. Shirley, Hill Cliffe.

div.head: DRINK AND POVERTY.
div.p: DRINK AND POVERTY.

Sir,—Tn your issue of the 7th inst., you report a speech made by Mr. Taylor at the Citizens' Temper- ance League meeting, in which he attempted to show by selected districts in Liverpool how "Drink was responsible for poverty." Only a very simple person, indeed, would be taken in by the illustration used. He takes a neighbour- hood in which the comfortable middle-class reside, and because it so happens that the public-houses are few, declares the prosperous condition of the residena to be the result of the few public-houses, when it is perfectly apparent that they would still be the comfort- ably-off middle-class, even if a public-house existed for every person in the district. He then takes a district where the inhabitants manage to eke out a painful existence on a few shillings per week, and declares, because it so happens that the ratio of public-houses is high, that drink is the cause of their poverty. 'I hat sort of argument is a libel on those whose lot in life is sufficiently hard to bear without adding insult to their hardships. The cry that drink is the cause of poverty is best described in the words of Father Bernard Vaughan, who said two or three years ago : " They were told by some that all this poverty was due to drink. What fudge and nonsense people talk! It was idiocy. There was not a word of truth in it." If proof is required of this, all one has to do is to look at some of the Prohibition States cf America, where the sale of drink is illegal, and where poverty and crime exist to a greater degree than in other States where drink is sold openly and legally. Further testimony is offered by Mr. Charles Booth, an acknowledged authority, in "Labour and Life if the People," when he points out that after carefully examining 4,000 cases of the " very poor," only 14 per cent. was due to drink and thriftlessness and 80 per cent. to unemployment, illness, large families and misfortune generally. The problem of poverty is an old one, and in a pro- portionate degree will always be with us ; but nothing will be done to assist its solution by the absurd cry that " drink is the cause of poverty," when it is the hopelessness and misery of the " very poor's " lot that drives some of them to excessive drinking for momentary relief from their hardohips. G. E. HOLMES. June 11th, 1013,

div.head: GUILDS OF HELP.
div.p: GUILDS OF HELP.
Warrington Represented at the Annual
Conference.

The National Association of Guilds of Help held its Annual Conference at Halifax at the end of last week, when several delegates were present from Weerrington. Four new Guilds became associated to the Association, and it was stated that several other towns are con- templating the formation of Guilds. Lancashire was well represented at the conference. The proceedings began with an evening meeting, at which Mr. Alexander Paterson, the author of the fascinating book " Across the Bridges," was the chief speaker. Seeing that he makes his home in the midst of a huge model-dwelling, in South London, ha speaks from an intimate acquaintance with the lives of the poor. His address was lit up with many flashes of humour, but its main effect was to sound a high note of sympathy for the poor in their troubles. ' The chief speaker was Mr. A. W. Whiteley, a well- known Halifax manufacturer, who for two years has been the president of the National Association of Guilds. His brother is chairman of the House of Commons Committees. The main session was held in a handsome Congrega- tional schoolroom, the walls of which were adorned with good copies of famous religious pictures. The Vicar of Halifax, Dr. Burn, presided in the morning. while the minister of the church occupied the chair in the afternoon. It was quite evident that in Halifax all sorts and conditions pull together for the oommonigood. The Guardians showed their goodwill by lending their Board Room for the business meeting of the Association. A singularly practical paper was given on "Landlord and tenant " by a solicitor from Chester. Mr. Grundy, of Manchester League of Help, read the paper which is likely to have the most widespread results. It was the more interesting because it was stated to be the joint production of three men. The paper advocated the drawing together of all societies engaged in organised personal service on civic lines. The practical outcome will be a joint conference of Guilds, Charity Organisation Societies and Social Welfare Councils. One meeting was specially arranged for questions and answers, an informal way of exchanging experiences of Guild work. A novel feature was an exhibition and demonstration of office administration intended specially for new societies. The programme included a motor trip for visitors who were not official delegates, and it closed with a garden party at the Open-air School for Halifax children. The business and hospitality arrangements ensured an excellent conference.
The Ex aminer, Saturday, June 14, 1913.

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.

NEW PASTOR OF BAPTIST CHURCIT.—We understand that the Rev. E. E. Lovell, of Whitchurch,bas accepted the unanimo us call to the pastorate of the Ly ram Baptist Church, and will enter upon his duties the first week in July. DIOCESAN FUND.-1 he annual sermons for the Diocesan Fund were preached at the Lymm Parish Church on Sunday, by the Rector (Rev. G. B. Thurston) The collections, which were the first taken for the Diocesan Fund under the new scheme of Church finance, amounted to over £l4. WOMEN'S TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION.—We are glad to see that the Lymm Branch of the National British Women's Temperance Association, which was formed last winter, is full of life and vigour, and the members have lost none of the enthusiasm with which the society was inaugurated. During the past week no fewer than twelve new members have been enrolled. LYMM BILL.--The Lymm Urban District Council Bill, which authorises the Council to purchase the Lymm Waterworks and certain properties of the Lymm listate Development Company, Ltd., and confers further powers on the Council in regard to their gas under- taking, passed its first reading in the House of Lords on the sth inst. It continued its successful passage through the Examining Committee, and MU? on Monday sent by that body for second reading. PRIMITIVE METHODIST QUARTERLY MEETIN(I.-011 Saturdar,the June session of the members of the Lymm Etnd Altrincham Primitive Methodist Circuit Quarterly Nreeting, was held at Broom Edge Chapel. In order to assist the funds of the circuit a public tea meeting was provided for the goodly number of persons who took advantage of the fine weather for an outing to this healthy spot. In the evening, at the conclusion of the business, the Circuit Steward, Mr. F. Kean. spoke of the able services that bad been rendered by the ministers who are leaving the district next month—the Rev. R. W. B. Whiteway, of Lymm, and the Rev. H. Haynes, of Altrincham—and proposed that a record of appreciation be entered in the minute hook. In seconding the proposition, Mr. G. L. Welford (Lymm) stated that the circuit bad gone through a very trying period of five Nears, and that by the co-operation of these two ministers and the laymen they were now entering into a less strenuous time. He expressed his belief in a more prosperous future. Messrs. Jackson (Dunham Massey), Hudson (Broadheath), and J. Perrin (Broom Edge), representing their societies, supported the motion. The Revs. R. W. B. Whiteway and H. 11a3 nes responded in a suitable manner.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

PENKETH TANNERY PRIZE BRASS BAND.—Stili another success attended the efforts of the local hand at the 13th annual brass band contest held at Darwen on Saturday. The test piece was "Bohemian Girl " or "Songs of sentiment," and quickstep (own choice), the adjudicator ‘ists Mr. !Wm. Adamson, Wingates. Mr. J. A. Greenwood conducted the Penketh band. The following were the results :—Quickstep: 1, Burnley Borough; 2, Nelson Old. Selection : 1, Nelson Old ; 2, Penketla Tannery; 3, Burnley Borough; 4, Atherton Temperance; 5, Heywood Old. Ttere were nine entries. PENKETH WF.SLEYAN CHURCH.—The Sunday School anniversary was celebrated on Sunday. Rain fell heavily in the morning, but there was an improvement in the afternoon, although the wind was bitterly cold. The preacher was the Rev. A. J. Costain (of Wallasey), who gave the children an excellent discourse in the morning, and delighted the congregation at the evening service with his impressive address. Special hymns were sung by the children and choir in a manner which did credit to all who took part, and not the least to Mr. George Carman, who has so successfully for several years undertaken the task of training the children. Miss Dodds and Miss D. Baker added to the interest of the evening services by rendering two solos in efficient style. In the afternoon, a sacred cantata entitled" A Day with our Lord " was given by the choir. The soloists were Miss Moston (contralto), Messrs. J. J. Foden and W. Tucker (tenor), F Ireland and N. Ray (bass). A quartette was sung by Misses A. and G. Bell and Messrs. N. Ray and J. Chatterton. The collections for the day amounted to £32 is. Bd.

div.head: PENKETH PARISH COUNCIL.
div.p: PENKETH PARISH COUNCIL.

A meeting of the above Council was held in the Council Schools on Monday evening. There were present : Dr. Murray (chairman), Messrs. J. G. Withinshaw (vice-chairman), Richard Routledge, James Woodward and E. Foster (clerk).

RP.DUCTION OF THE UNIO'N CALL. Arising out of the suggestion at the previous Council meeting re the question of reduction of the union call for the parkh of Penketh, the Clerk stated that he had received a reply stating that the matter was having attention. SUGGESTED SCHOOL MANAGERS' REPORT.

Mr. Foster said he had received the following reply from the Earlestown Educational Sub-Committee.,.with regard to the Council's request of an annual report from the school managers, 're eenketh Council bchool:— " In reply to your letter as to the annual report of Pen keth Council School Managers, I regret this cannot be given, as the Parish Council is not concerned what- ever in the school management. There must surely be some miLconception of the powers of your authority that led to making an application such as is contained in your letters. " 'Air. Routledge pointed out that he only intended his proposition to apply to the two local school managers, who were elected on the committees by the Parish Council.
Nothing further was done in the matter. FIDDLER'S FERRY DRoWNING FATALITY.

The Clerk read letters referring to the above from the Deputy Coroner (Mr. F. A. Jones), of Ormskirk, and the London and North-Western Railway Company, as follows :—"Coroner's Offices, Ormskirk.—l held an inquest yesterday on William Murdock, who fell into the canal at the wharf at Fiddler's Ferry, on the 21st inst., and the jury added to their verdict the following rider We represent U the Penketh Parish Council that some life-saving appliances should be provided at the place where the deceased fell in. Kindly bring this matter before your Council. " The London and North-Western Railway Company stated in a letter dated May 2nd, 1913, from the Chief Engineer, at Euston, that they had had the matter looked into, and found that life-saving apparatus (either lifebuoys or long poles with hooks at one end) was provided at a number of places on the canal, one of the poles being placed at No. 11 bridge, Fiddler's Ferry, which is close to the spot where William Murdock is supposed to have fallen Into the canal. This would seem to be sufficient for the place in question, hut it did not appear that anyone saw William Murdock fall into the canal who could have rendered assistance.

div.head: RECREATION GROUND SHELTERS.
div.p: RECREATION GROUND SHELTERS.
Dr. Murray proposed that the Council advertise the shed for sale.
Mr. Withinshaw seconded, and it was carried. DANGEROUS CROSS ROADS.

On the proposition of Mr. Withinshaw, it was decided that the Clerk write the Motor Union asking them to place a sign at the Co-operative Stores corner, to warn drivers, with the addition that the usual ten-mile limit fixtures through the village be placed from the Post Office to the west side of the Crown and Cushion Inn.

div.head: NTRO BUS.
div.p: A NTRO BUS.

SUNDAY SCHOOL SERMONS.—The Rev. W.A. Beckett, of Warrington, preached the annual Sunday school sermons at the Wesleyan Church on Sunday. Special hymns were sung by the Sunday school scholars and cboir. Miss 13olshaw wal at the organ. The collections, which amounted to .£6 7s. Bd., were in aid of the Sunday school treat lund.

FUNERAL OF Mg'. HENRY BAREER.—The funeral took place at Antrobus Church, on Saturday, of the late Mrs. Barber, of Pole-lane-ends. The Vicar (the Rev. J. Holden) officiated. Mrs. Barber was held in high esteem in the district. There was a good attendance of relatives and friends.

OUR CHILDREN AND THEIR TRAINING. Nobody can pretend, says a writer in Pear- son's Magazine, ;that our system of elementary education has proved an apparent success. Schools are judged by their fruits. We have only to look at the 'children Iturned out from elemen- tary schools, to hear them talk, and see how they athuse themselves, to know that the schools have apparently failed in their national duty. School life clashes with home life. In the poor !town schools the teacher wages a ceaseless battle be- tween school .and slum home. A child goes to school about thirty hours a week. If a child of the slums, the rest of the time is spent in the gutter, or, worso the home. School is the only factor in the child's life to combat dirt, im- morality, and irreligion. "The child is wanited," to quote a head teacher's words, "to nurse the unhappy infants of court and alley, while their mothers wash— always for others; to sell matches, that their scniors may secure the selfish oblivion which a kindly society has provided at every corner; to beg when the law of supply and demand forbids that a father ,should work. So the evanescent impressions of the schools are daily blurred by a longer, more real, spontaneous life \in a vicious home atmosphere." And school life clashes with the trade, profes- sion, or occupation on which the child must em- bark. If the parents do not destroy the flower of character which the schoolmaster • has un- folded, it is more than probable that, the child's first employer is free :to do so. These problems are not to be solved by a stroke of the pen. Real reforms will only, come when we have compul- sory continuation schools, carrying on education to seventeen or eighteen, together with drastic limitation of the hours of child labour, for after long hours in faCtory, shop, or office, children would reap small benefit from evening schools.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.
Annual Meeting of the Northern
Union.
WARRINGTON CONGRATULATED ON PLUCKY FIGHT IN THE FINAL.

The annual meeting cot' the Northern Rugby Union was held on Tuesday in Manchester. The statement of accounts showed that the balance in hand had teen increased from £1,732 to £1,891, and, in moving the adoption of the accqunts. Mr. W. Lyon (Hull) said that they could congratulate themselves on having had a very successful season. WARRINGTON PRAISED.

The financial results had been good and the play of the clubs of a very high order. The final at Headingley was one of the best he had ever seen, and while Huddersfield were to be congtatulated on their win Warrington deserved praise for the splendid game they played. The success of the Huddersfield and Wigan clubs showed that the play ing of an open, scientific game led to financial success ; and while the Union had not, owing to the unsatisfactory state of the transfer laws sod other reatocs, accepted an invitation to send a team to Australia there was no doubt that in the near future they would send a team which would uphold the credit of the Old Country. The accounts were passed without discussion. CONSTITUTION OF UNION COMMITTEE.

On behalf of the Salford and Swinton clubs an altera- tion to by-law 2 was moved, the important part being : "The Union Committee shall consist of twenty members nine from Yorkshire, nine from Lancashire, and two from other counties or districts at the discretion of the Committee. Clubs in membership shall be entitled to nominate one repretentative." _ . .

The Manchester and District League proposed that the rule should read : "The U, ion Committee shall consist of sixteen members, six from Yorkshire clubs, six from Lancashire clubs, one from a Yorkshire Junior Uni,n, one from a Lancashire Junior Union, and two from other counties or districts at the discretion of the Committee." Only four voted for this, and the Salford and Swinton amendment was defeated by 21 votes aeainst 18. The Union Committee proposed to add to by-law 2 the words " such representative shall not be a paid official of the club." It was explained that this pro- posal was not meant to be retrospective, and the motion was carried.

It was decided to alter by-law 10 to prevent any by- law of the game and challenge cup rule from being altered, rescinded, or added to without the consent of at least two-thirds of those present at a general meet- ing. It was also resolved that the challenge cup rule 25 should be altered to make it agree with the revised by-law.

div.head: QUESTION OF PAYMENTS.
div.p: A QUESTION OF PAYMENTS.

Mr. Cook moved that " the terms of payment must not be by annual or weekly payments, but must be per match only," be inserted in professional law 3. Mr. Cook said it was proposed to make a law of what had Leen the practice of many clubs, and to prevent the making or agreements such as had been made recently. Ile believed that some recent agreements were likely to be reds for the backs of those who made them, but it was not suggested that the new rule should be retrospec- tive. The proposal was carried.

div.head: COLONIAL PLAYERS.
div.p: COLONIAL PLAYERS.

On behalf of the Wigan and Huddersfield clubs it was proposed to rescind the following resolution recently passed by the General Committee :—" No player who hag played football in New Zealand or Australia shall in future be registered to take part in League football in England under the Northern Union code until he has a residential qualification in this country of two years." In support of this it was stated that as many of the Northern Union clubs kad to compete with Association clubs, who, according to the state of their finances, could go into the market for the best players, it was foolish to prevent them from doing their best to get good players. South Wales had been drained dry, and there were not enough good juniors to fill the vacancies. They had to think of drawing the public and not of sentiment. Mr. J. H. Smith said the committee's resolution was for the general benefit of all the clubs in the Union He did not agree that sufficient juniors could not be found ; the fact was that some clubs did not tak enough trouble to discover them. it was stated by other speakers that the improvement in the game was not brought about by the inclusion of Colonial players in their teams, and it was pointed out that certain clubs who had dabbled in Colonial stock were not very successful lest season. Oldham, for instance, bad lost about £1,500. Trio proposal was defeated 14 10 votes against 16. MR. H. ASHTON'S RESIGNATION.

At a meeting of the General Committee a letter was rend from Mr. Harry Ashton, of Warrington, tendering his resignation from the committee, and tho Secretary was instructed to thank him for his splendid services to the game. Mr. F. Osborne, of Warrington, was appointed to fill Mr. Ashton's place on the committee

div.head: CUP TIES.
div.p: THE CUP TIES.

The dates for cup ties were fixed as follows : Qualifying rounds : First, December 6th ; second, December 27th ; third, January 10th; fourth, January 31st; fifth, February 14th. Competition proper : First round, February 28th ; second, March 14th ; third, March 21st ; semi-final, April 4th ; final, April 25th. Complaints were received from junior clubs about the wholesale abandonment of their matches during April as the result of their players being attracted by workshops competitions, and it was decided to send a circular t etter to clubs promoting such competitions drawing attention to the hardships suffered by junior clubs.

div.head: ANGLING NOTES.
div.p: ANGLING NOTES.
Warrington Workingmen's Angling Association (N.A. Centre).

Last week-end WPS a failure as far as the catees were concerned. Beyond a trout or two that were to use for weighing purposes, and a few small eels,nothing was reported. It is a great pity that no pike have been we;ghed in at the Bay Horse, as there is a valuable "special " going P.-begging, and we have only one more week-end in which to secure it. The annual picnic from headquarters took aboitt, thirty anglers to Llangollen, who would otherwise have been out at their favourite fisheries. About fifty made the j iurney, the pic-nic being open to all customers of headqnsrters, and we should not be surprised if the trip resulted in the enrolment of a few more members, as the remarks were general that angler. were fortunate to have such a pretty place for their sport. It wits the first time many of the novices had visited the famous fishery,but a movement is already on foot to have a match for customers of headquarters who have not yet joined the society. The drive and the catering were well managed by Messrs. Ellison and Brooks, and to crown all, Mr. Walker, of the Old Nags Head, Chester, after catering in splendid style for the party, is forwarding a medal to the society for the novices. A novice is held to be one who has never secured a Ist, 2nd or 3rd prize in any bona-fide society. The Bay Horse club has decided to have a match in addition to those already on the list, the first being for the shield, to be held on July 13th, at Hartford. The other dates are: Opening match, July 27th, annual match September 11th. These dates are the same as the date for the centre and Cooper's Arms. Customers of the Bay Horse club are invited to fish a match on the day of the shield contest. They are to fish one hour after the club have concluded their match. NEW CLUB ROOM.
The opening of the new club room is to tnke niece on June 24th, when certain officials of the Northern Anglers will be present.

div.head: "I REMEMBER
div.p: "I REMEMBER
REMINISCENCES AND STORIES OF
OLD WARRINGTON.
GLEANED FROM MANY QUARTERS.

The Old Church-street Workhouse. Dear Sir,—Your "I remember" column is calculated to give decided jogs to old memories like mine. A very good thing, too, I should say, for there are many things that old folks can recall, which their descendants will be quite glad to have. Such a story as the one about Whitby's stumps must certainly add to the gaiety of posterity; the only difficulty will be that when Market Gate becomes a gay and beautiful circle people won't believe the tale. Several times when reading about old Warrington, the lines of Tom Hood have been set jingling through my mind—the lines, I suppose, which inspired your title :
I remember, I remember, The house where I was born, The little window where the sun Came peeping in at morn.

I was born in Church-street rather more than seventy years ago. lam afraid I can- not tell you much that is of value, but I thought your readers might like to have a reference to the old Workhouse which in those days stood in Church-street.

div.head: WORKHOUSE.
div.p: THE WORKHOUSE.

The building was about as plain as a build- ing could well be. It had three stories and along each of them about eight plain windows. I don't know what the old place was built for, possibly it was built as a Workhouse, but there was not a single beautiful feature about it. The only thing that relieved the plainness was an old- fashioned porch which projected over the door. The front was usually plastered over with bills announcing all sorts of events and containing police and public notices. It stood next to the Bull's Head Inn, upon the land which is DOW the yard of Messrs Sankey. I have a general remembrance of the ' interior, though I never ascended the stairs. The entrance hall was large, and a small room was portioned off it as a waiting-room. On the right-hand side was the dining-room with plain tables, and to the left was the Board Room. Behind the dining-room was the kitchen, and behind that the big wash- house, which was a pretty busy and steamy place on the numerous wash days. Behind the Board Room on the left was the children's room. Behind it was the school- room where the "Workhouse boys" were taught. These rooms on the one side and the washhouse and kitchen on the other formed two wings which ran out from the main building. At the back was a large open space and I garden. This could be reached by a passage which ran along the right-hand side of the Workhouse from Church-street. Beyond the garden was the Infirmary. This, I suppose, was the Workhouse Infirmary. The Infirmary for the town was in Orford-street, and the Dispensary in Buttermarket-street. The Workhouse Infirmary was not a big place. The old women inmates wore white caps and looked very well. An artist could have made some good pictures by copying the old folks as they sat out in the sun or gathered round the tables for meals. The building was old and shabby, but somehow it looked appropriate as the home of these old folks. In my youthful days it was usual to call the Workhouse the Bastile. Beyond the Bull's Head (which was then thatched, I think) there were some brick cottages, and then, extending ap the street towards the National School, were some whitewashed cottages, some of them thatched. The houses which replaced them are good houses, but they can never look half so good and picturesque as the thatched ones did.

Williamson-square was built, and was a snug place to live in and considered quite respectable. The people who built what are now considered rookeries, in their day were regarded as philanthropists, who built snug and cheap and very desirable little houses for the working-classes. And if we could put back the gardens and open spaces which then existed I don't know but that we might not so regard them yet. There was no tall spire to look at in those days. The church had a square tower and looked much better and more modest than the present one. I would rather see a church with a tower that belongs to it than see .a building with a spire three times too big. Church-street used to have its lively time at the holding of the Church-street Fair. This annual event brought great crowds of all sorts of desirables and undesirables. It was discontinued when I was a child and I cannot say very much about it.

div.head: STOMACH TROUBLES DUE
div.p: STOMACH TROUBLES DUE
TO ACIDITY.
SO SAYS EMINENT SPECIALIST.

So-called stomach troubles, such as indigestion, wind, stomach-ache and inability to retain food instead of indicating that the stomach is out of order are in nine cases out of ten simply evidence that fermentation is taking place in the food contents of the stomach, causing the formation of gas and acids. Wind distends the stomach, and causes that full, oppressive feeling sometimes known as heartburn, while the acid irritates and inflames the delicate lining of the s'omach. The stomach, however, is not at fault. The trouble lies entirely in the fermer.ting food. Such fermentation is unnatural, and acid formation is not only unnatural, but may involve the most serious conscquences if not prevented. To prevent or stop fermentation of the food contents of the stomach and to neutralise the acid, and render it bland and harm- less, half a teaspoonful of bisurated magnesia,prohably the beet and most effective antacid known, should be taken in a quarter of a glass of hot or cold water immediately after eating, or whenever wind or acidity is felt. This stops the fermentation, and neutralises the acidity in a few moments. Fermentation, wind and acidity are dangerous and unnecessary. Stop or prevent them by the use of a proper antacid, such as bisurated magnesia, which can be obtained from any chemist, and thus enable the stomach to do its work properly without being hindered by poisonous gas and dangerous acids.—M.F.P.

div.head: IS IT A NIGHTINGALE?
div.p: IS IT A NIGHTINGALE?

A nightingale is reported to have been heard in Pendlebury-lane, or Lord Crawford's Haigh Castle, near Wigan. It is, of course, a very unusual thing for a nightingale to stray so far North on the Trent, but five years ago the same locality had a similar visitant, the bird charming the whole neighbourhood by its song nightly for a week or more.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, June 14, 1913.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, June 14, 1913.
GRAPPENHALL AND ITS CHURCH.
Chaste Workmar ship of Seven Centuries Ago That Still Wins Admiration.

div.head: WILLIAM BOYDELL, CRUSADER.
div.p: WILLIAM BOYDELL, CRUSADER.
BY MR. ARTH

THE BOYDELL CHAPEL. To the Norman Church at Grappenhall, a very interesting addition was made in the year 1334. This was the Boydell Chapel, built on the south side, and of which some valuable portions remain. TO CELEBRATE MASS FOR EVER.

To reveal the origin of the chapel I must take you back again into the realm of charters and show you William Boydell arranging for a chaplain to celebrate mass for over for the repose of his soul. The document is too interesting to be omitted : Be it known to all men that I, Wm. Boydell the younger, have covenanted to find one honest chaplain to celebrate divine mysteries for ever for the soul of Wm. Boydell, my father, the soul of Nicolaa, my mother, and the souls of the faithful dead in the Chapel of Gropenhsle, built by the said lord William, my father. Ard for the better security of this matter, I William Boyden, junior, have sworn on the Holy Cross, in the Collegiate Church of St. John in Chester, in the preset ce of the aforesaid William, my father, William of Mulneton, Robert de Hawardyn, and Henry, Clerk, given at Chester, 19 January, 1334. This shows the Chapel as having been built by William Boydell the elder and endowed by William the younger. The building was placed against the south wall and would have a separate entrance.

div.head: R MOUNFIELD.
div.p: R MOUNFIELD.

saint would be in the minds of the eccles- iastics of the twelfth century by reason of a discussion as to the custody of his remains. It is said that in A. D. 958 Archbishop Odo discovered his bones in a neglected condition at Ripon and carried them to Canterbury, leaving as many bones behind as would work sufficient miracles for the Northerners. Modern Christians don't give themselves anxiety as to the comfort of the bones of the saints, but at that period the possession of relics was a matter of importance, and the fact that Wilfrid's fragments went to Canter- bury argued for the superiority of that city over York.

div.head: ORIENTATION.
div.p: ORIENTATION.

The dedication of a church usually affected its orientation. Perhaps I had better put this in simpler terms. Churches were always built with the altar to the east, but they were not placed due east and west as by a compass. The centre line of the church was arranged so as to point to that spot on the horizon on which the sun rose on the festival of the patron saint. Such has been the usual belief, but it is only right that I should say that the subject of variations in orientation presents many difficulties, and some good antiquarians have given up hopes of a solution. The orientation of Grappenhall fits a day
Photograph by

in April and August. It may, therefore, have been intended to suit St. Wilfrid's birth- day in August or the removal of his bones to Canterbury, which took place in April. REBUILDING IN THE 16TH CENTURY. The Norman Church which I have described remained until the beginning of the sixteenth century. Then came an almost entire rebuilding. The date A.D. 1539, carved upon one of the pillars, is supposed to record the completion of this large task. The builder placed the north pillars upon the foundation of the old wall and built out a north aisle. The south wall was treated in the way I have described, the pillars and arches being inserted in it, and the top portion with its gurgoyles and corbel table being left. The massive tower rose at the west end, as we see it now, save that it once had eight pinnacles. On the string course which encircles it is a large face probably that of a cat. Possibly, it is a coat of arms, and it has been suggested that it represents a pun on the name Caterich, a familiar name and property in the parish. Since 1539, various changes have occurred. The Boydell Chapel lost its identity by the lengthening of the east aisle. The walls of the nave have been raised and clerestory windows inserted, and a large vestry has been built in which is placed the old east window of the church. THE BELLS.
The tower has six bells, five of which are dated 1700 and one 1718. These are the inscriptions : R.S. THO SUTTON THO MERREY C.W. 1718.
JOHN BOARDMAN, Rector, 1700. HENRICUS BAGLEY, noes ficit 1700. HENRICUS BAGLEY, of Ecton, neare Northampton, made mee, 1700.
THOMAS BLACKBURNE and THOMAS SVTTON, Chvrchwardens, 1700. I to the Chvrch the living call, And to the grave doe summon all. THE YEW TREE.
Other features might detain us if there were time. The stocks are a well-preserved relic, and there is the fine sundial dated 1747 with its motto " Pulvis et umbra sumus."

But these antiquities are mere striplings in comparison to the yew tree under whose shade they stand. There would be material for quite a small lecture in this rugged yet kindly giant were there but time to give it. The age of many churchyard yews is beyond all calculation. Wordsworth reminds us that these trees furnished " . . weapons for bands That drew their souding bows at Agincourt, Perhaps at earlier Crecy or Poictiers." This is no poetic exaggeration, for the life of an ordinary yew is 400 years, and one still lives at Parley Dale which experts declare to have weathered milleniums.

It is very possible that the Grappenhall yew may have given shelter to the William Boydell who rode away in chain armour to fight the Saracens in the stirring days of the 13th century. C3llectors of epitaphs may increase their stock from the churchyard, but this is another of the smaller interests which I must leave untouched.

Seeing Grappenhall, as we do, upon a fair spring day, you will agree that it is a place to linger in and a place to be loved. Provid- ence has surely kept it as a restorative for jaded nerves; a place where Gray might have written his "Elegy," or Wordsworth his "Yew Trees." May quietness prevail, may its sleeping warrior long rest undisturbed by the hooting of motor horns and undistressed by the smell of petrol. And may its "yew tree's shade" and pleasing antiquities be long preserved to delight other generations as they delight us this afternoon.
• • ^ * •-• • • Burrell.

div.head: WILLIAM BOYDELL'S EFFIGY
div.p: WILLIAM BOYDELL'S EFFIGY

But when the building was enlarged in the sixteenth century the Chapel was merged in the aisle. Sixty years ago the aisle was extended eastwards and by this process the east wall of the Chapel was removed. It is for us, therefore, to see how much is left of the ancient Boyden Chapel after this drastic mutilation.

Though the relics are few, every antiquary would agree that they are very valuable. First, there is the window, the second from the east end of the aisle. This is a good and characteristic piece of fourteenth century architecture.

BEAUTIFUL ANCIENT GLASS. Very happily, too, we have some of the ancient glass. The most beautiful is that which represents, under canopies,the Apostle Peter with keys; James, represented as a pilgrim with a palmer's staff and escalloped hat; Barnabas, with a flaying knife and his skin in his hand, in token that he had been flayed : and Thomas and Philip. Mary Magdalene, with her ointment, and John the Baptist fill large places in this interesting window.

It was usual to represent the Apostle I James as a pilgrim. From the fact that ' pilgrims bore a palm branch they were called palmers, and they are usually shown with a scallop shell upon the hat. Both the palmer's staff and a hat adorned with a shell appear in this picture of James. But the best example of the glass with which the medieval builders adorned their churches is preseryed in the door of the organ screen. The figure is that of a female saint, with clasped hands, ermine dress, and a halo. There is no emblem to give identity. Tbe colours are golden yellow and brown. This relic, the chaste workmanship of seven centuries ago, gives us much room for thought and admiration. _ _ _ _ _
- - It is said that before the Reformation Grappenhall was famous for its glass, but these are the only fragments that are left. PRE-REFORMATION RELICS.

Other pre-Reformation relics have a modest place under the shadow of the organ, and are often missed by the casual visitor. Built into the wall are a piscina and credence table. Of course, this is not their true place. They would originally occupy a position near to the altar, or were possibly in the Boydell Chapel. The piscina, I may explain, was a sacred _ _ . . .

lavatory of the Church. In it the priest washed the altar vessels and washed his hands after the observance of the Mass. It was pierced to allow the water to drain through the wall of the Church. The credence was a small projecting table which held the emblems. The old Church would have also before the Reformation a stoup for holy water, but this has not survived. THE EFFIGY OF WILLIAM BOYDELL. We must now study a famous relic which once rested in the Boydell Chapel, and after a sojourn in the Warrington Museum, and a process of restoration, lies within the altar rails. The effigy is that of William Fitzwilliam Boydell, Crusader and lord of Grappenhall six and a half centuries ago. He is represented as a warrior who rgsts after his battles. He is in chain armour and his head rests upon a helm. This was the William Boydell who married Alice of Dutton, and I who died in 1272. It is from the crossed legs of the figure that we assume that he took part in the Crusades. The heroes who had been once to Palestine to fight the Saracens were represented with legs crossed at the ankles. Those who had been twice were shown with legs crossed below the knees, and those who had made three expeditions were shown crossed above the knees. But this can hardly be taken as a proof, for it is sometimes found that a vow to go or a very pious wish to go was commemorated after death by the crossing of the legs. Some antiquarians regard the leg-crossing as a mere fashion in effigies, but most people would conclude that a straining of the human figure so drastic as this must have had some significance. It does seem as though the Boydells had something to do with the Holy Wars, for later on they placed a Saracen's Head upon their crest. The familiar "Saracen's Head" at IWilderspool, it may be said in parenthesis, is an echo of the days when the nobles went out to try to deliver Palestine out of the hands of the Turk. DEDICATED TO ST. WILFRID.
I am forgetting to mention that the Church is dedicated to St. Wilfrid. This Northern
