WHEN THE CANARY DRESSES UP. I like to watch a canary at its toilet. It is quite a little entertainment. Of course, it is pretty much the same with any bird, but the canary is nearest to us and easiest to observe.

I notice that birds are very fastidious about their dress and are most careful to keep themselves tidy. There are no varieties in dress, of course, but the dress nature gives to them is arranged with splendid care. As a rule the gentlemen birds are more gay in their covering than the ladies, but they spend less time upon their toilet.

Suppose we watch the canary after its bath. Notice how each feather is cleaned, pulled and looked over, and watch how all the loose ones are taken out and dropped. All this is done by the bill, for a bird's neck is so flexible that it can be turned in all directions. For the head itself it will be noticed that the canary uses its foot. With it he combs his hair first on one side, then on the other scratching very fast as though to get all tangles out. Next comes an interesting process, which perhaps few people have noticed. It is not commonly known that a bird has a supply of hair oil. Complexion powders are not known in the bird world, but every bird, male and female, carries its own supply of hair oil.
They have a little pouch or sack on the back near the tail, and squeeze out the oil with the beak just as we should press a rubber bulb.

After the oil is loosened the bird lays it on the back between the wings and rubs her head against it, turning her neck in all direc- tions until every feather in her head is straight and shining. Some birds wear their hair done up high on their head, others push it out to a point as though trying to form a Chinaman's queue. Others comb it down plain and smooth. I need not say any more. The next time your canary takes a bath just watch the little programme for yourself.

div.head: LITERARY GLEANINGS.
div.p: LITERARY GLEANINGS.
A FARMER'S JOKE.

A Portland (Dorset) dairy farmer who had friction with the Sanitary Committee about cowshed regulations, which the farmers con- sider unreasonable, played an amusing joke on the members of the committee. The sanitary inspector issued notices of an intended inspec- tion for Saturday. The farmer made pre- parations for the visit by spreading linoleum over the floor of his cowhouse, displaying hearthrugs in convenient positions, hanging the walls with pictures, a mirror, and a motto 'Until we meet again," and furnish- ing the interior with chairs and a harmonium

-When the committee called he gravely asked them to wipe their feet on the doormat and explained that the harmonium was for the cow to play while the calf danced. The committee were so tickled that after vainly trying to hide their amusement, they had to retire. When they had gone the farmer informed his friends that they were so taken up with the decorations that they had for- gotten to examine the drains or to fulfil any of the objects of the inspection.

div.head: CLERGYMAN'S STORIES.
div.p: A CLERGYMAN'S STORIES.

The Rev. John M. Elvy,who has had forty years' connection with the Cathedral Church of Manchester, has just published a sixpenny brochure, in which, in the tersest of para- graphs, he recalls incidents of interest and relates anecdotes. Speaking of chistenings he says: "One day an urchin of about two years old was brought to me. When I attempted to take him, he was frightened and struggled violently. I asked the woman who brought him to hold him. She placed him over the font, and said by way of encouragement, Look at the pretty fish!' This is the best instance I have known of a pious fraud." A tale of a curious marriage follows

"A man put in the banns for a certain lady, and they were called out next Sunday. In the course of the week he came again, and said, You may take out those banns: I have found someone I like better.' The new lady's name was substituted, and the banns were published afresh the next Sunday. During the week after he came once more, and said, 'l'll go back to the old 'un; new 'un too skittish.' The ' old 'un ' was still willing to have him, and they were married. Whether they lived happily ever after has not been revealed."

A NEW STORY OF CECIL RHODES I AND THE KAISER. A new story of Cecil Rhodes has just crept into print. When Rhodes was visiting the Kaiser—l think it was in Berlin, and the morning that the former was departing—the Emperor said to him : "Rhodes, I wish you had been born a German." " ? " said Rhodes. "In order that I might make you my Foreign Minister," was the flattering reply. Rhodes pondered for a moment, and then said: "And I wish your Majesty had been born an Englishman." "Do you," said the Kaiser, "And why, may I ask?" "In order that I might make you my business manager," said the astute South African, who was able to find out the weak spot in au Emperor as easily as to tickle the fancy of a Hebrew speculator.

ANOTHER PARISH CLERK STORY. The Rev. H. P. Ditchfield tells in the June "Treasury" some stories about parish clerks. His own little church at Barkham was many years ago the scene of a deplorable episode. It was not unknown that the clerk on occa- sions used to patronise the village inn, which was kept by a parish worthy, Mrs. Collyer. One Sunday afternoon, when the weather was warm and the sermon long, the clerk slept and dreamed. He imagined himself the centre of an admiring company at the village inn. Hence, when the sermon was ended and the ascription said, and he was expected to utter a loud and sonorous "Amen," he startled the congregation by shouting, "Fill 'em again, Mrs. Collyer ; fill 'em again."

div.head: LITTLE THINGS.
div.p: LITTLE THINGS.

`Tis little things that matter, so they say. 'Tis little cares that harass life away, And little worries trace On every anxious face Those tiresome little wrinkes, day by day. 'Tis little things that matter, ah I I know Man needs unfailing patience here below. But try for wisdom's sake The best of life to make, And do not let small trials vex you so. But ever cherish pleasant little things, A little smile Love's radiance often brings. A little word and deed, Just suited to the need, Round Mem'ry's inner sanctuary clings.
MILITANT DAMAGE. JUDGMENT AGAINST W.S.P.U. FOR WINDOW-BREAKING.

The first of the actions brought by West End of London fira,s against leaders (past and present) of the Women's Social and Political Union, and also against the members of the Union, fur damage done in the window-breaking raid on March 1 last year ended on Saturday in a vet diet and judgment for £364 against all the defendants. On behalf of the members of the Union a stay of execution was granted so that they might take the case to the Court of Appeal. The Judge stated that the judgment was against those belonging to the Union at the date of the raid.— , nouneel for the plaintiffs, in his address to the jury, I had declared if the plaintiffs succeeded the Union would also be held liable for the huge amounts lost in more recent destruction of property, and the action would probably be "the first nail driven into the coffin" of the campaign and outrage.

div.head: TOWN CLERK'S DEATH ON DAUGHTER'S WEDDING DAY.
div.p: TOWN CLERK'S DEATH ON DAUGHTER'S WEDDING DAY.

The death occurred early on Tuesday, of Mr. Dan Sutcliffe, the Town Clerk of Todmorden, aged 70 years. A peculiarly sad feature of the bereavement is the fact that the same afternoon his daughter, Miss Frances Heena, was to have been married. All arrangements had been completed for the ceremony, which, of course, had to be postponed. Mr. Sutcliffe was a Noncon- formist, and identified himself with many of the religious organisrtions Cf the borough. He was also one of the oldest members of the Order of Rechabites in the district.

div.head: THREE TIMES I
div.p: THREE TIMES I

In his undergraduate days Professor Ramsay was a notable athlete, and on one occasion, when distributing prizes in the gymnasium of the Glasgow University, took occasion to pass some scathing remarks on the softness of the present generation, He illuminated his criticisms from Roman history.
"Gentlemen," cried the professor of humanity, "you should do as the ancient Romans. The youths of Rome used to gather on the banks of the Tiber every morning and swim three times across the river."
Voice from his audience: "What did they do about their clothes ? "

CURLY HEAD (four year old). " Very good he has been all morning," Said Curly Head's mother one day, As she looked at the dear little fellow On the nursery hearthrug at play, "See, here is a rosy cheeked apple, But don't eat it all alone, Go and offer half to a playmate Who hasn't got one of his own. Just half an hour after she asked him (For mothers never forget), "Well, how did you like your apple, And who did you share it with, pet," "Well I went to my little pussy, And whispered into her ear, I've got such a pretty red apple, So wouldn't you like half of it dear," "I'm glad that you tried,"said his mother, "To do just what you were told, But why did you go to pussy? You queer little two-year-old." Then two-year-old looked up bravely, Tho's his dear baby face was red, Came, "Pussies don't ever eat apples, And I wanted it all," he said.

BY WALTER WOOD.

r When the spy came in from the robbers' stronghold and demanded urgent audience of Major Lotman, of the Intelligence Department, Sergeant Raffin, who was drinking Soudan beer and reflecting unfavourably on the country and its brew, emptied his canteen on to the sand of the desert and remarked: "I'm not the lunatic you think for throwin' that rank marissa away. When a spy runs in like this, an' the chief stops stokin' to jaw with him, there's somethin' at the back of it. There's a bit of a durbar goin' on now—spy an' chief. Soon there'll be a scrap, an' the man whose brains are addled by marissa will get left, an' don't you forget it. Yes, sir." Sergeant Raffin hurried away in obedience to the call, which was from Major Durran,who had just dismissed the spy. Raffin had been attached to the Intelligence Department because he had shewn a wonderful power of understanding and dealing with the natives. He had been heard to say that there were two good men in Egypt, and that Durran was the other. "What sort of camels are those which were brought into the market-place this morning?" asked Durrnn.

smiled, and Mahn hated him atresn tor it. "You mean birds," he corrected, scornfully. "Ducks aren't birds, they're fowls." Durran dismounted and had a few curt words with the Mndir. to whom, as the nrincinal person in the place anu therelore one wno was not without an interest in the descent of the thieves, he made certain explanations and gave "arious instructinns. Then he went straight to the palace, taking with him the captain of the corps and Raffin and two men, also picks and shovels. , Under his chief's ettidance Raffia and the men laboured with pick and shovel until their very bones ached. But Raffin never groaned. So long as the eye of Durran was upon him he would have died rather than shew signs of being overcome. "Now," said Durran, whcri the work was done and the men gone, "you see what has happened? '4l's mined a spot in this building which is to on the main point of attack by the robbers. As a last extremity the mine will be fired—and you will fire it." "Yes, sir," said Baffin without enthusiasm. This so far as he could tell, meant that he would be out of the fighting; and fighting was as necessary to him as beer. "Here," continued Durran, "is a recess. You will stay in it, and when you get the order you will light this fuse. The dynamite will do the rest. Now remember my orders—you are to stay here without leaving until you get permission. You will fire the cartridges when I order you; but if I should not return or send within a reasonable time, you will use your own judgment. You understand?" "Yes, sir," answered Raffia. Durran and the captain walked off, and the sergeant took his station in the recess. There was a hole in the wall through which he could see what was happening, and what he saw was a thing which puzzled him. The whole of the camels were driven into an enclosure belonging to the Mudir, and the men, dismounted, were being hurried into huts so as to be out of sight. Raffin also saw that the captured thief had escaped, unseen for as he ran over the desert towards a neighbouring rocky hill he was neither pursued nor fired at. Raffin stamped in his wrath and disappointment, intt his orders were positive, and he could not Nor dare he fire the loaded rifle which was standing near him. He was _ still in an agony of fury and appre- %.ansion when he saw Durran and the spy walk out across the path by which the robber had escaped. The thief had made for the neighbour- ing hills. Thither also went Durran and his companion. Baffin rubbed his eyes. "Well! Of all the extryordinary performances!" he said. "If I didn't know that that was the major I should suppose he was a pal of the thieves. Talk about a man of mysteries! What's his game ? " Tenacious to his principle of personally recon- noitring any position in which he was specially interested, Durran was going to ascertain the strength and disposition of the robbers. His information told him that they were in the hills, waiting for the Midnight descent on the treasure. Ho believed that as he had made a detour into the town they did not know of his presence with a little British force; but he was unaware of the captured thief's escape—no one had had the courage to tell him—and was ignorant of the fact that that enterprising person was already warning Abu Lulah that his plan was hopeless of execu- tion for the present. Abu Lulah knew when luck was against him; he was also very careful of his own skin, and recollected that Durran 'Ffinikt,ahi was under promise to hang him on sight when caught. Abu therefore bowed to circumstances and ordered his band to make all speed home. But Abu Lulah was also avaricious. It occurred to his active mind that if his followers went home and feigned to resume their agricultural pursuits, of which they made violent pretence when danger threatened and work was vcry slack, Durran would withdraw his force. Furthermore, the thought suggested itself that it was foolish to divide treasure amongst many when one man alone—and that man himself—could use it to such undoubted advantage. Therefore he decided to have it all for his own use. "I will stay here till the English have gone," he said, "then I will return and be you back." The thieves, more anxious to escape than they were to credit the good faith of their leader, were making ready to depart when Durran's spy, who had been sent forward to learn what he could—an errand which he performed so un- willingly that Durran was forced to send him at the pistol-point—rejoined the band, with a smile on his face and fear in his heart. He had a plausible tale to tell, but the words died in his throat when Abu Lulah confronted him with the robber who was still believed to be a prisoner with the British. "We are pressed for time and cannot:listen," said Abu Lulah, with marked politeness. Than he whirled his sword round and struck the spy's head from his shoulders. "Now," he added, with a grim smile, "if any other man has anything to say just now, let him come forward. I will promise him the same sort of hearing. No? Well, then, go back that way." Ile swept an arm in a semi-circle, and Om swift-moving deseit men obeyed. Durran saw them scrambling over the hilly ground and making for a rendezvous five miles distant, where their camels an 1 horses were waiting to receive them. It was now dark, but the young moon gave light enough for seeing, and he observed that Abu Lulah did not go with his people but started boldly alone for the deserted palace. "Raffin will watch you, my beauty," murmured Durran, and with an easy mind he also hurried back. Quickly and silently he ordered the camels out again saddled up, and led the march round by the foot of the hills ta the camp of Abu Lulah. Here, in the shadow of the rocks, he dismounted his men and formed them into a little square, with the camels in the middle. That was an arrangement useful for emergency. "As soon as I give the:order," he said, in a low voice, "fire a single volley at a hundred yards, then use the sword. This work should be done without a man of you being hurt." The robbers were hurrying from the hill and spreading out on the plain towards their camp, laughing and chattering. Hands were on bridles and feet were in stirrups, when there was a loud, clear word of command from an unseen man. :ifty rifles, the flashes of which pitted the darkness at the foot of the hills, were followed by the wild cheers of as many voices, and after 'hat there came the cries of wounded men and the thud and clang of swords. The swoop was the work of a long minute. At the end of that time every robber who had not been killed or maimed was captured, every horse and camel which had not stampeded was secured. Durran scooped his captives up and carried them into the town. Meanwhile Abu Lulah had hastened to the palace. Time pressed, and he wanted to get his work done. Frequent visits had made him familiar with the hiding-place of the treasure, and he went straight to the spot, groping in the darkness. His hands as much as his eyes told him that .the ground had been disturbed, and he cursed beneath his breath. He paused and stood up, and looked about him, but saw no one and nothing. Bailin watched him in a sort of dream. Here was a thief, almost under his .very nose, palpably thieving; and yet, by virtue of his orders from Durran, he dare not even pounce upon and capture him. His duty was definite—to stay in his recess: until he was authorised to leave it. Raffin passed a dry hand across a drier mouth; but in that memorable moment he did not even think of thirst or beer. The rattle of rifle-fire and the cries of com- batants came over the plain from the hills. Abu Lulah ,understood all; so did Sergeant Baffin. "The English are over there! " exclaimed the robber, in a language—his own—which Baffin did not understand. "The major's bagged 'em!" murmured the sergeant. He wanted to shout "Hooray!" and fall on the robber; but he clenched his teeth and clutched his rifle instead. The robber bent down on his hands and knees and began to scratch away the loose earth like a terrier. Baffin felt a sudden chilling of the blood. He was a brave man; but he knew that dynamite cartridges were lying close to the robber's fingers, and that dynamite cartridges have a disastrows habit. of ,exulodimi on slight orovoca-

Raffin, who was cautious and methodical, said: "All sorts, sir," and produced a little note- book, from which he read: "At 4.30 a.m. this mornin' a sheik arrived with fifty transport camils an' seventy trotters. The trotters are for a chief, an' the sheik's haltin"ere to fake 'em up, so that he can deliver 'em in good condition."

"Go and tell the sheik that I will be with him in an hour," said Durran. "Have fifty of the best camels ready for me to see. I want them for three days, either to hire or buy; but, any- way, I mean to have them. Make that point clear. The interpreter will go with you." Itaffin took the interpreter with him to the market-place, where the camels were pic- turesquely huddled, and by virtue of his authority from Durran went straight to the heart of things. "Allah be with your," began the:sheik, througb the interpreter. "Same to him," responded Raffin. "Now then, let's cut the corner off compliments an' get to biz. What price the pick of these cam us P" "He says they are not for sale," explained the Interpreter, "and tint they belong to a high and mighty person in the country."

"bli, -no, they don't," -said Raffin. "They belong to a higher and mightier, an' that's Durran bintbashi, an' you'd better tell him so. They're wanted in the interests of the British Army, an' if he doesn't care to sell 'em he can let 'em out on loan; an' if he doesn't either sell or loan wo shall take'em, that's all. Tell him to take his choice, an' to buck up about it. Durran binahashi hasn't any time to waste on people like him."

The interpreter made known the situation. At the end of his explanation it had been agreed that the camels should be loaned to Major Durran for temporary British military purposes at so much per head. Further explanation was made to the sheik, of which the purport was not disclosed to Raffia by the interpreter, who had received certain secret instructions from the major. _

When Durran reached the market-place the chosen camels were awaiting his inspection. Two small, well-bred beasts, the pick of the steeds, were standing a little apart from the rest. These had been selected by Baffin for himself and his superior officer. Meanwhile Durran had chosen fifty men to form a camel corps for a swoop on a band of robbers from a neighbouring province. With one exeeption,every man was a good camel rider, as Darran's ordinary force included numerous members of a disbanded camel corps. The exception was Sergeant Rallin ; but he had had twelve years in the saddle in India, and in many ways the commanding officer regarded him as necessary to the success of this peculiar under- taking. The spy, who had come in, had been living with the robbers as one of them, and had furnished the intelligence that Abu Lulah, the leader of the band, had organised a descent on a town fifty miles away, whore some compact treasure was buried in the vaults of a forsaken palace. Precious stones were thole in plenty, but the hiding-place was so cunning that no outsider was supposed to know of it. Duir n knew—but Durran knew everything. He had kept an eye on this rich store for use when Government supplies ran short, and the news that it was to be raided and stolen troubled him as much as if the thieves had carried off his personal possessions. The further information that the robbers meant to put to the sword every man who resisted disturbed him but little. After all, that was part of the game which he was always playing, and men, being cheap, were easily replaced. _

What angered Durran most soroly at the outect was his unpromising situation. He was away from a base, with only two or three companies of infantry and no means of rapid locomotion. There was no railway, transit by the Nile was hopeless. The only way to get his troops to the threatened spot was on their legs. Given time and opportunity they could have accomplished this; but even Durran, who could do most things, could not march infantry fifty miles across a desert in a day, and that was needful if he meant to thwart the threatened onslaught. The robbers had planned their swoop for mid- night following that day, and Durran knew from experience that their chief was a remarkably good timekeeper. He solved the problem:l:when he had almost determined to endure the bitterness of a rare failure. He recollected that early in the morning a number of camels had been brought into the town, and were still there. It was the work of a minute for his resourceful brain to map out the scheme of a scratch camel corps, and, flying light, cut across the desert to the rendezvous, and when the thieves arrived, be in readiness to trap them. He had chosen his men while Sergeant Raffin had selected the camels, and now the corps was ready for a start. From the interpreter Durran learnt; another fact about the camels, a fact which interested him vastly, and which he meant to use to his own advantage in his own peculiar.way. With rations, water, forage, rifles, and ammunition the men went into the desert. Each rode a camel, and half-a-dozen spare brutes were taken to replace casualties and carry a few picks and shovels, the purpose of which was known to Durran alone.

The camel corps started at a strong pace, and Durran, who never spared either himself or anybody else, kept it up. He was the guide as well as the commander of the expedition. The spy and the interpreter went with him. Already the interpreter was being awkwardly questioned by Raffin, in whose mind a suspicion was grow- ing that there was some hidden meaning in a smile which he saw from time to time on the Egyptian's face. He reeaMed certain signs that had passed between the interpreter and the sheik, signs which he had observed without understand- ing. He was drowsily dwelling on them as the corps stumbled over a low, rocky black hill, when he saw a movement in some long grass near him. He bent down from his knifoboard saddle and dragged out a native who was in hiding. Raffin hauled him along to Durran, who learnt that he was a late member of the band of robbers who was now establishing a sound business of his own by attacking small caravans. _ .

The interpreter sugg-ested instant execution on the ground of expediency. "rut him on a spare camel," ordered Durran, "and, as he's your catch, Baffin, I shall make you responsible for him. I daresay I shall be able to use him later on. The man can be hanged or shot easily enough, if need be, but he can't:so conveniently be brought back to life." For a brief space the corps slept; then the roveillo was sounded and the camels resumed their trot They were kept at a merciless pace, but they had been well used beforehand, and were perfectly fit for work. In the end Durran finished his journey with half-a-dozen camels fewer that when ho started, hut amongst hie men there was not a single casualty. "Now," said the interpreter to Raffin, still smiling, "you watch and see Durran kill two ducks with one brick." Qnce more he

Com -.Dasn the beast! " Ile muttered, crouching in his recess. "Why can't he go and burrow somewhere else?"

Abu Lulah gave a cry of joy and leaped into the moonlight. He held a box in his hand. Raffin saw him clearly. The robber with eager fingers opened the box. Then he gave a savage shout, for the box was empty. Again Raffin rubbed his eyes. When they were re-nnened he saw that Abu Lulah was back at In. burrowing. It wad now uti is gr,ol. 1,... plot, tion assailed Raffin—the temptation to disobey Durrans orders—or rather interpret them to his own liking, and to fire the fuse. Sergeant Raffin was a man of action and resource, He was also ambitious, and saw an opportunity for promotion. The robber was over the mine the sergeant controlled the discharge. "Dash " he muttered, "I could easily say it was accidental !" He writhed in his hiding- place, and strove to put aside the craving which possessed him. Raffin was still the owner of a conscience, for he had been brought up in a narrow-minded family, and the precepts of his early life rose strong within him. "Yield not to temptation, for yieldin' is sin," he -murmured; "but fightin' isn't Sunday schoolin'. Hang it, I'll do it ! "

He furtively struck a match and fired the fuse. Then he waited to take his chance, for on one point of his orders he was adamant—he would not leave his recess without permission. At last the fuse burnt out, and the crash of the explosion shook the palace. Raffin was hurled away, and when he picked himself up he was helmctless and in rags. Durran's cold voice shocked him like an icy bath. "Have you seen Abu Lulah about here?" he asked.

Raiiin rubbed the dust from his eyes, and some of the dirt from his wrecked jacket. "He was squattin' there, sir," he answered, pointing to the smoking ruins. "What's left of him's in the ' debbriss '." _

A flash of merriment illumined Durran's cold, grey eyes. "The engineer's been nearly hoisted with his own petard," he said. "Yes, sir," agreed tho sergeant, "though I don't know it by that name. He's busted up, sir, if that's the same thing." Durran laughed. "Was it accident or design?" he asked. _ _

"Which does he want it to be ? " thought Raffin • but as the major was inscrutable he could not tell. He remained wise, and kept his mouth shut, feigning temporary deafness due to the explosion. "I couldn't have wished for anything more satisfactory," continued Durran, in an unusual glow of enthusiasm. "The man would have escaped—and I'm now spared the trouble of hanging him." The sergeant's deafness vanished. "That's the way I looked at it, sir," he said, "after a lot o' thinkin'. It's the practice of playing off your own .bat you're so fond of preachin'. Shall I tell off a party to collect him, sir ? " "I'll see to that," said Durran. "You go and get some fresh clothes, if you can find any." "I can do that, sir," Baffin assured him • and by commandeering a jacket from a private, to whose frank criticisms he turned a deaf ear, and a helmet from another, whose objections were crushed by an assertion that his features would look more becoming if crowned with a turban taken from a fallen robber, the sergeant had made himself presentable when Durran desired to see him before marching off. "You've been after Eracoits, I know," said Durran. "When you caught them as red-handed robbers, which was found the best way of dealing with them ? "

"There was nothing like a bit o' rope, sir— round the neck or across the back, accordin' to circumstances. The moral effect was marvellous. After that you could begin to talk to 'em. Some- times, if they were badly scared, you could let 'em off."

"Oh!" said Durran. Then he resolved that as Alm Lulah had been destroyed, the justice of the case would be met by giving one or two of the ringleaders a taste of Egyptian prisons and flogging one or two more before sending them about their business. As for the rest, they would be excellent material for absorbing into the Egyptian forces. The treasure, too, which he had quietly abstracted while the mine was being laid, would be of undoubted service. Raffle was still hovering near his superior when the captain came nil "What about the camels,— sir ? " asked the captain. "They are not in quite such good condition as if the sheik had delivered them himself," Durran answered; "but all things considered, they're in capital trim. We've only lost half-a-dozen, and the Mudir has got them a week sooner than if the Lizy brute had brought them." "I don't quite follow you, sir. Are the camel to be left here ? "

"Yes," said Durran, with twinkling eyes. "Don't you see through it?" "No sir." Well,. then, think it out." Sergeant Rani did see through it. lle with- drew silently, sought out the Egyptian inter- preter and took him aside. "Now, you blighted Gippy," he said. "I see daylight through your grin at last. Fancy Durran biinbashi doin' everybody in the eye like this! He commandeers these blighted camils an' actually delivers 'em to their own very owner! An' you knew it all the time!"

"Well," said the interpreter. "What of that? I had my orders to keep silent, and when Durran bimbashi orders, men obey." "I could kick myself silly for not eottonin' to the dodge," sr,id Raffin. "You might ha' told me, seem' as we did the interpretin' together in that stinkin' • market-place. Anything to drink goin' ? There are times when a man could drown himself in temperance." When the dismounted corps was trudging back across the desert Baffin caught sight of Durran, who was going stolidly along, with eyes bent to the sand and gravel. "Usual game---thinkin'," he muttered. "I wonder if he's plottin' to charge that Mudir feller so much a head for the prompt delivery o' them camils ? As for them diamonds an' rubies an' things he's bagged, I take it lie's got 'em in them innocent-lookin' pouches. By George! It's just the sort of ammunition I'd like to have served out to me! An' I'd take precious good care I didn't fire it off, either!" (THE END.]

div.head: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS.
div.p: WOMEN'S QUESTIONS.
Royalty Makes the Park and Row Resume Former Glories.

div.head: WOMAN'S DRESS CHAMPION.
div.p: A WOMAN'S DRESS CHAMPION.

London is rejoicing in one of the most brilliant seasons of recent times, and is now the hub of the social universe. The hig hotels are full to overflowing. These and the shops are crowded with foreigners and visitors from all parts of these Isles, and from every corner of the British Empire, while the streets are gay with well-dressed people, numbers of whom are frankly sightseers. The Park and Row have more than resumed their former glories, for the King and Princess Mary believe in the early morning con- stitutional on horseback, and this has induced many fashionable people to follow the Royal example. Just now, with the foliage on all sides at its freshest and crowded with fair equestriennes, Hyde Park is one of the sights of London. Princess Mary does not favour the cross- seat, and it must be admitted that tbe old-fashioned s'yle is better adapt, d t ) display the grace and figure of a gill r_r woman on horseback. There is, however, no doubt that the ride-a,tiide mode has come to stay, and is becoming iz.creasingly popular, both for the Park and for cross•country tiding. Many improve- ments have been made in the cut and style of the ride-astride coat, which is drawn into the figure by means of one seam on each side, and is, therefore, more shapely and becoming than its piedecessors

PBAISE FOR FEMININE FASHIONS. At last an eminent German professor has found the courage to say a good word for feminine fashions, ' which have been hitherto declared inimical to feminine health and be.ruty. As a nation we are in these times as subservient to our medical man as former genera- tions were to their spritual advisers, arrd are guided in our choice of foods, drinks, clothes and holiday resorts by the opinion of the family doctor. And yet ti ese opinions are as changeable as the weathervane, and those of one decade are in direct opposition to the prevailing convictions delivered with authority in the preceding ten years. It is quite comforting arid refreshing to be assured that high-heels----that have met with so much condemnation —keep the feet from contact with the damp earth, and protect the wearer from rheumatism and cola. That very low dresses are hralthy, the transparent blouse a protection from lung disease, and thin stockings and shoes most hygiene. Only cheap, badly cut shoes, meet with the Professor's disapproval. CHANGING FEMININE FASHIONS BENEFIT MEN. The corset, too, comes in for high praise. It distributes its presQure equally over the body, and, except when too tightly drawn, does not clush the waist, but preserves it fr2m being cut into by bands of dres-es, Sc. A good corset the Professor declares to he a Ihysical blessing, after which it is not surprising he should assert that fashions affect the feminine mind favourably and keep it and the brdy in health and equilibrium Indeed, fashions are a special source of strength], and the changes for which la mode ia usually reproached produce a healthy re-action on the mental faculties. They keep women young and fresh, and help the elasticity of the soul ; and, last hut not least, the 1 mter mortality of women may be directly traced to the beneficial influence of changing fashions. These have an animating and refreshing influence even on the men, who would be gainers if their modes were variable like those of womankind. The Professor hps arrived at the conclusion that if fashions were as detrimental to health and comfort as they are commonly believed to be, everybAy who followed them would by this time bo invalids or lunatics. ASCOT FASHIONS.

The midsummer month is here, the season in full swing, the Epsom meeting with Derby Day has come and gone, and Royal Ascot looms large in the world of fashion—for it is the great opportunity for the display ef all that is new and exquisitely beautiful in (Ire as. Designers reserve their cleverest and latest ereations for this event, which takea place when summer is in her pride, and the countryside glorious with golden sunshine, and glowing with the beauty of June's foliage and flowers. But the fickleness of the weather has to be taken into consideration, for the sun does not always shine on Ascot toilettes, and someth;ng more substantial than fairy-like creations of tulle, mousselilie, and gauze milt be prepared to meet the exigencies of our erratic climate. But there must be a novt I note, a subtle distinction in each ; then, after Ascot fashions settle down for a time, as at that event they reach their culminating point for the summer. Should the weather thr,.ugh June resemble that of the end of May, there will be a pre- ponderance of whi:e at Ascot, and marvellous indeed are the confections in tulle arid mousseline, embellished with wonderful embroideries, or decked with what appears to be a shower of crystals that have been prepared for many of fashion's leaders. ASCOT COAT.

Coats have become such an important part of a woman's wardrobe that the season's new designs are always awaited with some degree of expectation, and those confections prepared for Ascot arc regarded as deciding the style of this popular summer garment. This year the race cats appear to be considered of more importance than even the dresses, and never were they more gorgeous in colouring, or constructed of more perishable materials, but they serve to indicate the trend of fashion. One conspicuoua feature is ti e deep yoke of embroidery or brocade, in as many colours as Joseph's coat. The Medici collar, in a variety of shapes, is another feature, so is the fastening towards the left side. A novelty in c-ats constructed of maize-coloured crepe-de chine, is lined with black satin, and its appearance is decidedly effective. Draperies are fr«prently employed, and in some instances are suspended from the shoulders where they are kept in place by handsome buttons. This coat falls in wide loose folds at the back and i quite as full in front, but the material of which it is made is draphanous and very clinging, an that there is very little appearance of fulness. Yet it poin's to a greater width in styles that will be stall more pronounced in the coming autumn TABLE DECORATIONS.

Some fashionable women are decorating their tables with fruit instead cf flowers, the fr uit with its leaves being deposited upon the daintiest aid most costly squares of lace.Ot'y r hostesses are faithful to the lovely Nossoins of the seaFon, of which the lily of the valley is first favourite. Orchids, tulips, lilac, marguerites, and forget-me-nots, all make charming decorations, ;IA are very popular. The white rose is to be much used this srason, especially the kind called Frau Karl Druchlii. Coloured roses have for so long reigned snpreme that the revival cf the delicate white variety will be a welcome change.

div.head: ODDFELLOWS' MAIN.
div.p: ODDFELLOWS' MAIN.

The" William Savage" Lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows (Manchester Unity) held its first annual bowling main at the Norton Arms Hotel, Halton Castle, on Saturday. After a very pleasant drive through Moore, the party reached the Norton Arms at about 3 o'clock, and at once proceeded to business. The winner of the main was Bro. J. T. Ellison, with District Grand Master George Higham as runner-up. N.G. Peter Croft, Bro. W. E. Arnold, P.G. W. Paskyn, P.G. H. Stringer, and Bro. W. Broadhurst were also among the prize-winners. A consolation main was held for those knocked out in the first round and this was won by Past Grand Joseph Lowe. An excellent tea was provided by Host Birch. The return was made via Preston Brook.

div.head: WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB.
Vice-Presidents' Main.

This annual main again aroused great interest, and EOlllO capital games were witnessed, on Saturday, on the Liberal Club green. The prize-winners were as follows : 1, B. Webb ; 2, J. Graham; 3, W. Hayes ; 4, A. Gleave ; 5, J. Lea; 6, A. Gilbert; 7, R. Gallop ; 8, Jos. Wilkinson ; 9, E. A. Sanders ; 10, W. H. Dutton; 11, B. Foster; 12, G. H. Shaw ; 13, H. Greenieg ; 14, M. Tobin; 15, T. Millman ; and 16, T. Shaw. There was a record entry, and the games were played with a good spirit all through. When Mr. Thomas O'Brien stepped on to the green to referee for the final between B. Webb and J. Graham, a splendid reception was given to the contestants. B. Webb proved victorious by 13-7. An adjournment was then made to the new balcony leading on to the green from the billiard room, when / Councillor LINDLEY called upon Alr.Joseph Wilkinson, the chairman of the Bowling Committee, to present the prizes. div.head: WHAT IS WANTED.
div.p: WHAT IS WANTED.

Conversation in the railway carriage, says the "Manchester Guardian," had turned on necessary innovations in the calendar. Suddenly a stranger broke in on the discussion about a fixed Easter and said," What we need is eight quarter-days in the year." "We don't want any quarter-days," returned a passenger who presumably was behind with his rent. "Eight's what we want," said the stranger emphati- cally. " I'm in the furniture removing. For about six weeks in the year I've six times as much work as I can do, and for the rest of the year I've about a sixth uf the jobs I need to keep things going. Now if people 'd only get into the way of moving at the half-quarters you'd see this country grow prosperous."

COUNTY PALATINE OF CHESTER. VOTIOE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the next I_ll GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the COUNTY PALATINE OF CHESTER will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and fur the said County, on MONDAY, the 30th day o: June, 1913, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Foronoon, when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Petty Sessional Divisions of Broxton, Chester Castle, Dares- bury, Eddisbury, Nantwich, Runcorn, Winsford, and Wirral, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from the last-mentioned Divisions, will take place at such Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Chester District must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of the Court on MONDAY, the 30th day of .June, 1913, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon. THE COURT will be Adjourned to the COURT HOUSE, KNUTSFORD, on WEDNESDAY, the 2nd DAY OF JULY, 1913, at 10.30 o'clock in the Forenoon. The hearing of all Appeals arising within the Petty Sessional Divisions of Aitrincharu, Bucklow, Dukinfield, Middlewich, Sandbach, Congleton, Northwich, Prest- bury and Stockport, forming the Knutsford District, and the trials of all prisoners committed from such Divisions will take place at such Adjourned Sessions. The Grand and Petty Juries for the Knutsford Dis- trict must be in attendance at the Court House, Knots- ford, at the Court on WEDNESDAY, the 2nd day cf July, 1913, at 10.30 o'clock in the Forenoon. REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace of the County of Chester. Chester, 10th June, 1913.

COUNTY BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON.— PROCESSION OF SUNDAY SCHOLARS. JULY 4TH, 1913. VISIT OF HIS MAJESTY KING GEORGE V, JULY 7TH, 1913. By virtue of the powers given in that behalf by the Towns Police Clauses Act, 1347,and by Order of the Town Council, I DO HEREBY ORDER AND DIRECT that in order to prevent Accidents on the above occasions the following regulations be adopted, viz. :—On the occasion of the Public Procession of Sunday Scholars on Friday, the 4th July, 1913, no Cart, Carriage, Tram- car, Motor Car, Lurry, or other vehicle (excepting vehicles taking part in the procession, and mail carts), and no horse or other animal will be allowed to remain in or travel along or over any of the following streets between the hours of D a.m. and 12.30 p.m., viz. : Arpley-street, Kendrick-street, Barbauld-street, Legh-street, Bath-street, Museum-street, Bewsey-street, Palmyra-square, - Bold-street, Queen-street, Bridge-street, Rolleston-street, Buttermarket-street, Rylands-stree:, Cairo-street, Sankey-street, Church-street, Scotland-road, Edgeworth-street, Springfield-street, Friars'-gate, Suez-street, Froghall-lane, Tanners-lace, Golborne-street, Winmarleigh-street, Hanover-street, Winwick-street. Horsernarket-street. The above Order shall cease to apply to any of the above-named streets as soon as the procession in its proper order has passed along any such street. On the occasion of the Visit of His Majesty KING GEORGE V., on Monday, the 7th July, 1913, no Cart, Carriage, Tramcar' Motor Car, Lorry, or other Vehicle, and no horse or other animal will be allawed to enter, remain in, or travel along or over any of the following streets between the hours of One p.m. and 4.15 p.m., viz. :—Arpley-road, Bridge-street, Sankey-street, Liverpool-road. All streets leading into the above thoroughfares WILL BE CLOSED. BICYCLES and TRICYCLES are included in the term " vehicle "and must not be RIDDEN through any of the above-named streets during the hours specified. Any person wilfully acting in contravention of the above Order will be liable to a Penalty not exceeding Forty Shillings. Dated this 11th day of ;June, 1913. GEORGE WILLIAM JOSEPH, Mayor.

ON THE WING. Parliamentary Pigeon Race From Westminster to Yorkshire. The pigeon-flying contest between the Shipley division and the borough of Pontefract arranged by the respec- tive Liberal members, Mr. Percy Illingworth and Mr. , Handel Booth, took place on Saturday. when 180 birds— I 90 from each constituency—were liberated in New Palace Yard, Westminster, the Speaker acting as starter. The quickest Pontefract birds covered the distance in less than four hours, or at a speed of more than forty miles an hour. The honours fall to Pontefract, the official list of velocities being headed by ten Pontefrect birds, followed by six Shipley birds. The fastest l'outefract bird averaged 1.222 yards a minute and the fastest Shipley bird 1,073 yards a minute. The Shipley people attribute the wide differerme to the birds having been flown eastwards over country over which their birds bad not been trained, while the Pontefract birds had, and to their birds having to finish over a greater distance against a head wind. In London, at the start, the wind was south-west, but in Yorkshire, when the birds came along, it was blowing gustily from the north-west. West Lancashire Saturday Federation. The first race of the season organised by tnis club took place on Saturday to Neer Ferry, three boats entering—Comrade (la. Burthem), Nina (J. Whittaker) and Pastime (S. Measock). Warrington Win Their First Match Against Widnes. 'There was a large muster of spectators at the Corpora- tion baths on Thursday evening, when the Warrington Swimming Club opened their season, with a squadron race with Everton and a polo match with Widnes, in connection with the Liverpool and District Water Polo and Squadron League, second division. Tbe squadron teams were :—Warrington : N. Sisson, S. Roberts. T. Pemberton, J. Peers, E. Miller, C. Turner, S. Ince, J. Sanders. Everton : T. Cooper, E. Jones, J. Sails' T. Eaves, M. Jonas, F. Eleminshaw, J. Thomas, and R. E. Speers. Polo Teams.--Warrington : Jolley (goal), S. Ince and T. Pemberton (becks), J. Peers (halt-back), R. Pepper, H. Sisson and C. Turner (forwards). Widnes : Daintith (goal), Palmer arid Lloyd (backs), B. Fair- clough (half-back), Lavrick, Baker and Cheshire (forwards). The referee was Mr. W. Sutton (Warrington). THE RACE AND GAME. Warrington had no chance at all in the squadron race for Everton got away with the first two men and gradually increased their lead until Peers made a splendid effort and diminished the advantage to about half a length. However, the Everton men spurted for- ward and won by a length and a half. In the polo match Warrington proved that this season they are a team to be reckoned with their dribbling and defensive work being exceedingly good. They defended the shallow end in the first half and soon became aggressive. After three minutes play. Sisson received on the left and netted a beauty. Shortly afterwards the same player had hard lines, but Ince, obtaining possession in the middle of the bath, sent the leather clean through the sticks. Pepper added another just before the interval. Daintith, the IVidnes custodian, stopped many stinging shots, and was applauded for smart saves on nurnereus occasions, but the Warrington forwards were too much for him. If he bad had a good pair of backs in front of him, the adverse score would not have been so high. On resuming, Pepper sent the ball in end Daintith saved, but failed to clear properly, and Turner rushed in and recorded another goal for the locals. From a free throw for fouling, Pears secured and scored again for Warrington with a speedy shot. Close on time Lavrick scored for Widnes and the final came with the score :—Warrington, 5 goals ; Widnes, 1 goal. Warrington had the advantage both in pace and judgment,and if they maintain their form we have every trope of their finishing the season well.

WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT ASSOCIATION. Details of the draw appear on Page NOTES AND COMMENTS. Bull's Head Win Handsomely. High winds are never consistent with the beaming smile of a trundler, and it is no wonder that faces wore a somewhat downcast expression on the various greens last Saturday, when one comes to consider the boisterousness of the weather. But we have witnessed matches on worse days, and . the results last Saturday prove that the enthusiasm of local bowlers is equal to all circumstances and conditions. -- What a victory Lancashire gained over Derbyshire at Levenshuhne ! No one di,putes the fact that they have cause to crow over a win by 106 point,. There were only poor scores put up by the Derbyshire men, five of whom failed to record a double figure score and only two passed the 15 mark. G. Ball (jun.), the popular Cemetery player, had very little difficulty in putting paid to the account of P. Ellis, Derby, who only scored eight pints. At New Mills, however, the Lancastrians were having a very stiff time of it, for the Derbyshire men at home are " hot stuff." They were always a source of danger to their Lancashire opponents, and were only six shots short of winning the match. One noted the marked improvement since last year, when they did not register a single win. On Saturday all their players, with the exception of two, reached double figures, and Lancashire were fortunate in winning by four points, their aggregate win being one of 110 points. In this match Warrington was represented by two players, A. (Heave (Whitecross) and T Humphries (Rylands), both of whom won their games. When Derbyshire were 19 points ahead, Weave returned the winning card 21-17 against F. Dawson, Buxton, who played remarkably well and gave the Warringtonian very little latitude, Humphries was one of the last Lancashire men, arid after an exciting game beat C. Ratcliffe (Compstall) 21-19. In Warrington, the conditions for decent bowling were in no way the very best, but the games in the second round of the Warrington and District Associa- tion's competition were full of interest. The Senior Conservatives won by 34 points on the home and home matches with the Junior Conserva- tives. In the first match at the Bull's Head, the Church-street men gained a 74 point win over Fearn- head, and the return match will be played at Fearnhead this afternoon, At Sankey-street, the Seniors retired from the green with eleven scalps to their girdle, A. Scott being the only man on their side to lose. He fell to H. Bennett (Juniors), but he only lost his side two points, and the Seniors showed the fine majority of 91 to take with them to Orford-lane. In the majority of the games the Seniors recorded sweeping victories, H. Hughes, the captain, leading off with a brilliant 21-6 win against J. Gleave (Juniors) in 19 ends. J. Cooper (Juniors) had 14-5 at the 14th end against T. Horrabin, but here the Senior took the block and eventually peeled with 17 at the 25th end. The game now became intensely exciting, although Cooper tamed off a little in his play. Horrabin'e last run of nine evidently shattered him. However, he landed a single at the 29th end the game then being 20-18 favour of the Senior, who scored a beautiful single on the next length. D. Richardson (Seniors) had no small amount of difficulty in accounting for J. W. Monks, whom he beat by a couple of points in a 32 end game. It was even going all the way, the players peeling at 3,5, 10, and 17. At the 28th end Richardson led 19-17, but with two singles the Junior peeled again, only to fail to record any further points, the Sank( eestreet man gaining a couple of singles. H. Bennett, the only succeseful Junior, had to play exceedingly hard and consistently to gain the upper hand of A. Scott. The scores were even at 3,5, S, 11, and 14. At the 21st end Bennett got possession of the little 'un and ran his score to 18-14 only to be caught up again arid passed in three more ends. He peeled with a single on the next length, and, landing a double on the 29th end, won a two point victory. But the Juniors at Sankey-street and at home are two different teams. Once on the Orford-lane sward they soon showed their Seniors the art of bowling on a green, the peculiarities of which they so well know. Only three of the Seniors won their games, and their majority was reduced by 57. - The Juniors were inclined to be somewhat disheartened when J. Gleave, one of the first men on the green, was in arrears 4-10 at the 13th end in his game with J. H. Gittens, who was bowling well. However, Gleave had now some of the running and at the 26th end he led 15-14. The score was again equal at 16, but with a double and two singles Gleave gained a lead of 20-16 to win eventually by four points at the :_qth end. --- Bennett again won his game, beating J. Holland 21-18 in 29 ends. The former player had the best of matters all through, and at the 25th end he led by 20-14. Before the game was concluded, Holland managed to record 18 chalks to the delight of the senior followers, who had expected that Bennett would win by six or seven poiets. In the other games the seniors had very little chance but their majority was too much for the Orford- lane men who, although they made a plucky and determined stand, had to knuckle under to a 34 point defeat on both matches. -- Bull's Head go to Fearnhead to-day with a lead of 75 points, and although we do not doubt that the Farmer's Arms contingent will greatly diminish this advantage, we cannot see much prospect of them winning. The Bull's Head men are a staunch set of players and proved their merits on Saturday last. -- Practically speaking, there was only Bull's Head in it, for only three of the Fearnhead men won their games, five of the others failing to record more than nine points. One of the greatest surprises on Satur- day was the defeat of E. Eyes (Bull's Head) by H. Rateliffe,who settled the matter at the 29th end, winning by 21-12. In the earlier stages Eyes had the better of the situation, leading 10-18 at the 17th end. Once hold of the jack there was no holding Ratcliffe, who simply romped home. -- Thomas Davies (Fearnhead) put up a pluckly fight against T. Rigby, who played exceedingly well, lead- ing 10-6 and 14-S, at the 10th and 15th ends respec- tively. A run of three singles and a double by Davies and the scores were equal at the 22nd end, In four more ends the players peeled again with 17. and at ihe 2Sth end 18-18 was the state of the game Rigby ended the game by landing a beautiful double and a well-judged single in the next two lengths. Handles was in rare form to dispose of Jos. Weston by 21-2 in 18 ends. The Bull', Head man carried all before him and had two in on five occasions. --- John Weston (Fearnhead) did very little better, for he scored only three points against Jas. Isherwood, who won in 18 end.. Indeed, the Fearnhead men had

only the semblance of a look-in, but no doubt they will give the Church-street men a warm time of it to-day. In the Consolation Competition second round the only match played was between Rylands and King and Queen, the former team having to wipe cif a lead of live points to-day. H. Langley experierced hard lines in losing to J. Hingham (K. and Q.) by 16-21, for after having pulled up remarkably well from being in arrears 5-10 and 8-15, he was only two points behind the winner at the 27th end, when the scone was 10-18. The wire- worker, however, failed to add another point, and he lost by five points. -- A tight game Was played between G. Vernon (K.' and Q. and W. Roughley, the former fully deserving his four point win. The scores .Jere even at 4, 10 and 11, and only five doubles were landed. Rougbley made a plucky attempt to pull up, but Vernon knew the land well and lima his knowledge to decided advantage. The general expec'ation was that W. Langley would just about pull it cif with J. W. Brown, for he had the advantage practically all the way up to the 23rd length, when the score was 10 each. Langley gained a double to Brown a single, but the latter was not to shaken off and he stuck to his man with great tenacity, to land two singles and win by a trio of points. -- A similar game was played between F. Boscow and A. France (Rylands), the latter winning by 21-IS, after Boscow had lea. 17-14 at the 25th end. France, however, gained three beautiful singles, to win by the odd three chalks in 32 ends, amidst the applause of his fellow members of the team. We have every confidence that Rylands will give their oeponents a dose of real defeat to-day, for the King and Queen men's advantage is no slight that one of the wireworkers could easily wipe it off in a single game. -- RYLA.NDS' No. 2 PROVE TOUGH CUSTOMERS. ' The six matches played in the " Finlayson " Cup Competition of the Werrington Works Association, were a itnessed by a fair number of spectators on the Horse and Jockey Green, and one was surprised to see that Bewsey Ropery (No. 1), Armitage and Rigby, and Rylands (No. 2) were defeated in their matches. The first match between the Carpenters and Joiners and Ropery No. 1 was exceedingly well fought. The Joiners had an advantage of eight on the total handicap, and: considering that they only won by nine, the Ropery men have nothing to be ashamed of. They proved that on level terms they would no doubt have trounced the joiners. But credit was due to the joiners, for they played exceedingly well, and we do not think anyone was really dissatisfied with the result. S. Goslin (Joiners) (5; looked an easy winner, when in the first five ends with B. Perry (2) he led 10-2. Perry soon put a different aspect on the game which concluded at the 12th end, Goslin not having had a look in from the fifth end. -- A highly interesting game was played between J. Wilkinson (4) (Ropery) and D. Milling (4). At the fifth eud the Ropery man led 10-4, and at the 11th end he only needed one point to his opponent six. Milling got the jack and astonished the spectators by running out with three doubles and a single. An equally tight game was played between J. Brooks (4) (Ropery) and J. Hands (2), the joiner, after being in arrears 4-11, playing up remarkably well to finish at the 20th end a point behind. -- Howley Tannery, whose total handicap was one of 40 points heat the Longford No 1. men, handicapped at 40, by 10 points. F. Clare, the Howley skipper, drew first blood for his side by defeating H. Br omiey 15-14 after a very exciting game. The score was 13 each at the 13th end and to the finish it was touch and go. W. Robinson (4) (Howley) had all his work cut ost to dispose of C. Holt by 15-14 in 17 ends, and the Longford man is worthy of congratulation for the ' manner in which he hung on to his opponent. With a 16 point lead on the total handicap, Naylor's would indeed have been a poor side if they had not beaten the men from Armitage and Rigby's. They only just managed it by four points, and general surprise was voiced at the downfall of the A. and R. contingent. Despite the great handicaps they had to wipe away they recorded some capital wins, each maa distinguishing himself in a creditable manner. The chief complaint of Cockhedge was the handicap they had to face, but they took their defeat like men. The Corporation Gas Works men had not a ghost of a chance with the Fletcher's Moulders' representatives, for they only recorded two wins. The Moulders played hard to win by 51 points, and one of the best games in the match was between T. Evans (2) (Gas Works) and Regan (2). They kept even nearly all the way, but after flying led 13-8 at the 14th end, Evans fell away and after the 19th length, the game was 14 each. Regan got one in on the next end to win. The match between Orford Beam Shed and P. and K. Wheel Shop was a very good one, and, although having to c ,neede their opponents 9 points on the , handicap, the Wheel Shop men finally won by 25 Ipoints. --- Rylands' No. 2 were handicapped 19 points behind their opponents, Crosfield's Shipping, and on the first four games they looked like winning, but the tail end of the match went in favour of the Shipping men who finally triumphed by a trio of points. Some good games were witnessed and one would have liked to see the wireworker win, for they have played well in this competition. ST. AUSTIN'S F WIN BY ONE. The games in the " Peter Peacock " Challenge Cup Competition were highly interesting, and the closest win of the day was that of St. Austin's F who accounted for Whitecross .1 by 94-93, although they had to con- cede 10 points on the total handicap. The games were very exciting and the St. Austin's men were exceedingly proud of their achievement. --- Town Hall A are opponents to be considered. They beat the Latchford men by 51 points on Saturday, so future contestants beware ! -- St. John's D were four men short when they met Howley E, who, although, they only really won one game, gaineta 47 point victory. The other matches were- full of interesting incidents, St. Austin's A playing well to win by 21 points over St. Austin's E. Orford D disposed of the Fairfield C men by 34 points, their men being in rare form and playing their wocda well. Town Hall D did well to beat St. Austin's B by 24 points, and St. Austin's D were by far the better team against Latchford C, over whom they triumphed by 34 points. There is a full programme for to-day, and our only hope is that the weather clerk will be in a generous and considerate mood.
